passages.title: Local book verses

passages.context: Love and hate are simply different degrees of the same emotion. Heat and cold are both forms of temperature.
passages.title: Local book verses

passages.context: Understanding duality helps you transform your mental states by recognizing their spectrum.
passages.title: Local book verses

passages.title: Tao Te Ching

passages.context: When people see some things as beautiful, other things become ugly...
passages.title: Tao Te Ching

passages.context: Addition combines quantities. a + b is the sum. This is definitional arithmetic, not a computer-algebra system.
passages.title: topics

passages.context: Subtraction removes one quantity from another. a - b is the difference.
passages.title: topics

passages.context: Multiplication is repeated addition. a * b is the product.
passages.title: topics

passages.context: Division splits a quantity into equal parts. Division by zero is undefined.
passages.title: topics

passages.context: An exponent repeats multiplication. a^2 is a squared. a^0 is 1 for nonzero a.
passages.title: topics

passages.context: A variable is a symbol that stands for an unknown or changing number, often written as x or y.
passages.title: topics

passages.context: An equation says two expressions are equal. Solving it means finding values that make both sides the same.
passages.title: topics

passages.context: A triangle is a polygon with three sides. In a flat triangle the interior angles add up to 180 degrees.
passages.title: topics

passages.context: A circle is the set of points at a fixed radius from a center. Circumference is pi times the diameter. Area is pi times radius squared.
passages.title: topics

passages.context: In a right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides.
passages.title: topics

passages.context: A derivative is the instantaneous rate of change of a function. It is the slope of the tangent line.
passages.title: topics

passages.context: An integral accumulates a quantity. A definite integral is the signed area between a curve and the axis over an interval.
passages.title: topics

passages.context: A limit is the value a function approaches as its input approaches some point. Calculus builds on limits.
passages.title: topics

passages.context: Poison hemlock is a deadly poisonous plant in the carrot family, often mistaken for wild carrot, parsley, or parsnip. Also called Conium maculatum, poison parsley, tall white umbrella flower, hemlock plant. Look for smooth, hairless, hollow stalk with purple blotches; fern-like, finely divided leaves that smell musty when crushed.
passages.title: Poison hemlock

passages.context: Wild carrot is a common white umbrella wildflower with hairy stems and a carrot-smelling root, and it is easy to confuse with deadly hemlocks. Also called Daucus carota, Queen Anne's lace, bird's nest flower, wild carrot. Look for hairy, solid stems; carrot smell from a crushed root or leaf. Use it only as an identification lesson. A beginner should not eat any carrot-family plant from the wild.
passages.title: Wild carrot (Queen Anne's lace)

passages.context: Water hemlock is one of the most poisonous plants in North America; a small amount of the root can cause fatal seizures. Also called Cicuta maculata, spotted water hemlock, cowbane, deadly umbrella plant in wet ground. Look for grows in wet ground: stream banks, ditches, marshes; smooth hollow stems streaked or spotted with purple. Use only as a warning. Stay out of wet-ground carrot-family plants.
passages.title: Water hemlock

passages.context: Poison ivy is a common plant of New England with three-leaflet leaves and an oil, urushiol, that causes an itchy, blistering rash on contact. Also called leaves of three, Toxicodendron radicans, hairy rope vine, itchy vine, three leaf plant. Look for three leaflets, with the middle leaflet on a longer stalk; grows as a vine with hairy aerial roots, a shrub, or ground cover.
passages.title: Poison ivy

passages.context: Poison sumac is a swamp shrub with 7 to 13 smooth-edged leaflets and white berries; it causes the same rash as poison ivy. Also called Toxicodendron vernix, poison oak, swamp sumac, white berries sumac. Look for leaves of 7 to 13 smooth leaflets on a red stem; grows in wet swamps and bogs. Stay out of swamp shrubs you cannot name, and wash after contact like poison ivy.
passages.title: Poison sumac and poison oak

passages.context: A photo, an app, or a camera match can never confirm a wild mushroom is safe; deadly species resemble edible ones, and cooking does not remove most toxins. Also called can I eat this mushroom, is this mushroom edible, mushroom identification app, identify a mushroom. Look for many deadly species look like edible ones; key features like spore print, base, and habitat do not show in a photo.
passages.title: Never eat a wild mushroom from a photo

passages.context: The Jack-o'-lantern is an orange, poisonous mushroom that grows in clusters on wood and causes severe vomiting and cramps; it is often mistaken for a chanterelle. Also called Omphalotus illudens, orange poisonous mushroom, false chanterelle, orange mushroom on a stump. Look for orange, funnel-shaped caps growing in clusters from wood or buried roots; true, thin, sharp-edged gills running down the stem.
passages.title: Jack-o'-lantern mushroom (not a chanterelle)

passages.context: True chanterelles are golden, funnel-shaped mushrooms with blunt, forked ridges instead of thin gills, but only an expert should confirm them. Also called Cantharellus, golden chanterelle, false chanterelle, chanterelles in New England. Look for blunt, forked ridges that run down the stem and look like folds; grows from soil near trees, usually singly or scattered. Learn them in person with a local expert or society, never from a photo.
passages.title: Chanterelle and its look-alikes

passages.context: Destroying angels and death caps are deadly mushrooms; a small bite can destroy the liver, and symptoms may be delayed for hours. Also called Amanita bisporigera, Amanita phalloides, death cap, destroying angel, white mushroom in the woods. Look for white or greenish cap with white gills; a skirt-like ring on the stem and a cup or sac (volva) at the base, which may be buried.
passages.title: Destroying angel and death cap (deadly amanitas)

passages.context: If someone may have eaten a poisonous plant or mushroom, call Poison Control or 911 immediately, before symptoms appear. Also called ate a wild plant, child ate a berry, ate a mushroom and sick, pet ate a mushroom. Look for any wild plant or mushroom swallowed by a child or pet; vomiting, belly pain, drooling, confusion, or seizures.
passages.title: Someone may have eaten a poisonous plant or mushroom

passages.context: A wild plant is only safe to eat when a person has positively identified it by several features and ruled out its poisonous look-alikes; if you are unsure, the answer is no. Also called can I eat this plant, is this berry safe, wild plant edible, hungry and found a plant. Look for more than one feature checked: leaf, flower, fruit, stem, habitat; look-alikes ruled out.
passages.title: Is this plant safe to eat?

passages.context: Rules of thumb such as 'animals eat it', 'boiling makes it safe', or 'avoid red plants' are false and have killed people. Also called universal edibility test, animals eat it so it is safe, red berries rule, boiling removes poison, taste test. Look for animals can eat plants that poison people; boiling does not destroy many toxins.
passages.title: False rules about wild food

passages.context: Several New England berries are poisonous, including baneberry, pokeweed, bittersweet nightshade, yew, and Virginia creeper. Also called baneberry, doll's eyes, pokeweed berries, nightshade, yew berries. Look for baneberry: white or red berries with a dark dot on stalks; pokeweed: dark purple berries on pink stems. Teach children not to eat any wild berry, and keep these plants out of reach. Leave unknown berries alone.
passages.title: Toxic berries and fruits in New England

passages.context: Wild blueberries, blackberries, and raspberries are common New England fruits with few dangerous look-alikes, but always confirm them in person. Also called wild blueberries, blackberries, raspberry canes, wild berries Maine. Look for blueberry: small blue berry with a five-pointed crown on the end; blackberry and raspberry: clusters of tiny drupelets on thorny canes; raspberries pull off hollow.
passages.title: Blueberries, blackberries, and raspberries

passages.context: True morels have a honeycomb cap attached to a hollow stem, while false morels have a wrinkled, brain-like cap and cottony or chambered inside and can be toxic. Also called Morchella, false morel, Gyromitra, brain mushroom, morel hunting. Look for true morel: pitted honeycomb cap, hollow from tip to base when cut lengthwise; false morel: wrinkled, lobed cap that hangs free, with cottony or chambered interior.
passages.title: True morel versus false morel

passages.context: Fiddleheads are the coiled young fronds of the ostrich fern, a spring food in Maine; they must be identified correctly and cooked thoroughly or they can cause illness. Also called fiddlehead fern, ostrich fern, bracken fern, edible ferns. Look for a smooth stem with a deep U-shaped groove on the inside; brown papery scales on the coil.
passages.title: Fiddleheads (ostrich fern)

passages.context: Acorns are high in tannins that taste bitter and upset the stomach, so they must be shelled, ground, and leached in many changes of water before use. Also called eat acorns, acorn flour, tannins in acorns, white oak acorns. Look for bitter, astringent taste when raw; white oak acorns have less tannin. If you want to use acorns, follow a sourced method and expect hours of leaching. In a survival situation, they are not a first food.
passages.title: Acorns need proper leaching

passages.context: Hazelnuts, beechnuts, hickory nuts, black walnuts, and butternuts are native New England nuts, but they need positive identification and proper processing. Also called nuts you can eat, black walnut, butternut, beechnut, hickory. Look for each tree has distinct leaves, bark, and husk; black walnut and butternut have thick, stain-prone husks. Identify the tree in person, check for allergies, shell and eat only sound nuts.
passages.title: Wild nuts: hazelnut, beechnut, walnut, butternut

passages.context: Cattails are tall wetland plants with brown sausage-shaped spikes, but young shoots can be confused with poisonous wild iris. Also called Typha, bulrush, cattail shoots, wild iris lookalike. Look for brown cylindrical flower spike above long flat leaves; grows in standing water or marshes. Learn them with an expert; cattails absorb pollutants, so use only from clean water.
passages.title: Cattail and its look-alikes

passages.context: Dandelion and broadleaf plantain are common lawn and field weeds that can be eaten as greens when picked from clean, unsprayed places. Also called dandelion, edible weeds, plantain leaves. Look for dandelion: toothed rosette leaves and a single hollow stem with one yellow flower; plantain: oval ribbed leaves in a rosette with a spike of seeds. Pick young leaves from clean, unsprayed ground, wash them, and cook or eat as a small addition, not as free calories.
passages.title: Dandelion and plantain greens

passages.context: Plants can harm by contact (poison ivy, wild parsnip, giant hogweed), by eating (hemlocks, baneberry), or by smoke (burning poison ivy). Also called giant hogweed, wild parsnip burns, stinging nettle, poisonous plants overview. Look for wild parsnip and giant hogweed sap causes burns in sunlight; poison ivy oil causes a rash. Learn the plants of your area, wear long sleeves and gloves in brush, and wash exposed skin after contact. Keep children and pets from unknown plants.
passages.title: Plants that poison by contact, eating, or smoke

passages.context: Fly agaric is a red or orange Amanita mushroom with white warts that is poisonous and related to the deadly Amanitas. Also called Amanita muscaria, red mushroom with white spots, toadstool. Look for red or orange cap with white warts, white gills, a ring on the stem and a bulb at the base; warts are remnants of a veil and can wash off in rain. Learn it as a warning. Toxic. Related to the deadly Amanitas.
passages.title: Fly agaric

passages.context: Deadly galerina is a small brown mushroom on rotting wood that contains the same liver toxins as the death cap. Also called Galerina marginata, funeral bell, autumn skullcap. Look for small brown mushroom on rotting wood with a thin ring and rusty brown spores; cap 1 to 4 cm, sticky when wet. Learn it as a warning. Deadly. Grows on the same logs as honey mushrooms.
passages.title: Deadly galerina

passages.context: Webcaps are brown Cortinarius mushrooms with a cobweb veil, and some damage the kidneys days after eating. Also called Cortinarius, cortinarius, webcap. Look for rusty-brown spores, a web-like veil on young caps, often on the ground in woods; rusty-brown spore print. Learn it as a warning. Some are deadly to the kidneys. Never eat a brown mushroom you cannot identify.
passages.title: Webcaps (Cortinarius)

passages.context: Chicken of the woods is a bright orange and yellow shelf fungus on trees with pores, not gills. Also called Laetiporus, sulphur shelf, chicken mushroom, Laetiporus sulphureus. Look for bright orange and yellow shelves with no gills on trees, soft when young; no gills; tiny pores underneath. Use it as an identification and look-alike lesson; only an expert who sees it in person can confirm it. Some people react badly, and growths on conifers or eucalyptus can be harmful.
passages.title: Chicken of the woods

passages.context: Hen of the woods is a large gray-brown clustered mushroom at the base of oaks, with pores instead of gills. Also called maitake, Grifola frondosa, sheep's head. Look for big clump of grey-brown overlapping fronds at the base of oaks; pores instead of gills. Use it as an identification and look-alike lesson; only an expert who sees it in person can confirm it.
passages.title: Hen of the woods (maitake)

passages.context: A giant puffball is a round white mushroom with no stem or gills that is solid white inside when young. Also called puffball, Calvatia, puffballs, Calvatia gigantea. Look for round white ball with no stem or gills; solid white inside when cut. Use it as an identification and look-alike lesson; only an expert who sees it in person can confirm it. A young Amanita looks like a puffball. Cut it open: any outline of a cap and stem means leave it.
passages.title: Puffball

passages.context: Lion's mane is a white mushroom of hanging icicle-like spines that grows on hardwood trees. Also called Hericium, bearded tooth, pom pom mushroom. Look for white hanging icicle-like spines on trees; no cap and no gills. Use it as an identification and look-alike lesson; only an expert who sees it in person can confirm it.
passages.title: Lion's mane

passages.context: The oyster mushroom is a gray-tan shelf mushroom on wood with gills running down to a short side stem. Also called Pleurotus, oyster mushrooms, tree oyster, Pleurotus ostreatus. Look for shelf-shaped grey-tan caps with gills running down to a short side stem, on wood; white to lilac spore print. Use it as an identification and look-alike lesson; only an expert who sees it in person can confirm it. Do not confuse it with other shelf fungi that have gills.
passages.title: Oyster mushroom

passages.context: Turkey tail is a thin, tough shelf fungus on dead wood with colored bands and white pores underneath. Also called Trametes versicolor, turkey tails. Look for thin tough shelves with colored concentric bands and a white pore underside; tough and leathery, not fleshy. Use it as an identification lesson. Yehsa does not give doses or remedies with wild fungi.
passages.title: Turkey tail

passages.context: Birch polypore is a rounded gray-white shelf fungus on dead birch, used historically as a razor strop and tinder. Also called razor strop, Fomitopsis betulina, birch bracket. Look for rounded grey-white shelf on dead birch; the pore side is white. Use it as an identification lesson. Yehsa does not give doses or remedies with wild fungi. Survival history only. Do not eat it.
passages.title: Birch polypore (razor strop)

passages.context: Reishi, or hemlock varnish shelf, is a glossy red-brown shelf fungus on hemlock and other conifers. Also called hemlock varnish shelf, Ganoderma, lingzhi, Ganoderma tsugae. Look for glossy varnished red-brown shelf on a stalk or the side of a tree; shiny, varnished-looking top. Use it as an identification lesson. Yehsa does not give doses or remedies with wild fungi.
passages.title: Reishi (hemlock varnish shelf)

passages.context: Honey mushrooms are clusters of honey-colored capped mushrooms with a ring that grow on wood and roots. Also called Armillaria, honey fungus, bootlace fungus. Look for clusters of honey-coloured caps on wood with a ring; white spores. Use it as an identification and look-alike lesson; only an expert who sees it in person can confirm it. The deadly galerina looks like it.
passages.title: Honey mushroom

passages.context: Shaggy mane is a tall white shaggy-capped mushroom that melts into black ink as it ages. Also called Coprinus comatus, lawyer's wig, inky cap. Look for tall white cylinder cap with shaggy scales that melts into ink; gills turn black and dissolve from the bottom up. Use it as an identification and look-alike lesson; only an expert who sees it in person can confirm it.
passages.title: Shaggy mane

passages.context: A bolete is a fleshy mushroom with a sponge of pores instead of gills under the cap. Also called Boletus, boletes, porcini, king bolete. Look for fat stem with a sponge of pores instead of gills under the cap; pores instead of gills under the cap. Use it as an identification and look-alike lesson; only an expert who sees it in person can confirm it. Red-pored and bitter ones are toxic. Do not eat on a photo.
passages.title: Bolete

passages.context: The green-spored parasol is a large lawn mushroom whose gills turn green with age, and it causes the most mushroom poisonings in North America. Also called Chlorophyllum molybdites, false parasol, green-spored lepiota, vomiter. Look for big scaly cap with a ring; gills turn green with age. Learn it as a warning. The most common mushroom poisoning in North America.
passages.title: Green-spored parasol

passages.context: The hedgehog mushroom is a pale orange mushroom with soft spines under the cap instead of gills. Also called Hydnum repandum, sweet tooth, hedgehog. Look for pale orange cap with soft spines instead of gills; small spines under the cap instead of gills. Use it as an identification and look-alike lesson; only an expert who sees it in person can confirm it.
passages.title: Hedgehog mushroom

passages.context: Tinder fungus is a hoof-shaped gray woody shelf on birch and beech whose inner layer was used to carry fire. Also called horse hoof fungus, Fomes fomentarius, amadou, hoof fungus. Look for hoof-shaped grey woody shelf on birch and beech; used for tinder. Use it as an identification lesson. Yehsa does not give doses or remedies with wild fungi. Survival use for fire only.
passages.title: Tinder fungus

passages.context: Chaga is a black, cracked, charcoal-like growth on birch that is orange-brown inside. Also called Inonotus obliquus, clinker fungus, birch conk. Look for black charcoal-like crust on birch with an orange inside; cracked black outer crust. Use it as an identification lesson. Yehsa does not give doses or remedies with wild fungi.
passages.title: Chaga

passages.context: Ramps are wild leeks with two or three broad smooth leaves in spring and a strong onion-garlic smell. Also called wild leek, Allium tricoccum, ramp. Look for two or three broad smooth leaves per plant in spring, red-purple stalk base, strong onion and garlic smell; every leaf smells of onion when crushed.
passages.title: Ramps (wild leek)

passages.context: False hellebore is a wetland plant with large pleated leaves spiraling up the stem, and it is deadly. Also called Indian poke, Veratrum, green hellebore, corn lily, Veratrum viride. Look for big pleated leaves that wrap the stem in a spiral; wet woods and meadows. Learn it so you can avoid it and warn others. Sometimes mistaken for ramps. Deadly.
passages.title: False hellebore (Indian poke)

passages.context: Lily of the valley is a garden and wild plant with small white bell flowers, and every part is deadly to the heart. Also called lily of the valley, Convallaria, May bells, Convallaria majalis. Look for two smooth upright leaves, small white bells on an arching stem, red berries; no onion smell, unlike ramps. Learn it so you can avoid it and warn others. Mistaken for ramps. Every part is deadly.
passages.title: Lily of the valley

passages.context: Chicory is a roadside plant with sky-blue flowers on stiff stems whose leaves and roasted roots are used as food. Also called blue sailors, Cichorium, coffee weed, succory, Cichorium intybus. Look for sky blue flowers on stiff, nearly leafless stems along roadsides; milky sap.
passages.title: Chicory

passages.context: Red clover is a common field plant with round pink-purple flower heads and three leaflets marked with a pale V. Also called Trifolium pratense, clover. Look for pink-purple round flower heads; three leaflets with a pale V mark. Learn it as an identification first. Eat it only after you have matched every feature in person, ideally with someone who knows the plant, from ground that was not sprayed or beside a busy road, and start with a small amount.
passages.title: Red clover

passages.context: White clover is a low creeping lawn plant with round white flower heads and three leaflets. Also called Trifolium repens, Dutch clover, lawn clover. Look for low creeping plant, white round flower heads, three leaflets often with a pale band; stems creep and root along the ground.
passages.title: White clover

passages.context: Burdock is a large weed with huge heart-shaped leaves and hooked burrs that stick to clothing; its first-year root is eaten cooked. Also called Arctium, gobo, great burdock, beggar's buttons. Look for very large heart-shaped leaves, hooked burr heads, purple thistle-like flowers; leaves pale and woolly underneath.
passages.title: Burdock

passages.context: Foxglove is a garden and wild plant with a tall spike of tubular pink-purple flowers, and every part is deadly to the heart. Also called Digitalis, fairy gloves, purple foxglove, Digitalis purpurea. Look for fuzzy leaves in a rosette, tall spike of tubular pink-purple bells; spotted throat inside each bell. Learn it so you can avoid it and warn others. Deadly to the heart. Often confused with comfrey in the first year.
passages.title: Foxglove

passages.context: Comfrey is a hairy-leaved garden plant with curled clusters of bell flowers that contains liver-damaging compounds. Also called Symphytum, knitbone, boneset, Symphytum officinale. Look for rough hairy leaves, bell flowers in curled clusters; leaves run down onto the stem as wings. Learn it so you can avoid it and warn others. Contains liver-damaging compounds. Do not eat or brew it.
passages.title: Comfrey

passages.context: Wild iris, or blue flag, is a wetland plant with flat sword-shaped leaves in a fan, and it is poisonous. Also called blue flag, yellow flag, flag iris, Iris versicolor. Look for flat sword-shaped leaves in a fan; blue-violet or yellow flowers. Learn it so you can avoid it and warn others. Toxic if eaten. Often mistaken for cattail shoots.
passages.title: Wild iris (blue flag, yellow flag)

passages.context: Wild strawberry is a low native plant whose tiny red berries carry their seeds on the outside and taste like small garden strawberries. Also called Fragaria, woodland strawberry, wild strawberries, Fragaria virginiana. Look for three toothed leaflets, white five-petal flowers, tiny red berries with seeds on the outside; runners that root along the ground.
passages.title: Wild strawberry

passages.context: Brambles are the prickly canes of blackberries and raspberries, whose berries are built from many small beads. Also called blackberry, raspberry, Rubus, blackcap, dewberry. Look for arching prickly canes, toothed compound leaves, clustered berries made of tiny beads; raspberries pull off hollow like a cap; blackberries keep a white core.
passages.title: Blackberry and raspberry (Rubus)

passages.context: Lowbush blueberry is a small shrub of sunny barrens and woods whose blue berries end in a five-point crown. Also called lowbush blueberry, wild blueberry, huckleberry, Vaccinium angustifolium. Look for low shrub, small oval leaves, blue berries with a five-point crown at the tip; many tiny seeds inside, not one stone.
passages.title: Blueberry

passages.context: Cranberry is a trailing evergreen vine of bogs whose sour red berries ripen in fall. Also called wild cranberry, bog cranberry, Vaccinium macrocarpon. Look for trailing evergreen vine in bogs, tiny leaves, red berries; berries bounce and have air pockets inside.
passages.title: Cranberry

passages.context: Elderberry is a shrub with flat clusters of tiny white flowers and dark purple berries that are only safe to eat cooked and ripe. Also called elder, Sambucus, black elderberry, elderflower, Sambucus canadensis. Look for opposite compound leaves, flat clusters of white flowers, dark purple (or red) berries, pithy stems; stems have soft white pith inside.
passages.title: Elderberry

passages.context: Pokeweed is a tall plant with purple-red stems and drooping clusters of dark berries, and its berries, roots, and mature leaves are poisonous. Also called poke, pokeberry, poke salad, inkberry, Phytolacca. Look for purple-red stems, large leaves, drooping clusters of dark purple berries; can grow taller than a person in one season. Learn it so you can avoid it and warn others. Berries, roots and mature leaves are toxic.
passages.title: Pokeweed

passages.context: Staghorn sumac is a shrub with velvety twigs and upright cones of red fuzzy berries; it is not poison sumac. Also called red sumac, sumac berries, sumac lemonade, Rhus typhina. Look for fuzzy velvet twigs, long compound leaves, upright red fuzzy berry cones; berries are red and point up, never white and drooping.
passages.title: Staghorn sumac

passages.context: Virginia creeper is a climbing vine with five leaflets spread like a hand, often confused with poison ivy, and its berries are poisonous. Also called five-leaved ivy, woodbine, Parthenocissus, Parthenocissus quinquefolia. Look for five leaflets spread like a hand; climbing vine with tendrils. Learn it so you can avoid it and warn others. Berries are toxic. Sometimes mistaken for poison ivy.
passages.title: Virginia creeper

passages.context: Stinging nettle is a plant covered in fine stinging hairs that burn the skin on contact; cooking or drying removes the sting. Also called nettle, nettles, Urtica, Urtica dioica. Look for opposite toothed leaves with stinging hairs, square stem, small green flower strings; a burning, tingling rash right after you brush it.
passages.title: Stinging nettle

passages.context: Lambsquarters is a common garden weed whose diamond-shaped leaves have a white mealy coating underneath. Also called goosefoot, pigweed, wild spinach, Chenopodium, Chenopodium album. Look for diamond-shaped leaves with a white mealy powder underneath; water beads on the leaves.
passages.title: Lambsquarters

passages.context: Wood sorrel is a small plant with heart-shaped leaflets in threes and a sour, lemony taste from oxalic acid. Also called sour grass, Oxalis, yellow wood sorrel, sheep sorrel, Oxalis stricta. Look for heart-shaped leaflets in threes like a clover, small yellow or pink five-petal flowers; sour taste.
passages.title: Wood sorrel

passages.context: Jewelweed is a soft wet-ground plant with orange spotted trumpet flowers and seed pods that burst when touched. Also called spotted touch-me-not, touch-me-not, Impatiens capensis. Look for orange or yellow spotted trumpet flowers, pale watery stems, leaves bead up water; seed pods burst when touched.
passages.title: Jewelweed

passages.context: Bracken is a large common fern with triangular fronds; it is toxic and not a safe fiddlehead. Also called bracken fern, brake fern, Pteridium, Pteridium aquilinum. Look for large triangular fronds on a single stalk, fuzzy coiled shoots, open ground; young shoots are fuzzy, not smooth and grooved. Learn it so you can avoid it and warn others. Toxic and linked to cancer. Do not eat.
passages.title: Bracken fern

passages.context: Common milkweed is a tall plant with milky sap, broad paired leaves, and warty pods, and it is toxic raw. Also called milkweed, Asclepias syriaca, monarch plant. Look for thick stem with milky white sap, big opposite oval leaves, pink ball flower clusters, warty pods; pods full of silky seeds in fall. Learn it so you can avoid it and warn others. Toxic raw. Only a trained forager should use it, and not by photo.
passages.title: Common milkweed

passages.context: Dogbane is a milky-sapped plant with red-tinged stems and slim paired pods that is poisonous to the heart and looks like milkweed. Also called Indian hemp, hemp dogbane, Apocynum, Apocynum cannabinum. Look for red-tinged stems with milky sap, pointed opposite leaves, tiny white bells, slim paired pods; branches near the top, unlike young milkweed. Learn it so you can avoid it and warn others. Toxic to the heart. Looks like milkweed.
passages.title: Dogbane

passages.context: Mullein is a tall roadside plant with large, soft, gray, fuzzy leaves and a yellow flower spike in its second year. Also called common mullein, flannel leaf, cowboy toilet paper, Verbascum, Verbascum thapsus. Look for large grey fuzzy leaves in a rosette and a tall yellow flower spike in the second year; dry stalks stand through winter.
passages.title: Mullein

passages.context: St. John's wort is a yellow-flowered plant whose leaves show tiny see-through dots when held to the light. Also called Hypericum, St Johns wort, goatweed, Hypericum perforatum. Look for opposite small leaves with see-through dots when held to light; yellow five-petal flowers that stain purple.
passages.title: St. John's wort

passages.context: Self-heal is a low lawn and trail plant with a square stem and a spiky purple flower head. Also called heal-all, Prunella, selfheal, Prunella vulgaris. Look for low plant, square stem, spiky purple flower head with ruffled lips; opposite leaves on a square stem. Older manuals and folk use mention it, but Yehsa does not give doses or treatments with wild plants. Use it as an identification lesson, and use tested first-aid supplies for care.
passages.title: Self-heal

passages.context: Goldenrod is a tall late-summer plant with plumes of small yellow flowers; it is often blamed for hay fever caused by ragweed. Also called Solidago, goldenrods. Look for tall plume of tiny yellow flowers in late summer, alternate narrow leaves; stands in old fields and roadsides by the thousands. Older manuals and folk use mention it, but Yehsa does not give doses or treatments with wild plants. Use it as an identification lesson, and use tested first-aid supplies for care.
passages.title: Goldenrod

passages.context: White snakeroot is a woodland plant with fuzzy white fall flowers that poisons livestock and can pass into their milk. Also called snakeroot, Ageratina, milk sickness plant, Ageratina altissima. Look for opposite toothed leaves on a branching stem, fuzzy white flower clusters in autumn; grows in shade at woods edges. Learn it so you can avoid it and warn others. Poisons livestock and milk. Do not eat.
passages.title: White snakeroot

passages.context: Jerusalem artichoke is a tall wild sunflower whose knobby underground tubers are edible. Also called sunchoke, sunroot, Helianthus tuberosus. Look for tall rough sunflower-like plant with small yellow flowers and knobby tubers; leaves rough like sandpaper.
passages.title: Jerusalem artichoke

passages.context: Evening primrose is a tall plant with four-petal yellow flowers that open at dusk. Also called Oenothera, common evening primrose, Oenothera biennis. Look for tall plant with four-petal yellow flowers that open at dusk, reddish stem; first-year rosette with a pink-tinged midrib.
passages.title: Evening primrose

passages.context: Pineapple weed is a low weed of packed paths whose petal-less yellow-green flower cones smell like pineapple when crushed. Also called wild chamomile, disc mayweed, Matricaria discoidea. Look for low plant with feathery leaves, yellow-green cone flowers with no petals; smells like pineapple when crushed.
passages.title: Pineapple weed

passages.context: Wild bergamot is a mint-family wildflower with lavender shaggy flower heads and an oregano-like smell. Also called bee balm, Monarda, horsemint, Monarda fistulosa. Look for square stem, lavender shaggy flower heads, minty oregano smell; square stem and paired leaves like other mints. Older manuals and folk use mention it, but Yehsa does not give doses or treatments with wild plants. Use it as an identification lesson, and use tested first-aid supplies for care.
passages.title: Wild bergamot

passages.context: Mayapple is a spring woodland plant with umbrella-like leaves, and every part except the fully ripe fruit is poisonous. Also called American mandrake, Podophyllum, umbrella plant, Podophyllum peltatum. Look for umbrella-like lobed leaves, a single white flower under the leaves, one green-yellow fruit; grows in large colonies on the forest floor. Learn it so you can avoid it and warn others. Everything except the ripe fruit is toxic.
passages.title: Mayapple

passages.context: Bloodroot is an early-spring wildflower with one lobed leaf and a white flower whose root bleeds red-orange sap, and it is poisonous. Also called Sanguinaria, red puccoon, Sanguinaria canadensis. Look for one clasped rounded lobed leaf and a white eight-petal flower in early spring; red-orange sap. Learn it so you can avoid it and warn others. Toxic.
passages.title: Bloodroot

passages.context: Baneberry, or doll's eyes, is a woodland plant whose white or red berries on thick red stalks are deadly. Also called doll's eyes, white baneberry, red baneberry, Actaea, Actaea pachypoda. Look for compound toothed leaves, a white or red berry cluster on thick red stalks (doll's eyes); each white berry has a black dot like an eye. Learn it so you can avoid it and warn others. Berries are deadly.
passages.title: Baneberry

passages.context: Jimsonweed is a rank-smelling weed with large white trumpet flowers and spiny seed pods, and every part is deadly. Also called Datura, thorn apple, devil's trumpet, locoweed, Datura stramonium. Look for large white trumpet flowers, spiny egg-shaped seed pods, strong smell; grows in disturbed ground and barnyards. Learn it so you can avoid it and warn others. Every part is deadly.
passages.title: Jimsonweed

passages.context: Bittersweet nightshade is a climbing vine with small purple star flowers and red egg-shaped berries that are poisonous. Also called climbing nightshade, woody nightshade, Solanum dulcamara. Look for climbing vine, purple flowers with a yellow cone, red egg-shaped berries; green berries turn orange, then red. Learn it so you can avoid it and warn others. Berries are toxic.
passages.title: Bittersweet nightshade

passages.context: Monkshood is a garden and wild plant with hooded blue-purple flowers, and every part is deadly, even through the skin. Also called Aconitum, wolfsbane, aconite. Look for deeply cut leaves and tall spikes of hooded blue-purple flowers; top petal shaped like a monk's hood. Learn it so you can avoid it and warn others. Deadly. Even skin contact can numb or harm.
passages.title: Monkshood

passages.context: Giant hogweed is a huge carrot-family plant whose sap, with sunlight, causes severe burns and blisters on skin. Also called hogweed, Heracleum mantegazzianum. Look for huge: stem 5-10 cm wide with purple blotches and stiff hairs, umbrella flower head up to 1 m; can be taller than a person, with a flower umbrella over a meter across. Learn it so you can avoid it and warn others. Sap plus sunlight causes severe burns. Do not touch.
passages.title: Giant hogweed

passages.context: Cow parsnip is a large native carrot-family plant with maple-like leaves whose sap can burn sunlit skin. Also called Heracleum maximum, Indian celery. Look for big maple-like leaves, white flat umbrella, hairy hollow stem; smaller than giant hogweed, with a greener, less blotched stem. Learn it so you can avoid it and warn others. Sap can cause burns on sunny skin.
passages.title: Cow parsnip

passages.context: Wild parsnip is a yellow-flowered carrot-family roadside plant whose sap, with sunlight, causes burns and blisters. Also called Pastinaca, poison parsnip, Pastinaca sativa. Look for yellow umbrella flowers, grooved hollow stem, toothed leaflets; flat yellow umbrella flowers in midsummer. Learn it so you can avoid it and warn others. Sap plus sunlight causes burns and blisters.
passages.title: Wild parsnip

passages.context: Skunk cabbage is a wetland plant with a mottled hooded flower in late winter and big leaves that smell skunky when torn; it is toxic raw. Also called Symplocarpus, swamp cabbage, eastern skunk cabbage, Symplocarpus foetidus. Look for wet ground; mottled purple-maroon hooded flower in late winter. Learn it so you can avoid it and warn others. Toxic raw.
passages.title: Skunk cabbage

passages.context: Japanese knotweed is an invasive plant with hollow, bamboo-like jointed canes that forms dense stands. Also called knotweed, Fallopia japonica, Mexican bamboo, Reynoutria, Reynoutria japonica. Look for hollow bamboo-like reddish canes, heart-shaped leaves, dense stands; zigzag stems with a leaf at each joint.
passages.title: Japanese knotweed

passages.context: Curly dock is a common weed with long, wavy-edged leaves and a tall rust-red seed stalk. Also called yellow dock, sour dock, Rumex crispus, dock. Look for long leaves with wavy ruffled edges, tall rust-red seed stalk; papery sheath where each leaf meets the stem.
passages.title: Curly dock

passages.context: Wintergreen is a low evergreen ground plant whose glossy leaves smell of wintergreen when crushed and whose berries are red. Also called teaberry, checkerberry, Gaultheria, Gaultheria procumbens. Look for low evergreen with glossy leaves that smell of wintergreen when crushed; red berries.
passages.title: Wintergreen

passages.context: Wild rose is a prickly shrub with five-petal pink flowers that leave red rose hips in fall. Also called rose hips, pasture rose, Rosa, multiflora rose, Rosa carolina. Look for prickly canes, five-petal pink flowers, red rose hips; hips stay on the canes into winter.
passages.title: Wild rose

passages.context: Hawthorn is a thorny small tree with lobed leaves and small red apple-like fruits called haws. Also called Crataegus, thornapple, haws, whitethorn. Look for thorny small tree or shrub with lobed leaves and red apple-like haws; long straight thorns on the twigs.
passages.title: Hawthorn

passages.context: Mountain laurel is an evergreen shrub with clusters of pink-white cup flowers, and its leaves, flowers, and honey are poisonous. Also called Kalmia, calico bush, spoonwood, Kalmia latifolia. Look for evergreen glossy leaves, clusters of pink-white cup flowers; forms dense thickets on rocky slopes. Learn it so you can avoid it and warn others. Leaves, flowers and honey from it are toxic.
passages.title: Mountain laurel

passages.context: Sphagnum is the spongy bog moss that holds many times its weight in water. Also called peat moss, bog moss, sphagnum moss, Sphagnum. Look for pale green to red spongy moss in bogs that holds a lot of water; grows in bogs in green, red, or brown carpets.
passages.title: Sphagnum moss

passages.context: Usnea, or old man's beard, is a pale green hair-like lichen on branches whose strands have a white elastic core. Also called old man's beard, beard lichen, Usnea lichen, Usnea. Look for pale green hair-like lichen on branches; pull it and the core is a white elastic thread. Older manuals and folk use mention it, but Yehsa does not give doses or treatments with wild plants. Use it as an identification lesson, and use tested first-aid supplies for care.
passages.title: Old man's beard (Usnea)

passages.context: Cleavers is a sprawling plant whose square stems and narrow whorled leaves stick to clothing with tiny hooks. Also called bedstraw, stickyweed, goosegrass, Galium, Galium aparine. Look for sprawling square stem with whorls of narrow leaves that cling by tiny hooks; sticks to your sleeve when you brush it.
passages.title: Cleavers

passages.context: Canada moonseed is a climbing vine with grape-like berries that are deadly; each berry holds one crescent-shaped seed. Also called moonseed vine, Menispermum, yellow parilla, Menispermum canadense. Look for climbing vine with big lobed leaves, dark blue-black berries each with a single crescent seed; no tendrils, unlike grape. Learn it so you can avoid it and warn others. Looks like wild grape. Grapes have several seeds and tendrils. Moonseed has neither.
passages.title: Canada moonseed

passages.context: Wild grape is a climbing vine with tendrils, toothed lobed leaves, and bunches of small dark grapes. Also called riverbank grape, fox grape, Vitis, Vitis riparia. Look for climbing vine with tendrils, toothed lobed leaves, round berries in a bunch; shreddy bark on older vines.
passages.title: Wild grape

passages.context: Thistle is a spiny plant with round purple flower heads whose peeled young stems and roots are edible. Also called bull thistle, Cirsium, spear thistle, Cirsium vulgare. Look for spiny leaves and stem, round purple flower heads; fluffy seed heads in late summer.
passages.title: Thistle

passages.context: Spotted spurge is a flat mat-forming weed whose milky sap irritates skin and which is toxic if eaten. Also called Euphorbia, spotted spurge, prostrate spurge, Euphorbia maculata. Look for flat mat of small oval leaves with a dark spot, milky sap; thin wiry stems, not fat and succulent. Learn it so you can avoid it and warn others. Sap irritates. Mistaken for purslane.
passages.title: Spotted spurge (Euphorbia)

passages.context: Purslane is a low succulent weed with thick paddle-shaped leaves and reddish stems, a common edible green. Also called Portulaca, pigweed, verdolaga, little hogweed, Portulaca oleracea. Look for flat mat of thick succulent paddle leaves with reddish stems; clear sap.
passages.title: Purslane

passages.context: Chickweed is a small, soft, sprawling weed with tiny white star flowers and a single line of hairs along the stem. Also called Stellaria media, common chickweed, starweed. Look for low plant with small oval leaves and one line of hairs along the stem; tiny white deep-notched petals.
passages.title: Chickweed

passages.context: Common mallow is a low weed with round lobed leaves and small pale pink flowers that leave cheese-wheel shaped seeds. Also called cheeseweed, Malva, buttonweed, Malva neglecta. Look for round lobed leaves on long stalks, small pale pink flowers, round cheese-wheel fruits; slimy texture when the leaves are chewed or crushed.
passages.title: Common mallow

passages.context: Garlic mustard is an invasive woodland plant whose heart-shaped leaves smell of garlic when crushed. Also called Alliaria, hedge garlic, jack-by-the-hedge, Alliaria petiolata. Look for heart-shaped toothed leaves smelling of garlic, small white four-petal flowers; first-year rosettes stay green through winter.
passages.title: Garlic mustard

passages.context: Common juniper is a low, spreading evergreen shrub with sharp needles in threes and blue berry-like cones. Also called juniper, Juniperus communis, juniper berries. Look for low spreading evergreen shrub with sharp needles in threes and blue berry-like cones; needles have a white stripe on top. Knowing the tree helps you pick firewood, shelter sites, and landmarks. Do not mix it up with yew, which is deadly.
passages.title: Common juniper

passages.context: Canada yew is a low evergreen shrub with flat needles and red fleshy berries whose seeds, needles, and bark are deadly. Also called Canada yew, ground hemlock, Taxus, yew berries, Taxus canadensis. Look for flat dark green needles with two pale lines underneath, red fleshy cup berries; low shrub. Knowing the tree helps you pick firewood, shelter sites, and landmarks. Needles, seeds and bark are deadly.
passages.title: Yew (Canada yew)

passages.context: Balsam fir is a northern evergreen with flat, blunt, fragrant needles and resin blisters on smooth bark. Also called fir, Abies balsamea, Christmas tree fir, balsam. Look for flat blunt needles with two white lines underneath, upright cones, smooth bark with resin blisters, spicy smell; cones sit upright on top branches. Resin blisters burn well as fire starter, and boughs make soft bedding.
passages.title: Balsam fir

passages.context: Red spruce is a northern evergreen with stiff, square needles that roll between the fingers and small hanging cones. Also called spruce, Picea rubens, eastern spruce. Look for square four-sided stiff needles that roll between your fingers, hanging cones, reddish scaly bark; sharp needles on small woody pegs. Spruce boughs make shelter roofing and bedding; resin helps start fires.
passages.title: Red spruce

passages.context: White spruce is a northern evergreen with blue-green four-sided needles that smell strong when crushed. Also called Picea glauca, cat spruce, skunk spruce. Look for four-sided blue-green needles, slim hanging cones; needles smell strongly when crushed. Spruce boughs make shelter roofing and bedding; spruce roots make cordage.
passages.title: White spruce

passages.context: Black spruce is a slim bog spruce with short needles and small round cones that stay on the tree for years. Also called bog spruce, Picea mariana. Look for bog tree with a thin top, short needles, small round cones that stay on the tree; club-like dense top. Its presence usually means wet, boggy ground, so plan a route around it.
passages.title: Black spruce

passages.context: Eastern white pine is a tall evergreen with soft needles in bundles of five and long slim cones. Also called white pine, Pinus strobus, eastern pine. Look for soft needles in bundles of five, long slim cones, tiered branches; one needle bundle has five needles, like the letters in white. Pitch from wounds is a fire starter, and inner bark is a famine food.
passages.title: Eastern white pine

passages.context: Red pine is an evergreen with long needles in pairs that snap cleanly when bent and orange-red flaky bark. Also called Norway pine, Pinus resinosa. Look for long needles in bundles of two that snap cleanly, orange-red flaky bark; often in straight planted rows. Dead lower limbs are dry fuel, and fatwood makes strong tinder.
passages.title: Red pine

passages.context: Eastern hemlock is a shade-loving evergreen tree with short flat needles; it is not the poisonous hemlock plants. Also called hemlock tree, Tsuga canadensis, Canada hemlock. Look for flat short needles with two white lines underneath on tiny stalks, tiny cones, drooping top; tiny cones at the branch tips. Dense hemlock gives good shelter from wind and snow. The tree is not the poison hemlock plants. Poison and water hemlock are herbs with umbrella flowers.
passages.title: Eastern hemlock (the tree)

passages.context: Eastern red cedar is a juniper tree with scaly leaves, blue berry-like cones, and fragrant reddish wood. Also called red cedar, Juniperus virginiana, aromatic cedar. Look for scaly green leaves or sharp awls, blue berry-like cones, shredding reddish bark; narrow cone shape in old fields. Shredded bark makes good tinder.
passages.title: Eastern red cedar

passages.context: Northern white cedar is an evergreen with flat fans of scale-like leaves and stringy bark, common in wet ground. Also called arborvitae, Thuja, swamp cedar, Thuja occidentalis. Look for flat fans of scale-like leaves, small cones, stringy bark; wet ground. Its inner bark makes cordage and tinder.
passages.title: Northern white cedar

passages.context: Tamarack is a larch, a conifer whose soft tufted needles turn gold and drop each fall. Also called larch, eastern larch, Larix laricina, hackmatack. Look for soft needles in tufts that turn gold and drop in autumn; bare in winter, unlike other conifers. It marks wet, boggy ground.
passages.title: Tamarack (larch)

passages.context: Sugar maple is a hardwood with five-lobed leaves and rounded gaps, tapped in late winter for maple syrup. Also called hard maple, rock maple, Acer saccharum. Look for five-lobed leaf with smooth rounded gaps, opposite branches, grey furrowed bark; winged seeds in pairs. It is excellent firewood and the classic syrup tree.
passages.title: Sugar maple

passages.context: Red maple is a common hardwood with three- to five-lobed toothed leaves and red twigs, buds, and fall color. Also called swamp maple, soft maple, Acer rubrum. Look for three- to five-lobed leaf with toothed edges and sharp gaps, red twigs and buds; red flowers before the leaves in spring. Its sap can be boiled for syrup too, with a lower sugar content.
passages.title: Red maple

passages.context: Paper birch is a hardwood with white bark that peels in papery sheets and burns even when damp. Also called white birch, canoe birch, Betula papyrifera. Look for white bark peeling in papery sheets with dark marks; toothed oval leaves. Peel bark only from dead or downed trees; it is one of the best natural tinders.
passages.title: Paper birch

passages.context: Yellow birch is a hardwood with silver-yellow bark peeling in curly strips and twigs that smell of wintergreen. Also called Betula alleghaniensis, gold birch. Look for silver-yellow bark that peels in curly strips; twigs smell of wintergreen when scratched. Curly bark shreds catch a spark and burn wet.
passages.title: Yellow birch

passages.context: American beech is a hardwood with smooth gray bark and pale papery leaves that cling through winter. Also called beech, Fagus grandifolia, beechnut tree. Look for smooth blue-grey bark, toothed oval leaves with straight veins, pale leaves that stay in winter; long pointed cigar-shaped buds. Its small triangular beechnuts are edible in fall.
passages.title: American beech

passages.context: White oak is a hardwood with rounded leaf lobes and pale, scaly bark. Also called Quercus alba, white oaks. Look for rounded leaf lobes, pale scaly bark; acorns mature in one year and are less bitter. Acorns need leaching before eating.
passages.title: White oak

passages.context: Northern red oak is a hardwood with pointed, bristle-tipped leaf lobes and ridged bark with shiny stripes. Also called northern red oak, Quercus rubra. Look for pointed leaf lobes with bristle tips, ridged bark with pale stripes; acorns take two years to ripen and are bitter. Acorns need long leaching before eating.
passages.title: Red oak

passages.context: American elm is a hardwood with lopsided, double-toothed leaves and a vase-shaped crown. Also called elm, Ulmus americana, white elm. Look for leaves with uneven bases and double teeth, vase shape; many killed by Dutch elm disease. Inner bark makes cordage.
passages.title: American elm

passages.context: White ash is a hardwood with opposite compound leaves and bark ridged in a diamond pattern. Also called ash, Fraxinus americana, American ash. Look for opposite compound leaves, diamond-pattern bark; opposite branches, unlike most trees. Ash splits easily and burns well even when fairly green.
passages.title: White ash

passages.context: Quaking aspen is a hardwood with round leaves that tremble on flat stalks and smooth pale green-white bark. Also called aspen, trembling aspen, popple, Populus tremuloides. Look for round leaves on flat stalks that tremble, smooth pale green-white bark; grows in clones of many trunks. Its bark rubs off a white powder some use as sunblock in a pinch.
passages.title: Quaking aspen

passages.context: Black cherry is a hardwood with dark, flaky bark like burnt potato chips; its wilted leaves, pits, and bark are poisonous. Also called wild black cherry, Prunus serotina, rum cherry. Look for dark scaly bark like burnt potato chips, glossy toothed leaves, dark berries; almond smell when a twig is scratched. Only the ripe fruit flesh is eaten, never the pits. Leaves, pits and bark contain cyanide compounds. Wilted leaves are dangerous.
passages.title: Black cherry

passages.context: Shagbark hickory is a hardwood whose bark hangs in long loose plates and whose nuts are sweet and edible. Also called hickory, Carya ovata. Look for long loose plates of bark curling at the ends; compound leaves. Hickory is top firewood and smoking wood.
passages.title: Shagbark hickory

passages.context: Basswood is a hardwood with large lopsided heart-shaped leaves and fragrant summer flowers. Also called linden, lime tree, Tilia americana, bee tree. Look for large heart-shaped lopsided leaves, nut-like balls hanging from a leafy strip; nutlets hang from a leaf-like strip. Its inner bark is one of the best natural cordage fibers.
passages.title: Basswood (linden)

passages.context: Black walnut is a hardwood with long compound leaves and round green-husked nuts whose meat is edible. Also called walnut, Juglans nigra. Look for compound leaves of many leaflets, dark ridged bark, round green husked nuts; husks stain hands dark brown. Its roots release a chemical that stunts many plants beneath it.
passages.title: Black walnut

passages.context: Sassafras is a small tree with three leaf shapes on one tree and a spicy, root-beer smell when crushed. Also called Sassafras albidum, mitten tree. Look for leaves of three shapes on one tree (oval, mitten, three-lobed); spicy smell when crushed. The root contains safrole, which FDA has banned as a food additive, so do not brew it.
passages.title: Sassafras

passages.context: American sycamore is a large streamside tree whose bark flakes off in white, green, and brown patches. Also called buttonwood, plane tree, Platanus occidentalis. Look for bark flaking off in patches of white and brown, big lobed leaves, ball fruits; white upper limbs visible from far away. It almost always grows near water.
passages.title: American sycamore

passages.context: Witch hazel is an understory shrub with wavy-edged leaves and yellow ribbon flowers in late fall. Also called Hamamelis, winterbloom, Hamamelis virginiana. Look for wavy-edged uneven leaves, yellow ribbon flowers in late autumn; flowers after the leaves drop. Knowing the tree helps you pick firewood, shelter sites, and landmarks.
passages.title: Witch hazel

passages.context: Do not eat a plant you have not identified. Edible species can have toxic lookalikes. This is an offline caution, not a field guide or medical advice.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Plantago, often called plantain, is a common lawn weed with parallel veins. Crushed plantain (Plantago) leaves are a traditional poultice for an itchy insect bite, and only after the plant is identified. Not a treatment.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Willow bark (Salix) is traditionally used for aches, not as a medicine. Salicin from willow is described as an analgesic, and astringent tannins show up in the bark. Identify the tree before any use. This is not a dose or a substitute for emergency care.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Milky sap, bulb leaves, or umbrella flower clusters are reasons to stop and not taste a plant. Cultivated food is safer than foraging when identification is uncertain.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Yarrow (Achillea millefolium) is a field plant for a small bleeding scrape, and only after the plant is identified. Feathery leaves and a flat white flower cluster are the usual look, and lookalikes are easy to mistake. Do not use a plant you have not identified. This is not a dose or a substitute for emergency care.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Wild carrot (Queen Anne's lace) can look like poison hemlock and water hemlock, which are deadly. Poison hemlock has smooth purple-spotted stems and a musty smell. Water hemlock grows in wet ground and has chambered roots. Wild carrot often has one dark floret in the center and a hairy stem. Never taste an umbrella-flowered plant. A picture is not an identification. Call emergency services if any was eaten.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Death camas is a toxic bulb that can look like a wild onion. A wild onion smells strongly of onion when the bulb or leaf is crushed. Death camas does not smell like onion and its flowers are not an onion umbel. If there is no onion smell, do not eat it. Call emergency services if a bulb was eaten. A picture is not an identification.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Many toxic plants share milky sap, bulb leaves, or white umbrella flower clusters. Never taste a plant to identify it. A small amount of water hemlock, poison hemlock, or death camas can be deadly. Identify every part, and if anyone eats an unknown plant, call emergency services. This is not a dose.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: A cumulonimbus is a very tall, dense storm cloud with a flat anvil top that produces thunderstorms, lightning, heavy rain, hail, and sometimes tornadoes. Also called thunderhead, thunderstorm cloud, anvil cloud, towering storm cloud. Look for towering cauliflower shape that reaches very high; flat, spreading anvil at the top.
passages.title: Cumulonimbus (thunderhead)

passages.context: Cumulus are puffy, flat-bottomed clouds with a cotton-ball look that usually mean fair weather unless they grow tall. Also called fair weather clouds, puffy clouds, cotton ball clouds. Look for distinct, rounded puffs with sharp edges; flat bases. Small, scattered cumulus mean fair weather. If they build taller through the day and darken, watch for afternoon showers or storms.
passages.title: Cumulus clouds

passages.context: Stratus is a flat, gray, featureless layer of low cloud, like fog that has lifted off the ground. Also called low gray clouds, overcast low sky, gray blanket cloud, high fog. Look for uniform gray layer with no shape; very low base, sometimes touching hills. Expect gloomy, damp, cool conditions with little wind and perhaps drizzle. Visibility is poor, so use care navigating.
passages.title: Stratus clouds and fog

passages.context: Nimbostratus is a thick, dark gray layer that blocks the sun and brings steady rain or snow for hours. Also called rain clouds, steady rain cloud, dark gray rain layer. Look for dark, even gray sky with no visible sun; steady, continuous rain or snow. Plan for long, soaking rain: set up shelter, keep gear dry, and avoid low spots and dry washes that can flood.
passages.title: Nimbostratus

passages.context: Cirrus are thin, wispy, white streaks high in the sky made of ice crystals, and they often come before a change in weather. Also called mares tails, wispy high clouds, feathery clouds, ice crystal clouds. Look for thin white hair-like streaks; very high in a blue sky. A few mean fair weather. If they thicken and lower into a sheet over a day, a warm front and rain may follow in about 24 hours.
passages.title: Cirrus clouds

passages.context: Cirrostratus is a thin, milky veil of high cloud that makes a ring (halo) around the sun or moon, and it often means rain or snow is coming within a day. Also called ring around the moon, halo around the sun, milky sky, sun dog. Look for bright ring around the sun or moon; thin, milky sheet across the sky. Expect weather to turn within roughly 12 to 24 hours. Use the time to prepare shelter and gear.
passages.title: Cirrostratus and halo around the sun or moon

passages.context: Altocumulus are white or gray patches or rolls of cloud at mid-levels, and in a warm humid morning they can mean afternoon thunderstorms. Also called mackerel sky, sheep back clouds, patchy mid-level clouds, castellanus. Look for rows or patches of rounded cloudlets; mid-level, smaller than cumulus. If you see turrets or they appear on a warm, sticky morning, watch for storms by afternoon.
passages.title: Altocumulus (mackerel sky)

passages.context: Altostratus is a gray or blue-gray mid-level sheet through which the sun appears dimly, like looking through frosted glass. Also called watery sun, gray veil, sun looks like through ground glass. Look for gray sheet with a dim, watery sun; no halo. It usually thickens ahead of a warm front, so expect steady rain or snow within several hours.
passages.title: Altostratus

passages.context: Stratocumulus are low, lumpy gray and white clouds in rolls or patches that cover much of the sky, often with little rain. Also called low lumpy gray clouds, rolls of low cloud. Look for rounded masses joined in rows; gray with brighter gaps. Usually dry or light drizzle at most. Conditions often clear toward evening.
passages.title: Stratocumulus

passages.context: A lenticular is a smooth, lens-shaped cloud that sits over or downwind of mountains where strong winds flow in waves. Also called UFO cloud, lens shaped cloud, stacked pancake cloud, wave cloud. Look for smooth lens or stacked-plate shape; stays in one place while air streams through. Treat it as a sign of strong winds aloft and possibly rough air and gusty winds at the summit or downwind. Weather may be changing.
passages.title: Lenticular cloud

passages.context: Mammatus are pouch-like bulges that hang from the underside of a cloud, usually a thunderstorm anvil. Also called pouch clouds, bubbly cloud underside, udder clouds. Look for lumpy pouches under an anvil; often seen after a storm has passed. They mark a strong storm system. Stay alert for severe weather and move to shelter if a storm is still near.
passages.title: Mammatus clouds

passages.context: A shelf cloud is a low, wedge-shaped wall of cloud on the leading edge of a thunderstorm's cold outflow, with strong straight-line winds right behind it. Also called arcus cloud, roll cloud, wall of cloud ahead of storm, storm front line. Look for long horizontal band with a smooth leading edge; dark, ragged cloud behind it. Take shelter now. Damaging gusts, heavy rain, and hail arrive within minutes of the shelf cloud.
passages.title: Shelf cloud and gust front

passages.context: A wall cloud is a localized lowering of the rain-free base of a thunderstorm, and rotation there can lead to a tornado; a funnel cloud is a rotating condensation funnel that has not reached the ground. Also called rotating cloud base, funnel cloud, lowering under a storm, wall cloud tornado. Look for a lowering that looks like a wall under the storm base; visible rotation or rapid upward motion.
passages.title: Wall cloud and funnel cloud

passages.context: Contrails are the trails of cloud behind high aircraft; if they stay long and spread, the high air is moist and weather may change. Also called vapor trails, airplane trails spreading, long contrails. Look for short, quickly vanishing contrails mean dry upper air; long lasting, spreading trails mean moist upper air. Use them as a hint of a coming change, along with other signs like wind shift and falling pressure.
passages.title: Contrails as a sign

passages.context: Fog is a cloud at ground level; it forms when air cools to its dew point, most often on calm, clear nights or when moist air moves over a cold surface. Also called morning fog, mist, fog in valleys, fog on the water, low visibility. Look for radiation or valley fog: calm, clear night, fog in low spots; advection fog: warm moist air moving over cold water or land.
passages.title: Fog: radiation, advection, and valley fog

passages.context: A thunderstorm grows from rising warm moist air, matures with heavy rain and lightning, and then weakens as downdrafts cut off the updraft. Also called how a thunderstorm forms, towering cumulus, downdraft, storm stages. Look for towering cumulus growing fast; anvil top and rain, hail, and lightning at maturity. Watch for fast-growing towers on warm afternoons and plan to be off ridges early. Storms often last 30 minutes to an hour but can repeat along a line.
passages.title: Thunderstorm life cycle

passages.context: Count the seconds from a lightning flash to its thunder; every five seconds is about one mile (three seconds is about one kilometer). Also called how far away is the lightning, count between flash and thunder, 30 30 rule, thunder distance. Look for see the flash, start counting; hear the thunder, stop. If you hear thunder, you are close enough to be struck. Go to safe shelter and wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.
passages.title: Flash-to-bang: counting the distance to lightning

passages.context: Tornado signs are a dark, greenish sky, large hail, a rotating wall cloud, a loud roar, and a debris cloud at ground level. Also called how to know a tornado is coming, green sky, debris cloud, roaring sound like a freight train. Look for dark, green-tinged sky and large hail; rotating, lowering cloud base. If a tornado warning is issued or you see these signs, go to shelter now. A tornado watch means conditions are favorable, so stay alert.
passages.title: Tornado warning signs

passages.context: In a tornado, get to the lowest floor of a sturdy building, in an interior room away from windows, and protect your head and neck. Also called what to do in a tornado, tornado shelter, basement during a tornado, caught outside in a tornado. Look for interior room, closet, or bathroom on the lowest floor; basement or storm shelter is best.
passages.title: Tornado safety

passages.context: The EF scale rates a tornado from EF0 to EF5 by the damage it causes and the wind speeds estimated from it. Also called tornado rating, EF5, how strong is a tornado. Look for EF0: 65 to 85 mph, light damage; EF2: 111 to 135 mph, considerable damage. Use it to understand reports after a tornado. The rating is assigned after the damage survey, not in advance.
passages.title: Enhanced Fujita (EF) scale

passages.context: The Saffir-Simpson scale rates hurricanes from category 1 to 5 by sustained wind speed, but flooding and storm surge cause most deaths. Also called category 3 hurricane, how strong is a hurricane, typhoon, cyclone wind speeds. Look for category 1: 74 to 95 mph; category 3: 111 to 129 mph, a major hurricane. Prepare early by category and by the local storm surge and rainfall forecasts. Follow evacuation orders for surge zones.
passages.title: Hurricane categories (Saffir-Simpson)

passages.context: Storm surge is the rise in sea level pushed ashore by a hurricane's winds, and it is the biggest killer in hurricanes. Also called hurricane flooding from the sea, wall of water, coastal flooding. Look for water rising far above normal high tide; strongest to the right of the storm's track in the north hemisphere. Leave when told to evacuate a surge zone, and go inland or uphill. Plan the route before the storm.
passages.title: Storm surge

passages.context: Hurricane safety means knowing your evacuation zone, leaving early if told to, and sheltering in a safe interior room if you stay. Also called hurricane preparedness, what to do in a hurricane, tropical storm prep. Look for know your zone and route; supplies for several days: water, food, medicine, radio, power bank.
passages.title: Hurricane safety

passages.context: A watch means conditions are favorable for the hazard; a warning means it is happening or about to happen; an advisory means it will be a nuisance. Also called difference between a watch and a warning, tornado watch, flood warning, weather alert meaning. Look for watch: be prepared; warning: take action now. When a warning is issued for your location, act at once. When a watch is issued, review your plan and keep a radio on.
passages.title: Watch, warning, and advisory

passages.context: NOAA Weather Radio broadcasts National Weather Service forecasts and alerts around the clock on seven VHF frequencies. Also called weather radio, same alert radio, emergency alert radio. Look for frequencies between 162.400 and 162.550 MHz; a tone alert and SAME code for your county. Keep a weather radio with fresh batteries, set to your county's SAME code, as a way to get warnings when cell service and power are out.
passages.title: NOAA Weather Radio

passages.context: A blizzard is a storm with sustained winds or gusts of 35 mph or more and low visibility from falling or blowing snow for at least three hours. Also called whiteout, heavy snow storm, stuck in a snowstorm, winter storm. Look for falling or blowing snow with very low visibility; strong winds and drifting. Stay inside, stay put in a vehicle if stranded (run the engine only briefly with the tailpipe clear), and keep warm and hydrated. Use layers, a hat, and bright markers.
passages.title: Blizzard and winter storm safety

passages.context: Freezing rain falls as liquid and freezes on contact, coating everything with ice; it is far more damaging than sleet. Also called glaze ice, icy roads, sleet versus freezing rain, ice on power lines. Look for glazed trees, wires, and roads; sleet bounces and rattles, freezing rain coats and sticks. Stay off roads, stay clear of trees and power lines, and prepare for outages. Keep warm and do not use generators indoors.
passages.title: Freezing rain and ice storms

passages.context: Wind chill is how cold the air feels on bare skin because wind carries away body heat; it affects people and animals, not objects. Also called feels like temperature, cold wind, frostbite time. Look for a stronger wind makes the same temperature feel colder; at around minus 20 F (minus 29 C) wind chill, frostbite can occur in about 30 minutes. Dress for the wind chill: windproof outer layer, covered skin, and warm insulation, and check for frostbite on exposed skin.
passages.title: Wind chill

passages.context: The heat index combines air temperature and humidity to show how hot it really feels, because sweat cannot cool you when the air is humid. Also called feels like in the heat, humid and hot, heat advisory. Look for high humidity makes it feel hotter; heat index above 103 F (39 C) is dangerous. Do hard work in the early morning or evening, rest in the shade, and drink water. Check on older people, children, and pets.
passages.title: Heat index

passages.context: The dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated and dew or fog forms; a higher dew point means muggier air. Also called dewpoint, why is it sticky, dew on the grass, fog forms when. Look for dew point under 10 C (50 F): dry, comfortable; above 18 C (65 F): sticky. If the night temperature will fall to the dew point, expect dew or fog and condensation on gear. Put gear in a tent or bag to keep it dry.
passages.title: Dew point and humidity

passages.context: A barometer measures air pressure; how it changes over a few hours tells more than the number itself. Also called falling pressure, rising pressure, barometer, altimeter weather change, pressure drop. Look for falling slowly: clouds and weather deteriorating; falling fast: a storm is near. Note the pressure every few hours. A fast fall, such as 3 hPa or more in three hours, calls for preparing for rough weather. Watch altimeter drift as a pressure change.
passages.title: Reading the barometer trend

passages.context: A cold front is the leading edge of a cooler air mass that pushes under warmer air, causing a narrow band of storms, a wind shift, and a drop in temperature. Also called front passing, storm line, temperature drop and wind shift, squall line. Look for a line of towering clouds and showers or storms; wind shifts to the west or northwest in the northern hemisphere.
passages.title: Cold front

passages.context: A warm front is where warm air slides over cooler air, bringing a long period of thickening clouds and steady rain or snow, then milder weather. Also called slow moving rain, thickening clouds, steady rain ahead of warm air. Look for cirrus, then cirrostratus, then altostratus, then nimbostratus; pressure falls steadily. Expect a day or so of build-up, then hours of steady precipitation and warmer, muggier air after it passes.
passages.title: Warm front

passages.context: Wind shifts show a passing front: in the northern hemisphere, stand with your back to the wind and the low pressure is on your left. Also called wind changed direction, wind backing, which way is the low pressure, how to find the storm. Look for wind backing (counterclockwise) with falling pressure ahead of a low; sudden shift to the northwest with a cold front.
passages.title: Wind shifts and Buys Ballot's law

passages.context: The Beaufort scale describes wind force from 0 (calm) to 12 (hurricane) using what you can see. Also called wind force, gale, how strong is the wind, wind speed words. Look for force 4: moderate breeze, dust and small branches move (11-16 knots); force 6: strong breeze, large branches sway, umbrellas hard to use (22-27 knots). Use it to judge conditions and decide to stay off the water, ridgelines, and exposed trails at force 6 and above.
passages.title: Beaufort wind scale

passages.context: Mountain weather changes fast: temperatures fall with height, winds strengthen, and storms often build by early afternoon. Also called weather in the mountains, storms on peaks, summit weather, afternoon thunderstorms. Look for temperature drops about 6.5 C per 1,000 m (3.5 F per 1,000 ft); afternoon cumulus towers in summer. Start early, be off summits and ridges by noon, and turn back when clouds build. Carry rain and warm layers even on fair days.
passages.title: Mountain weather

passages.context: A microburst is a small, intense downdraft from a thunderstorm that spreads out at the ground and can knock down trees in one direction. Also called straight-line winds, sudden gust, storm winds knocked trees down. Look for sudden strong wind at the leading edge of a storm; dust or rain streaking down. Move away from trees and into a sturdy shelter at the first sign of a strong, sudden gust ahead of a storm.
passages.title: Microburst and downburst

passages.context: A flash flood is a rapid rise of water, often from storms miles upstream, and it can reach you under a clear sky. Also called flood watch, rising creek, dry wash flood, slot canyon flood, dry gully. Look for heavy rain upstream, rising and muddy creeks; a rumbling roar in a canyon, or debris in the water. Move to high ground at once, avoid canyons and washes in storm season, and never drive or walk through floodwater. Turn around, don't drown.
passages.title: Flash flood risk

passages.context: Wildfire smoke contains fine particles that can harm the lungs and heart; the air quality index (AQI) shows when to limit time outside. Also called smoky air, air quality index, AQI, fire smoke, N95 for smoke. Look for AQI above 100 is unhealthy for sensitive groups; above 150 is unhealthy for all. Stay indoors with windows closed, run a HEPA filter, and use a well-fitted N95 respirator outside if you must. Limit exertion.
passages.title: Wildfire smoke and air quality

passages.context: For a wildfire, leave early when told to or when smoke and flames are near; waiting is the biggest mistake. Also called fire is coming, wildfire go bag, leave before the fire, fire evacuation zone. Look for official evacuation order or warning; smoke, ember showers, and a wind shift toward you. Take people, pets, medicines, papers, and a go bag, close windows and doors, and follow known evacuation routes. Tell someone where you are going.
passages.title: Wildfire evacuation

passages.context: A haboob is a wall of dust pushed ahead of a thunderstorm's outflow, dropping visibility to near zero within seconds. Also called dust wall, sandstorm, blowing dust. Look for a towering brown wall approaching; sudden strong gusts and a drop in visibility. Pull off the road as far as you can, turn off lights, set the parking brake, and keep your foot off the brake pedal. Cover your nose and mouth.
passages.title: Dust storm (haboob)

passages.context: On calm clear nights, cold air sinks and pools in valleys while the slopes above stay warmer; this is a temperature inversion. Also called cold in the valley at night, frost hollows, smoke lies flat, inversion. Look for smoke or fog layers lie flat; valley floors much colder than the slopes. Camp on the slope or bench, not the valley floor. Frost and fog form in the low spots first.
passages.title: Temperature inversion and cold air pooling

passages.context: Some old sayings work because they match real changes in air pressure and moisture; others are myths. Also called red sky at night, cows lying down, birds flying low, weather sayings, ants before rain. Look for red sky at night, shepherd's delight: often works in mid-latitudes where weather moves west to east; a ring around the moon: thin high cloud ahead of a front.
passages.title: Folk weather signs: what holds up

passages.context: Lightning can strike the same place many times, can reach 10 miles from a storm, and rubber tires do not protect you; a hard-topped metal vehicle does. Also called does lightning strike twice, rubber tires protect, if the sky is clear lightning cannot hit, bolt from the blue. Look for bolts from the blue strike under clear skies near a storm; tall isolated objects are struck repeatedly.
passages.title: Lightning myths

passages.context: In a storm outage, keep warm, use flashlights, keep fridge and freezer doors closed, and run generators outside, far from the house. Also called lights are out, storm knocked out power, candles safety, fridge during outage. Look for flashlights and battery lantern, not candles; closed fridge keeps food safe about four hours, a full freezer about 48 hours.
passages.title: Power outage basics in a storm

passages.context: The weather trend is the direction air pressure and the sky are moving over the last few hours, read from this phone's barometer together with the saved forecast and how old it is. Also called weather trend, is the weather getting worse, will it rain, pressure trend, barometer says. Look for pressure falling 1 hPa or more per hour: weather is worsening, often rain or wind; pressure steady: no big change soon.
passages.title: What is the weather trend?

passages.context: A saved forecast or alert is a snapshot; it gets less reliable with age, and every NWS alert carries its own expiry time. Also called is the forecast out of date, stale forecast, when was the alert issued, alert expires. Look for the issue time on the forecast; the 'until' or expiry time on an alert.
passages.title: How old is the saved forecast or alert?

passages.context: Hypothermia can happen well above freezing: cool air plus rain, wind, and wet clothes steals body heat fast. Also called cold and wet, hypothermia at 50 degrees, rain and wind chill, cold drizzle. Look for air temperatures from 30 to 50 F (minus 1 to 10 C) with rain or wind; shivering, clumsiness, and mumbling. Put on a waterproof shell and a hat, swap wet layers for dry ones, eat and drink, and get out of the wind. Stop and warm up at the first shivering.
passages.title: Hypothermia in mild but wet weather
