passages.context: Fog cuts visibility, hides landmarks, and can make a known place unfamiliar; it also muffles sound. Also called foggy morning hunt, can't see in the fog, low light and mist. Look for valley fog at dawn on calm clear mornings; visibility dropping below a few hundred feet.
passages.title: Fog and low visibility on a hunt or hike

passages.context: If thunder is heard, get to a vehicle, a building, or low ground at once, and get off the water, ridges, and open fields. Also called storm while hunting, lightning in the woods, storm on the boat, lightning on the lake. Look for thunder or a flash within 30 seconds; dark towers and a sudden cool breeze.
passages.title: A thunderstorm starts while you are hunting or on the water

passages.context: After ice or wind storms, ice-loaded limbs and downed lines are the main hazards, and any line on the ground should be treated as live. Also called tree limb down, power line on the ground, ice storm cleanup, widowmaker after a storm. Look for ice-coated or cracked limbs overhead; wires on the ground or hanging in trees.
passages.title: Ice, branches, and downed lines after a storm

passages.context: A red flag warning means warm temperatures, very low humidity, and strong winds are creating critical fire conditions. Also called red flag warning, fire weather watch, dry windy day, drought and fire risk. Look for low humidity, dry vegetation, and gusty winds; a burn ban or an NWS red flag warning. Do not burn outdoors, keep vehicles off dry grass, and have an escape route ready. Check local burn bans. Put out any fire completely.
passages.title: Red flag warning and fire weather

passages.context: Rain on deep snow plus warm air can melt it fast and send a surge of water into streams, and ice jams can back up rivers. Also called thaw flooding, ice jam, snowmelt flood, spring flood. Look for warm rain on a deep snowpack; rapidly rising streams and cracking river ice. Stay away from rivers and stream banks, move to higher ground if water rises, and avoid crossing flooded roads. Move vehicles and valuables from low spots early.
passages.title: Rain on snow and ice jam flooding

passages.context: A small craft advisory warns that winds or seas are hazardous for small boats, and a marine forecast gives wind, seas, and visibility for coastal waters. Also called small craft advisory, coastal waters forecast, boating weather, choppy seas. Look for winds around 20 to 33 knots and rough seas; fog and reduced visibility.
passages.title: Marine and small-craft forecast

passages.context: Dew forms when surfaces cool to the dew point, and frost forms when they cool below freezing on a clear, calm night. Also called will it freeze tonight, frost forecast, ground frost, heavy dew. Look for clear skies and calm winds cool the ground fastest; wet grass or a white coating at dawn. Expect a frost when the forecast low is near 36 F (2 C) on a clear, calm night. Cover gear, bring water filters and batteries inside, and sleep above the cold air in the valley.
passages.title: Dew, frost, and overnight lows

passages.context: A whiteout is a loss of depth and horizon in blowing snow or flat light, and it makes it easy to lose direction or walk off an edge. Also called can't see in the snow, blowing snow, snow squall, white out. Look for no visible horizon or shadows; blowing snow and low visibility. Stop moving unless you are on a sure handrail such as a fence or a wall. Put on warm layers, take shelter, and wait for visibility to improve. Use a compass if you must move.
passages.title: Whiteout

passages.context: A better local forecast comes from combining pressure trend, wind shift, cloud change, and temperature rather than relying on any one sign. Also called how do I forecast the weather myself, signs of a storm coming, weather clues, predict rain. Look for falling pressure plus thickening high cloud: wet weather in a day; backing wind plus low, dark cloud: worsening.
passages.title: Using pressure, wind, and clouds together

passages.context: Remnants of tropical storms and nor'easters bring heavy rain, wind, and high tides that flood coasts and rivers well inland. Also called hurricane remnants, nor'easter, coastal flood, storm tide. Look for tropical storm or nor'easter in the forecast; heavy rain bands and rising rivers. Follow evacuation orders, move to higher ground, secure outside items, and avoid flooded roads. Have supplies for several days.
passages.title: Tropical storm remnants and coastal flooding

passages.context: Biomes are broad living landscapes: forest, grassland, desert, tundra, and coast, set by climate and water more than by towns. Plants and the ground underfoot tell you which pattern you are in. A biome is not a line you can pace to a city limit. Weather still changes inside it.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Terrain is the shape you walk: flat, rolling, steep, broken, swampy, or cliffed. Steep ground costs time. Broken rock hides ankles. Soft ground hides depth. Choose the line that keeps you on ground you can see. This is a travel cue, not a soil survey or a road map.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: A watershed is the land that drains to one stream, lake, or coast. Ridges are the divides. Water runs away from them into the basin. Following a creek downhill moves you toward that basin's trunk stream, not necessarily toward help. A drainage is not a trail.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: A coast is where land meets a large body of water. Tides, cliffs, and headlands change the walkable strip through the day. A headland is a natural landmark. A harbor town is not stored here. Stay off wet rock when the sea is rising, and do not guess a tide table you do not have.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Mountains stack climate. Higher is usually colder, windier, and slower. A pass is a low saddle between higher ground. A peak is a landmark only while you can still see it. Weather arrives fast on ridges. Turn back when the route you can see runs out. This is not a climb grade.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Deserts are water-poor landscapes, hot or cold, where shade and the water you carry matter more than speed. Washes can flood from rain you do not see. Walk the firm edge of a wash, not its throat. Do not chase a shimmer toward a town. Night can turn sharply cold.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Forests hide the sun and the distant ridge. Travel is slower, and a handrail such as a stream or a ridge matters more than a bearing you cannot check. Moss is not a compass. Mark the way back while the last sure point is still in sight. This is not a timber or trail catalog.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Arctic and tundra country is open, cold, and often wet underfoot, with few trees to use as landmarks. When the horizon disappears, a short bearing and a counted pace are safer than a long walk. Summer light can last all day. Winter dark does the opposite. Ice is not a path this note approves.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: River cues: a V of ripples often points at a rock, and smooth dark water can be deep. The outside of a bend cuts the bank. The inside piles gravel. Current is a force, not a trail. Wade only at a wide shallow place you have walked, and do not enter flood water.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Useful landmarks are natural and stable: a peak, a saddle, a lone butte, a confluence, a waterfall, a headland, a lake outlet. Name them on the map you carry and in a waypoint you save yourself. This store has no city, street, or business directory. If the landmark clouds over, rejoin a handrail.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Climate bands follow latitude and altitude in a rough way: tropical, subtropical, temperate, polar, plus dry belts where rain rarely falls. A band says what the season tends to do, not what tomorrow's storm will do. Height can copy a colder band. Watch the sky you actually have.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Magnetic declination is the angle between magnetic north and true north at a place. It changes slowly over years and with where you stand. A compass needle points magnetic. A map's meridians are the true frame. Set the declination printed on your map before you trust a bearing. There is no live declination feed.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: True north follows the planet's axis, toward the geographic pole. Magnetic north is where the needle points, and the gap between them is declination. East declination means magnetic north sits east of true north. Add east declination to a magnetic bearing to plot true. A position lock is a point, not a north reference.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Contour lines join points of equal elevation. Lines close together mean steep ground. Wide gaps mean flatter ground. A V in the contours often points upstream in a valley. Index contours are the labeled ones. They show shape, not a trail name. The interval is printed on the map you carry.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Map and compass: set the map to the land, lay the compass edge on the line you mean to walk, turn the housing to north on the map, then turn your body until the needle agrees. Walk a short leg to a landmark you named and count paces. This is a method sketch, not a course certificate.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Elevation is height above a datum, often mean sea level. A GPS altitude, when a consented fix includes one, is a rough height and is weaker than the horizontal fix. If the lock has no altitude, say so and do not invent one. Contours show shape. A barometer drifts with the weather.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: A great-circle course is the shortest path on a sphere between two latitudes and longitudes. The initial bearing is the direction you start, and it can change as you travel. Reverse bearing is the direction back. These tools use that spherical estimate. They do not follow roads and they do not download tiles.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: A track log is a list of your own points, saved on this device only after you consent. Distance is the sum of the great-circle legs. Elapsed time is counted only when those points carry timestamps. It is not someone else's path, and it is not sent anywhere unless you say so in your own words.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Landscape navigation here is terrain, water, coast, and sky: distance, bearing, waypoints, and a track you record yourself. It deliberately has no city map, no street list, and no points of interest that go stale as towns change. If you need a town, use a map you brought, not this store.
passages.title: notes

passages.context: Cleaning a wound means flushing dirt and germs out with plenty of clean running water after bleeding is under control. Also called wash a cut, rinse a scrape, irrigate a wound. Look for bleeding has stopped or is controlled; visible dirt or grit in the wound. Rinse for several minutes with clean water, use mild soap on the skin around it, and lift out loose grit with clean tweezers. Pat dry and cover.
passages.title: Cleaning a wound

passages.context: A wound is likely infected when it gets worse over days instead of better, with growing redness, warmth, swelling, pus, or pain. Also called infected cut, cellulitis, pus in a wound, red streaks. Look for redness that spreads outward from the wound; warmth, swelling, and increasing pain after the first day or two.
passages.title: Signs a wound is infected

passages.context: Sepsis is the body's dangerous overreaction to an infection, and it can quickly harm organs and cause death if not treated. Also called blood poisoning, septic, infection spreading through the body. Look for fever or shivering, or feeling very cold; fast heartbeat and fast breathing. Treat it as an emergency in anyone with a known or suspected infection who has these signs. Get to hospital care fast; sepsis needs medical treatment.
passages.title: Sepsis warning signs

passages.context: A dressing is the clean pad that sits on the wound, and a bandage is what holds it in place without cutting off blood flow. Also called dressing a wound, wrap a cut, cover a wound, gauze. Look for clean, non-stick or gauze pad; wrap snug but loose enough for a finger beneath. Cover the wound with a clean dressing, wrap over it firmly, and check the fingers or toes beyond it for color, warmth, and feeling every little while.
passages.title: Bandaging a wound

passages.context: A pressure bandage is a thick pad held over a bleeding wound with a firm wrap, so you can keep pressure on without your hands. Also called emergency bandage, israeli bandage, wrap that stops bleeding. Look for thick pad directly on the wound; firm wrap that presses the pad down. Use it after direct pressure when bleeding is steady and you need your hands free. Add more padding on top if blood soaks through; do not remove the first layer.
passages.title: Pressure bandage

passages.context: Arterial bleeding is blood from an artery: bright red and often spurting with each heartbeat, and it can be fatal within minutes. Also called spurting blood, bright red bleeding, life-threatening bleeding. Look for bright red blood that spurts or pulses; blood that quickly pools or soaks clothing.
passages.title: Arterial bleeding

passages.context: Internal bleeding is blood loss inside the body that you cannot see, often after a hard blow, a fall, a crash, or a deep injury to the torso. Also called bleeding inside the body, hidden bleeding, blood loss you cannot see. Look for bruising, swelling, or a hard painful belly after a blow; pale, cold, clammy skin, fast weak pulse, dizziness.
passages.title: Internal bleeding

passages.context: A serious belly injury can damage organs and bleed inside, and an open wound can let intestines show. Also called stomach wound, bowel sticking out, gut injury, blow to the belly. Look for open wound or protruding bowel; a rigid, swollen, very painful belly. Keep the person lying on their back with knees bent if comfortable, cover any exposed organs loosely with a clean moist cloth, and get emergency help.
passages.title: Belly (abdominal) wound or injury

passages.context: A penetrating chest wound can let air into the chest around the lung, making breathing hard and getting worse. Also called punctured lung, stab to the chest, penetrating chest injury, pneumothorax. Look for hole in the chest, sometimes with a sucking sound or bubbling blood; trouble breathing and chest pain.
passages.title: Chest wound (sucking chest wound)

passages.context: An embedded object plugs the wound it caused, and pulling it out can release heavy bleeding. Also called impaled object, stabbed, something stuck in the leg, embedded object. Look for object visibly stuck in the body; bleeding around, not through, the object. Leave it in place. Pad around it to hold it still and stop it moving, control bleeding by pressing around it, and get emergency help.
passages.title: Object stuck in a wound

passages.context: After an amputation, the first job is to stop the bleeding and treat shock; the severed part is saved wrapped and cool so it might be reattached. Also called severed finger, cut off hand, body part cut off, avulsion. Look for heavy bleeding from the stump; a separated finger, hand, or limb.
passages.title: Amputation: care of the person and the part

passages.context: A crush injury is damage from a heavy weight pressing a body part, and releasing a long-trapped limb can suddenly cause shock or kidney trouble. Also called pinned under something, trapped limb, crushed leg, building collapse injury. Look for limb pinned under a heavy object; swelling, numbness, and pain. Get emergency help first. If trapped less than about 15 minutes and the load is safe to lift, free the person, control bleeding, and treat for shock. Keep them still.
passages.title: Crush injury

passages.context: A fracture is a break or crack in a bone, and the signs are pain that is worse with movement, swelling, bruising, and an odd shape or loss of use. Also called fracture, broken arm, broken leg, did I break it, cracked bone. Look for sharp pain at one spot that is worse with use; swelling, bruising, and a limb that looks bent or short.
passages.title: Signs of a broken bone

passages.context: An open fracture is a broken bone with an open wound, which means a high risk of infection and bleeding. Also called bone sticking out, compound fracture, bone through skin. Look for bone end visible or a wound over a deformed limb; bleeding at the break. Control bleeding with pressure around the bone, not on it. Cover the wound loosely with a clean moist dressing, splint without pushing the bone back, and get emergency help.
passages.title: Open (compound) fracture

passages.context: A sling holds the forearm up, and a swathe is a second bandage that binds the arm against the chest so it cannot swing. Also called arm sling, triangle bandage sling, broken collarbone sling, shoulder injury support. Look for a triangular bandage or a shirt tail; forearm rests higher than the elbow. Use it for a broken arm, collarbone, shoulder or dislocation, after you have checked the fingers for color and feeling. Put padding between the arm and body.
passages.title: Sling and swathe

passages.context: A dislocation is when the ends of the bones in a joint are forced out of place, leaving the joint looking wrong and unable to move. Also called dislocated shoulder, dislocated finger, joint out of place, popped out of socket. Look for joint looks deformed or out of position; severe pain and swelling and unable to move it. Support the joint in the position found with padding and a sling or splint, apply a cool pack for pain, and get it put back by a clinician.
passages.title: Dislocated joint

passages.context: A concussion is a mild brain injury from a blow or jolt to the head, and the danger is that a serious bleed can build slowly. Also called hit head, bump on the head, knocked out, head trauma, brain injury. Look for headache, dizziness, confusion, or memory gaps; nausea or vomiting, or blurred vision.
passages.title: Concussion and head injury

passages.context: An unresponsive person who is still breathing normally needs their airway kept open and an ambulance, because they can choke on their own tongue or vomit. Also called passed out, fainted, not waking up, unresponsive. Look for does not respond to voice or a shoulder tap; chest rises and falls with normal breathing.
passages.title: Person who is unconscious but breathing

passages.context: Fainting is a short loss of consciousness when the brain briefly gets too little blood, often from standing too long, heat, fear, pain, or dehydration. Also called passing out, about to faint, blacked out, lightheaded and dizzy. Look for lightheaded, pale, sweaty, vision narrowing; collapse that lasts under a minute or two.
passages.title: Fainting

passages.context: A speck or grit in the eye usually washes out with tears or clean water, and anything stuck or sharp needs a clinician. Also called speck in eye, grit in eye, eyelash in eye, foreign body in eye, eye pain. Look for watering, blinking, redness, a gritty feel; pain that is worse when blinking. Do not rub. Blink, then flush the eye with clean water or saline for several minutes. Pull the upper lid over the lower to let lashes sweep it out.
passages.title: Something in the eye

passages.context: Snow blindness is a painful sunburn of the surface of the eye from bright ultraviolet light reflecting off snow, ice, or water. Also called sun burned eyes, photokeratitis, eye sunburn, welder flash. Look for gritty, burning pain and tears hours after exposure; red, swollen lids and sensitivity to light. Get out of the light, cover both eyes with a dark soft cloth, rest, and use cool damp cloths for comfort. Prevent it with dark tinted glasses with side shields.
passages.title: Snow blindness

passages.context: A knocked-out adult tooth can sometimes be saved if it is kept moist and put back or seen by a dentist within about an hour. Also called lost a tooth, avulsed tooth, broken tooth, tooth fell out. Look for a whole tooth out with the root attached; bleeding in the socket. Pick up the tooth by the crown, not the root. Rinse gently with milk or saline if dirty and try to push it back into the socket; otherwise keep it in milk or against the cheek. See a dentist right away.
passages.title: Knocked-out tooth

passages.context: A toothache is pain from decay, a crack, or an abscess, and swelling or fever means the infection may be spreading. Also called tooth pain, abscess, swollen gum, dental pain. Look for steady throbbing pain, worse with hot or cold; swollen gum or cheek, a bad taste. Rinse with warm salt water, keep the mouth clean, and use over-the-counter pain relievers as directed on the label. See a dentist as soon as you can.
passages.title: Toothache in the field

passages.context: A fishhook is barbed, so pulling straight back tears the skin; it is pushed through or backed out along its curve. Also called hook in finger, fish hook stuck, hook in skin. Look for hook embedded in finger, arm, or face; barb under the skin. For a shallow hook, push the point through, snip off the barb with clippers, and back the shaft out. Clean the wound and cover it. Check your tetanus status.
passages.title: Fishhook removal

passages.context: Tetanus is a serious infection from bacteria in soil and dirt that enter a wound, and it is prevented by vaccination with boosters. Also called lockjaw, tetanus booster, rusty nail, dirty wound vaccine. Look for a dirty, deep, or puncture wound; animal bite or rusty or soil-contaminated injury. Ask a clinician about a booster after a dirty or deep wound, usually if you have not had one in the last five years for dirty wounds or ten years for clean ones.
passages.title: Tetanus and wounds

passages.context: An animal bite can cause infection and, from wild animals, rabies, so it needs washing and a call to a clinician or health department. Also called dog bite, cat bite, bitten by a wild animal, rabies exposure, bat in the house. Look for puncture or torn skin from teeth or claws; a wild, strange-acting, or unprovoked animal.
passages.title: Animal bite

passages.context: A splinter is a small piece of wood, thorn, or glass in the skin that is removed with clean tweezers along the angle it went in. Also called sliver, thorn in the skin, wood splinter, cactus spines. Look for a visible end sticking out; tenderness at the spot. Wash the skin, clean the tweezers with alcohol or boiling water, pull the splinter out in the line it entered, and wash again. Tape can lift fine cactus spines.
passages.title: Splinter removal

passages.context: A blister is a fluid-filled pocket from friction or heat, and a hot spot is the warm, tender patch that warns one is coming. Also called foot blister, rubbing boot, hot spot on heel, blister on foot. Look for a warm, red, tender patch where a boot rubs; a raised bubble of clear fluid.
passages.title: Blisters and hot spots

passages.context: Foot care is keeping feet dry, clean, and padded so friction, wet, and cold do not disable you. Also called sore feet, care for feet when hiking, preventing blisters, dry socks. Look for changing to dry socks at breaks; trimmed toenails and well-fitting boots. Stop at the first hot spot, dry feet at rests, rotate socks, and use powder or tape where you rub. Air feet at night and dry socks against your body.
passages.title: Foot care on the trail

passages.context: Trench foot is damage to the feet from long exposure to wet and cold, even above freezing, and it can lead to tissue loss. Also called wet foot injury, immersion foot, feet numb and swollen from wet. Look for cold, numb, tingling feet that may look pale, blue, or red; swelling and a heavy, 'wooden' feel. Get out of wet footwear, dry and gently warm the feet, keep them raised and clean, and get medical care. Prevent it with dry socks and regular foot checks.
passages.title: Trench foot (immersion foot)

passages.context: Sunburn is skin damage from ultraviolet light that shows up as red, painful skin hours after exposure. Also called burned by the sun, red skin, sun poisoning. Look for red, hot, painful skin that appears hours later; blisters on bad burns. Get out of the sun, cool the skin with cool water, drink fluids, and use moisturizer. Cover up and keep burned skin out of the sun. Prevent it with shade, clothing, a hat, and sunscreen.
passages.title: Sunburn

passages.context: The recovery position lays an unresponsive person who is breathing on their side so the tongue falls forward and fluid drains out of the mouth. Also called lateral position, roll someone on their side, put them on their side, keep airway open. Look for person is unresponsive but breathing normally; lying on their side with the top leg bent for stability.
passages.title: Recovery position

passages.context: Heat exhaustion is the body overheating from heat and fluid loss, with heavy sweating, weakness, and dizziness. It can progress to heat stroke. Also called overheated, heavy sweating and weak, too hot and dizzy, heat sickness. Look for heavy sweating, pale or clammy skin; headache, dizziness, nausea, and weakness. Move to shade or a cool place, loosen clothes, cool with wet cloths or a fan, and give small sips of water. Rest and do not go back to hard work that day.
passages.title: Heat exhaustion

passages.context: Heat stroke is a life-threatening emergency in which the body temperature rises dangerously high and the brain is affected. Also called sunstroke, hyperthermia, very hot skin and confused, body overheated. Look for hot, red, dry or damp skin; sweating may stop; confusion, slurred speech, or odd behavior.
passages.title: Heat stroke

passages.context: Heat cramps are painful muscle spasms during or after hard work in the heat, usually from fluid and salt loss. Also called muscle cramps in the heat, leg cramps from sweating, cramping while hiking. Look for cramping in the legs, arms, or belly; heavy sweating. Stop, rest in the shade, stretch and gently massage the cramping muscle, and sip water or a drink with electrolytes.
passages.title: Heat cramps

passages.context: Staying hydrated means drinking steadily so urine stays pale; thirst lags behind, so drink before you are thirsty during work or heat. Also called how much water to drink, drink more water, thirst, pale urine. Look for pale yellow urine means good hydration; dark urine, headache, dry mouth, and tiredness mean you need more. Sip regularly through the day and more in heat, at altitude, or when ill. Add food and some salt when sweating heavily for hours.
passages.title: Staying hydrated

passages.context: Drinking far more water than you sweat out can dilute the salt in the blood, causing headache, nausea, and confusion. Also called drinking too much water, hyponatremia, overhydration. Look for headache, nausea, and bloated feeling after drinking lots of water; confusion, weakness, or seizures in severe cases. Stop drinking plain water and eat salty snacks. Get medical help for confusion or severe symptoms.
passages.title: Water intoxication (low blood sodium)

passages.context: Hypothermia is when body temperature falls below normal, and the signs progress from shivering to clumsiness and confusion to stopped shivering. Also called too cold, shivering uncontrollably, umbles, stumbling and mumbling, cold exposure. Look for mild: shivering, cold hands, clumsy; moderate: stumbling, slurred speech, apathy, confusion.
passages.title: Hypothermia: mild to severe

passages.context: Rewarming a cold person means stopping heat loss first and then adding gentle heat to the trunk, not to the limbs. Also called warm someone up, how to warm a hypothermic person, sleeping bag with another person. Look for dry insulation under and over them; warm packs or bottles wrapped in cloth at chest, armpits, groin.
passages.title: Rewarming a cold person

passages.context: Drowning is trouble breathing from submersion; the first moves are to reach the person safely, then get them breathing again. Also called near drowning, pulled from water, pulled someone out of the water, cold water immersion. Look for person in the water who is quiet, vertical, and not waving; not breathing or breathing with difficulty after being rescued.
passages.title: Drowning rescue and first aid

passages.context: An electric shock can stop the heart and cause internal burns that are bigger than they look, so every significant shock needs a medical check. Also called electrocuted, got shocked, downed power line, live wire. Look for person still touching a live source or near a downed wire; burns at the entry and exit points.
passages.title: Electrical shock

passages.context: A lightning strike victim does not carry a charge, and they often need CPR because the heart or breathing may stop. Also called struck by lightning, lightning injury, hit by lightning. Look for unconscious or not breathing; burns, confusion, hearing or vision loss. Move them to a safer place away from the storm, call for help, check breathing and pulse, and start CPR if needed. Treat burns and fractures after the person is breathing.
passages.title: Lightning strike victim

passages.context: Carbon monoxide is an invisible, odorless gas from burning fuel that keeps blood from carrying oxygen. Also called CO poisoning, gas stove in tent, generator fumes, headache and dizzy in a closed room, carbon monoxide. Look for headache, dizziness, nausea, confusion; several people ill at the same time, or pets sick.
passages.title: Carbon monoxide poisoning

passages.context: Breathing smoke can burn the airway and carry poisonous gases, even if the skin is not burned. Also called breathed smoke, house fire fumes, smoke in the lungs. Look for coughing, hoarse voice, black spit; singed nose hairs or soot around the mouth and nose. Move the person into fresh air, call emergency services, and keep them sitting upright and calm. Start CPR if they stop breathing.
passages.title: Smoke inhalation

passages.context: Burns are graded by depth: first-degree is red and dry, second-degree blisters, and third-degree is white, brown, or charred and may be numb. Also called how bad is the burn, burn blisters, charred skin, degrees of burns. Look for first degree: red, dry, painful, no blisters; second degree: blisters, moist, very painful.
passages.title: Burn severity: first, second, third degree

passages.context: A chemical burn keeps damaging skin until the chemical is removed, so flushing starts immediately. Also called acid on skin, bleach on skin, lye, caustic burn. Look for burning, redness, or blistering after contact; chemical container or label nearby. Remove contaminated clothing, brush off dry powder first, and flush with lots of cool running water for at least 20 minutes. Cover loosely and call poison control or emergency services.
passages.title: Chemical burn on the skin

passages.context: A stroke is a blocked or burst blood vessel in the brain, and fast treatment limits the damage. Also called face drooping, slurred speech, arm weakness, mini stroke, TIA. Look for Face drooping on one side; Arm weakness or drifting down. Note the time symptoms started, call emergency services immediately, keep the person calm and seated or lying with the head slightly raised, and do not give food or drink.
passages.title: Stroke signs (FAST)

passages.context: An asthma attack is a tightening of the airways that makes breathing hard and noisy. Also called wheezing, cannot breathe tight chest, inhaler, shortness of breath. Look for wheezing, coughing, tight chest; struggling to speak a full sentence. Sit the person upright, help them use their own quick-relief inhaler as directed, keep them calm, and move them away from triggers. Call emergency help if it does not ease.
passages.title: Asthma attack

passages.context: Anaphylaxis is a rapid, whole-body allergic reaction that can close the airway and drop blood pressure. Also called allergic reaction, swelling of throat, hives and trouble breathing, bee sting allergy, peanut allergy. Look for hives, swelling of the face, lips or tongue; wheezing, throat tightness, trouble breathing.
passages.title: Severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) signs

passages.context: A sting injects venom that causes pain and swelling; a honeybee leaves its stinger and venom sac in the skin. Also called bee sting, hornet sting, stung by a wasp, stinger. Look for sharp pain, a red welt, and local swelling; a small black stinger in the skin. Move away from the nest, scrape the stinger out with a card edge or fingernail, wash, and apply a cool pack. Watch for allergy signs for at least 30 minutes.
passages.title: Bee and wasp stings

passages.context: Most spiders are harmless, but black widows and brown recluses have bites that need medical care. Also called spider bite, black widow, brown recluse, venomous spider. Look for black widow: shiny black spider with a red hourglass underneath; severe cramps and sweating; brown recluse: tan spider with a violin mark; a blister that can turn into a sore.
passages.title: Black widow and brown recluse bites

passages.context: Most scorpion stings hurt like a bee sting, but the bark scorpion of the US Southwest can cause serious nerve symptoms, especially in children. Also called stung by a scorpion, bark scorpion. Look for sharp burning pain, numbness, and tingling; drooling, odd eye movements, or twitching muscles in severe stings. Wash with soap and water, apply a cool pack, keep the area still, and get medical advice or call poison control. Shake out shoes and clothes in scorpion country.
passages.title: Scorpion sting

passages.context: Poison ivy, oak, and sumac carry an oil called urushiol that causes an itchy, blistering rash on contact. Also called itchy rash from a plant, leaves of three, urushiol, contact dermatitis. Look for streaks or patches of itchy red bumps and blisters; rash shows up hours to days after touching the plant. Wash skin with soap and cool water as soon as you can, then wash clothing and tools. Cool compresses and calamine can ease the itch.
passages.title: Poison ivy, oak, and sumac rash

passages.context: Jellyfish tentacles carry stinging cells that keep firing; treat by removing them and soaking in hot water, not by rubbing. Also called jellyfish, portuguese man o war, stingray, sea urchin. Look for lines of welts where a tentacle touched; burning pain and itching. Rinse the area with seawater (not fresh water), pick off tentacles with tweezers or a gloved hand, and soak in hot water, as hot as is comfortable, for 20 to 45 minutes. Vinegar helps with some species.
passages.title: Jellyfish and marine stings

passages.context: Low blood sugar in a person with diabetes causes shakiness, sweating, and confusion and is fixed fast with sugar. Also called hypoglycemia, diabetic passed out, shaky and sweaty, insulin shock, blood sugar low. Look for shaky, sweaty, hungry, and anxious; confusion, slurred speech, or odd behavior. If they are awake and can swallow, give fast sugar such as juice, glucose tablets, or regular soda, then a snack. Call for help if it does not improve in about 15 minutes.
passages.title: Low blood sugar (diabetic emergency)

passages.context: A fever is a body temperature of about 38 C (100.4 F) or higher, usually a sign the body is fighting an infection. Also called high temperature, running a fever, hot and chills. Look for hot skin, chills, sweating, and aches; temperature above 38 C (100.4 F). Rest, drink fluids, and dress lightly. Over-the-counter fever reducers can help if used as the label says. Watch for signs of getting worse.
passages.title: Fever in an adult

passages.context: Vomiting and diarrhea are the body's way of clearing a gut infection or toxin; the main danger is dehydration. Also called stomach bug, food poisoning, traveler's diarrhea, gastroenteritis, upset stomach. Look for frequent loose stools or vomiting; dry mouth, dark urine, dizziness. Rest, take frequent small sips of clean water or oral rehydration solution, and eat bland food when you can. Wash hands carefully and keep clear of food prep.
passages.title: Vomiting and diarrhea

passages.context: Most belly pain is minor, but pain that is severe, constant, or moving to the lower right can be appendicitis or another emergency. Also called stomach ache, appendicitis, severe stomach pain, belly pain. Look for pain that starts near the navel and moves to the lower right; rigid, tender belly, fever, vomiting. Rest, take nothing by mouth if you may need surgery, and get medical care quickly if pain is severe or getting worse.
passages.title: Belly pain: when it is urgent

passages.context: When a baby is crowning and cannot be reached by help in time, you can support the delivery, keep the baby warm, and wait for emergency services. Also called baby coming now, giving birth, delivery in the field, woman in labor. Look for contractions a minute or two apart, urge to push; the baby's head is visible.
passages.title: Emergency childbirth

passages.context: A newborn loses heat quickly, so drying, warming, and watching the breathing are the first jobs. Also called baby just born, keep a newborn warm, infant born outside. Look for baby cries or breathes within seconds; wet, slippery, and cold skin. Dry the baby, wrap in warm dry cloths with the head covered, and hold skin-to-skin against the mother. Keep the face clear and note the time of birth.
passages.title: Care of a newborn

passages.context: Bleeding, severe pain, or fainting in a pregnant woman can be serious and needs medical help. Also called bleeding while pregnant, miscarriage, pregnancy emergency. Look for vaginal bleeding with cramps or pain; dizzy, pale, faint, or severe one-sided belly pain. Have her lie down on her left side, keep her warm and calm, and get emergency help. Note how many pads she is soaking.
passages.title: Heavy bleeding in pregnancy

passages.context: Altitude sickness is an illness from too little oxygen at height; mild forms ease with rest, but fluid on the lungs or brain is life-threatening. Also called AMS, HAPE, HACE, mountain sickness, can't breathe at altitude. Look for mild: headache, nausea, poor sleep, tiredness; HAPE: breathlessness at rest, wet cough, pink froth. Stop climbing, rest, drink water, and descend if symptoms are getting worse. Dangerous forms need immediate descent.
passages.title: Altitude sickness: mild versus dangerous

passages.context: For a swallowed poison, the quickest help is poison control or emergency services, who tell you exactly what to do for that substance. Also called swallowed something poisonous, child ate pills, drank cleaner, poison control. Look for an opened container, plants, berries, or pills nearby; vomiting, drowsiness, confusion, or burns around the mouth.
passages.title: Swallowed poison or overdose

passages.context: Heavy bleeding is blood that spurts, pools, soaks through cloth, or does not slow after 10 minutes of firm pressure; a minor cut slows and stops with pressure. Also called is the bleeding serious, how bad is the bleeding, bleeding will not stop, bleeding a lot. Look for spurting, pulsing, or fast flowing blood; blood soaking through several layers or pooling on the ground.
passages.title: Heavy bleeding versus a minor cut

passages.context: A tourniquet is a tight band, ideally a commercial windlass device, and a last resort for life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg when firm direct pressure has not stopped it. Also called CAT tourniquet, windlass tourniquet, TQ, strap to stop bleeding, tourniquet time. Look for life-threatening bleeding from an arm or leg; a traumatic amputation.
passages.title: How to apply a tourniquet

passages.context: If blood keeps flowing after a tourniquet is on, it is usually not tight enough or not high enough, and the fix is to tighten it or add a second one. Also called tourniquet not working, still bleeding with tourniquet, second tourniquet, tourniquet too loose. Look for blood still flowing or spurting below the band; a pulse can still be felt below it.
passages.title: Bleeding continues after a tourniquet

passages.context: Packing means pushing gauze or clean cloth deep into a bleeding wound and pressing hard on it; it is used where a tourniquet will not work, such as the neck, armpit, or groin. Also called pack the wound, gauze in the wound, hemostatic gauze, wound that tourniquet cannot reach, neck bleeding. Look for deep wound at the neck, armpit, groin, or the top of a limb; blood welling from the depth of the wound.
passages.title: Packing a wound and pressure dressing

passages.context: For an infant under one year, a choking rescue uses five back blows and five chest thrusts, not abdominal thrusts; a child over one uses abdominal thrusts like an adult. Also called baby choking, toddler choking, back blows infant, chest thrusts infant. Look for cannot cry, cough, or breathe, silent or high-pitched noise; blue lips or face.
passages.title: Choking in a child or infant

passages.context: CPR for children and infants keeps blood and oxygen moving; it is similar to adult CPR but uses less force, and breaths matter more because children often stop breathing first. Also called baby CPR, infant not breathing, child not breathing, rescue breaths for a baby. Look for not breathing or only gasping; limp and unresponsive.
passages.title: CPR for a child or infant

passages.context: An AED is a portable device that checks the heart's rhythm and, if needed, gives a shock; it talks you through each step. Also called defibrillator, automated external defibrillator, heart paddles, shock machine. Look for person is unresponsive and not breathing normally; voice prompts after you turn it on.
passages.title: Using an AED

passages.context: An opioid overdose slows or stops breathing, and naloxone (Narcan) is a medicine that can reverse it for a short time. Also called narcan, overdose, passed out from pills, blue lips pinpoint pupils, fentanyl overdose. Look for will not wake, slow or stopped breathing; blue or gray lips and skin.
passages.title: Opioid overdose and naloxone

passages.context: A fracture is a broken bone, a sprain is a stretched or torn ligament, and a dislocation is a joint forced out of place; the field answer is the same: stabilize and get care. Also called is it broken or sprained, sprain versus fracture, twisted ankle or broken ankle. Look for fracture: point pain on the bone, deformity, cannot bear weight; sprain: pain and swelling at a joint, some use possible.
passages.title: Broken bone, sprain, or dislocation?

passages.context: Babies lose heat fast, and a cold infant may have bright red, cold skin and very low energy, not just shivering. Also called baby too cold, newborn cold, bright red cold skin baby, low energy baby. Look for bright red, cold skin; very low energy, weak cry, or refusing to feed. Take the baby indoors, remove damp clothing, and hold the baby skin to skin under dry blankets, with the head and a hat covered. Warm the room. Get urgent care at once.
passages.title: Cold baby: infant hypothermia

passages.context: Frostbitten skin is numb and easily damaged; rubbing, high heat, or thawing then re-freezing makes it worse. Also called rub frostbite, thaw frozen fingers, stove on frostbite, heating pad frostbite. Look for pale, waxy, hard, or blotchy skin that is numb; tingling and then loss of feeling.
passages.title: Frostbite: what not to do

passages.context: Cold-water shock is the gasp and panic in the first minute after falling into very cold water, and it can cause drowning before hypothermia sets in. Also called fell through the ice, fell in cold water, capsized, cold shock, cold water immersion. Look for a sudden gasp, rapid breathing, and panic; swimming ability lost within minutes.
passages.title: Cold-water shock and near-drowning

passages.context: When you call 911, stay on the line and give your location and what happened; the dispatcher will tell you what to do next. Also called what to say when I call 911, how to call for help, emergency call, giving my location. Look for your exact location, with a road, landmark, or GPS coordinates; what happened and how many people are hurt.
passages.title: Talking to a 911 dispatcher

passages.context: Clear information helps a clinician decide fast: when it started, what makes it worse or better, what medicines and allergies the person has. Also called what to tell the doctor, how to explain symptoms, medical history for an emergency crew. Look for start time and how it began; what makes it better or worse.
passages.title: Describing symptoms clearly to a clinician

passages.context: For a missed dose, an expired medicine, or a drug interaction, read the label and ask a pharmacist; never share prescription drugs. Also called missed a pill, expired medicine, share a prescription, can I take this with that. Look for label directions for a missed dose; an expiration date. Check the label or the pharmacist or Poison Control line for a missed dose, and keep medicines in a cool, dry place. Ask a pharmacist before mixing medicines. Keep a list of what you take.
passages.title: Medication basics: missed dose, expired, sharing

passages.context: Lyme disease is spread by blacklegged (deer) ticks, and an expanding red rash, often with fever, chills, and aches, can appear three to thirty days after a bite. Also called bullseye rash, erythema migrans, tick fever, deer tick bite, Lyme. Look for a red expanding rash, sometimes with a clear center; fever, chills, headache, and tiredness.
passages.title: Lyme disease signs after a tick bite

passages.context: Preventing tick bites means covering skin, using repellent, and checking your whole body after being outdoors. Also called tick check, permethrin, stay safe from ticks, repellent for ticks. Look for tick season from spring through fall, with nymphs most active in late spring and summer; brush, leaf litter, and tall grass.
passages.title: Preventing tick bites

passages.context: New England has very few venomous snakes: the timber rattlesnake and the northern copperhead in a few southern areas; most snakes are harmless. Also called timber rattlesnake, northern copperhead, snake bit me, venomous snake, garter snake bite. Look for venomous bites leave two puncture marks with swelling and severe pain; timber rattlesnake has a rattle and a heavy body.
passages.title: Snakebite in New England

passages.context: A puncture wound is narrow and deep, closes quickly, and traps germs, so it can get infected and may need a tetanus shot. Also called stepped on a nail, puncture in the foot, deep puncture. Look for a small hole with little bleeding; pain that gets worse in the next days. Let it bleed a little, wash with soap and clean water, and cover. See a clinician the same day for a deep wound, a rusty or dirty object, or a wound in the foot. Ask about a tetanus shot.
passages.title: Nail or tool puncture wound

passages.context: High blood sugar builds slowly with thirst, frequent urination, tiredness, and fruity breath, and it can become a medical emergency. Also called hyperglycemia, diabetic ketoacidosis, very thirsty and frequent urination, fruity breath. Look for extreme thirst and frequent urination; nausea, belly pain, and fast deep breathing.
passages.title: High blood sugar (diabetic emergency)

passages.context: Ear or sinus pain after swimming or a cold is often a mild infection, but severe pain, fever, or discharge needs a clinician. Also called swimmer's ear, earache, sinus pressure, ear infection. Look for ear pain that hurts when you pull on it; stuffy nose and pressure around the eyes. Keep the ear dry, use a warm compress, and take over-the-counter pain medicine as the label says. See a clinician if pain lasts more than a day or two or if there is fever or drainage.
passages.title: Ear or sinus pain after a swim or a cold

passages.context: Frostnip is a mild cold injury that turns skin pale and numb but is reversible with warming; frostbite is a deeper freeze injury. Also called cold fingers pale, nose turned white, ears numb. Look for frostnip: pale or red skin that tingles and returns to normal when warmed; frostbite: hard, waxy, numb skin that stays white or gray.
passages.title: Frostnip versus frostbite

passages.context: Start CPR for anyone who is unresponsive and not breathing, or only gasping, and call 911 first. Also called should I do CPR, no pulse, not breathing what do I do, hands only CPR. Look for no response to a shout or shoulder tap; not breathing, or only occasional gasps.
passages.title: When to start CPR

passages.context: Yehsa medical entries are offline reference labels for a personal survival agent. They are not a diagnosis, a prescription, or a substitute for emergency services. In an emergency, contact local emergency services.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: Serious bleeding needs direct pressure with clean cloth and urgent human help. This note does not teach surgery or medication dosing.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: Clean water matters before wound rinsing or rehydration. Boil water when you can. This is a field reminder, not clinical instruction.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: A mosquito bite is usually a small itchy spot. Wash it with clean water. Swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing, needs a person and emergency services, not a plant.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: A tourniquet is a last resort for life-threatening limb bleeding, when direct pressure with clean cloth does not stop the blood. Put it between the wound and the heart, and note the time it went on. Do not loosen it in the field. This is not surgery and not a substitute for emergency care.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: Frostbite is frozen skin, often fingers, toes, ears, or the nose. Get to shelter and put on dry layers. Do not rub the skin, and do not rub snow on it. Warm it against healthy skin or in warm, not hot, water, and do not walk on a thawed foot if you still must travel; this is not a substitute for emergency care.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: A splint keeps a suspected broken bone still, such as a broken arm or leg. Pad it, include the joints above and below, and tie it snug enough to stop motion without cutting off circulation. Skin beyond it should stay warm and able to feel. Do not set the bone; this is not surgery or a substitute for emergency care.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: A nosebleed: sit up, lean forward, and pinch the soft part of the nose for ten minutes or more. Do not tilt the head back. Spit blood instead of swallowing it. Call emergency services if bleeding will not stop, started after a head injury, or the person is dizzy or weak.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: Choking: if an adult or child cannot cough, speak, or breathe, give abdominal thrusts until the object comes out or they become unresponsive, then start CPR and call emergency services. For an infant, use back blows and chest thrusts, not abdominal thrusts. Call emergency services.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: Start CPR when a person is unresponsive and not breathing normally. Call emergency services. Compress the center of the chest at 100 to 120 per minute. Adult depth is about 5 cm (2 inches). A child is about 5 cm. An infant is about 4 cm (1.5 inches). If you are trained, give 30 compressions then 2 breaths. This is not a certification.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: Anaphylaxis can include trouble breathing, swelling of the face or throat, or collapse. Use an epinephrine auto-injector as the label printed on the device says, into the outer thigh, and hold it for the time the label states. Call emergency services. This note gives no other drug dose.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: Shock: pale, cold, fast pulse, or confusion after injury or illness. Have the person lie down, keep them warm, and raise the legs if no injury makes that unsafe. Do not give food or drink. Call emergency services.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: During a seizure, keep the person from hitting nearby objects, do not restrain them, and do not put anything in the mouth. Time the seizure. Call emergency services if it lasts more than a few minutes, repeats, or the person is injured, pregnant, or does not wake.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: Chemical in an eye: flush with clean running water for many minutes, from the nose outward, and remove contact lenses if that is easy. Do not use drops you have not been told to use. Call emergency services or a poison center.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: Altitude sickness: headache, nausea, or unusual tiredness after going higher. Stop climbing, rest, and descend. Confusion, trouble walking, or breathlessness at rest needs emergency services and a descent. This is not a drug dose.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: Heart attack signs can include chest pressure, pain spreading to the arm, neck, or jaw, shortness of breath, sweat, or nausea. Call emergency services immediately and have the person rest. Do not wait to see if it passes. This is not a diagnosis.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: A burn: cool it with cool running water, not ice. Do not put butter, oil, or ointment on it. Cover it with a clean cloth. Call emergency services for a large burn, a burn on the face, hands, or genitals, or any burn with breathing trouble.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: Tick removal: use fine tweezers, grasp the tick close to the skin, and pull straight out with steady pressure. Do not twist, burn, or cover the tick with oil. Wash the skin. Watch for a spreading rash or fever and get medical care. This is not a diagnosis.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: Oral rehydration for dehydration from diarrhea, using clean water: one liter of water, six level teaspoons of sugar, and half a level teaspoon of salt. Sip it. Call emergency services if the person is confused, cannot drink, or is a limp infant. This is not a drug dose.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: A sprain: rest, ice wrapped in cloth, a snug compression bandage, and elevation (RICE). Do not force the joint. Call emergency services or a clinician if the limb looks deformed, will not bear weight, or the pain is severe.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: Spinal precautions: if the neck or back may be injured, do not move the person, do not twist the head, and keep them still. Call emergency services. Only move them if the place itself is immediately dangerous, and then keep the head and body in line.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: A cut may need stitches when it gapes open, is deep, is on the face, keeps bleeding through pressure, or has something stuck in it. Cover it with clean cloth and call emergency services or a clinician. This note does not teach how to stitch.
passages.title: reference

passages.context: During the greater part of the winter of 1914-15, the fighting along the western front had been almost constant, but had resulted in little that either side could justly assert to be a success. The rigors inevitable in such a mode of warfare had become almost beyond human endurance, and commanders on both sides looked forward to a more active campaign.
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: An immense amount of ammunition had been stored by the French in and around Perthes in anticipation of a forward movement; and, by the second week of February, a quarter of a million men of the French army had been assembled near that place. They were opposite a section of the German trenches which was about twelve miles long, extending from Ville-sur-Tourbe in the Argonne to the village of Souain. Early in the year this section had been held by only two divisions of Rhinelan
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: Because of the chalk formation of the soil in this section of the front, the excessive moisture of this season of the year drained rapidly, leaving exposed an undulating section on which were small forests of fir trees. The nature of the ground made it an easy matter to move troops even in winter. General Joffre took advantage of this fact, and assembled a quarter of a million men against the German lines in Champagne. This caused the German commanders to mass troops just in
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: The Germans sought to reply by bringing up twenty-two batteries of heavy guns and sixty-four field batteries; but the French gunners kept command of the field. In the twenty days' battle--from February 16 to March 7, 1915--the French won scarcely a mile of ground; but they found and buried 10,000 German dead. The French staff estimated that 60,000 German soldiers had been put out of action. The German staff admitted they had lost more men in this action than in the campaign i

passages.context: In the last week of February, 1915, it had been learned by General Joffre that General von Falkenhayn of the German forces had withdrawn from Neuve Chapelle, and the section north of La Bassée six batteries of field artillery, six battalions of the Prussian Guard, and two heavy batteries of the Prussian Guard. These had been withdrawn for the purpose of checking the supposed French advance at Perthes, as already narrated. Hence, it was known that the English, in command of Si
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: The British officers in the region of Neuve Chapelle received complete instructions on March 8, 1915, in regard to an offensive which they were to start on the 10th. These instructions were supplemental to a communication which had been sent on February 19 by the British commander in chief to Sir Douglas Haig, the commander of the First Army. Neuve Chapelle was to be the immediate objective of the prospective engagement. This place is about four miles north of La Bassée at th
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: The land in this part of France is marshy and crossed by dykes; but, to the eastward, the ground rises slowly to a ridge, on the western border of which are two spurs. Aubers is at the apex of one; and Illies at the apex of the other. Both of these villages were held by the Germans. The ridge extends northeast, beyond the junction of the spurs, from Fournes to within two miles southwest of Lille. Along the ridge is the road to Lille, Roubaix, and Tourcoing, all of which are a
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: The River Des Layes runs behind Neuve Chapelle to the southeast; and, behind the river, a half mile from the straggling village, is a wood known as the Bois du Biez. Almost at right angles to the river, on the west, the main road from Estaires to La Bassée skirts Neuve Chapelle. There is a triangle of roads north of the village where there were a few large houses with walls, gardens, and orchards. At this point the Germans had fortified themselves to flank the approaches to t
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: The German trenches were in excellent positions, but were occupied by only a comparatively few soldiers; it was the German plan to keep large bodies of troops in reserve, so that they might be sent to any sector where the need seemed most likely. They have asserted they had only four battalions in the front line here; but that statement is denied by the British.
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: The British plan of attack embraced a heavy bombardment to demoralize their enemy and prevent reenforcement. This was to be followed by an infantry attack. It was expected that the Germans would be surprised to such an extent it would be impossible for them to make much resistance. Units of the First Army were to make the main attack, supported by the Second Army. The support included a division of cavalry. Among the large force of heavy artillery for the opening bombardment
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: Three hundred and fifty guns at short range began a most terrific bombardment March 10, 1915, at 7.30 a. m. It is said that the discharges of the artillery was so frequent that it seemed as if some gigantic machine gun was in action. Shortly after this bombardment started, the German trenches were covered by a great cloud of smoke and dust and a pall of green lyddite fumes. The first line of German trenches, against which the fire was directed, became great shapeless furrows
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: This was the condition all along the line except on the extreme northern end where the artillery fire was less effective, owing, it was said, to a lack of proper preparation by the British staff. This terrific artillery fire was continued for thirty-five minutes; and then the range was changed from the first line of German trenches to the village of Neuve Chapelle itself. Thereupon the British infantry advanced and made prisoners of the few Germans left alive in the first lin
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: Where the wire entanglements had been swept away, the Second Lincolnshire and the Berkshire regiments were the first to reach the German trenches. These regiments then turned to the right and left, and thus permitted the Royal Irish Rifles and the Rifle Brigade to go on toward the village.
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: In order to understand the infantry attack in detail it is necessary to know the manner in which the British troops were distributed before they made their dash at the ruined trenches of the Germans. Two brigades of the Eighth Division, the Twenty-fifth to the right and the Twenty-third to the left, were due west of Neuve Chapelle. On a front a mile and a half long to the south of them was the Meerut Division, supported by the Lahore Division. The Garhwal Brigade was on the l
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: The trenches opposite the Twenty-fifth were taken with practically no fighting. The Germans who had manned them were either killed or too dazed to offer resistance. As has already been told, the Second Royal Berkshires and the Second Lincolns took the first line of trenches in front of them, and opened the middle of their line to permit the Second Rifle Brigade and the First Irish Rifles to dash on to the village. The British artillery range was lengthened, thereby preventing
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: These men of the Twenty-fifth Brigade found terrible scenes of destruction. The village had been knocked literally into a rubbish heap. Even the dead in the village churchyard had been plowed from their graves by the terrific bombardment.
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: The Garhwal Brigade captured the first line of trenches on the right, and the Third Gurkhas, on the southern outskirts of the village, met the Rifle Brigade. Then it dashed on to the Bois du Biez, passing another rubbish heap which once had been the hamlet known as Port Arthur.
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: The attack on the left, however, resulted less successfully for the British forces. As indicated above, the preparation for the bombardment at this part of the line had been inadequate for the purpose which the general in command had sought to achieve. Thus on the northeast corner of Neuve Chapelle the German trenches and the wire entanglements in front of them had been damaged but little. The British forces on this part of the line included the Second Devons, the Second West

passages.context: The Middlesex, on the right, met with the same obstruction and lost many of its men and officers while waiting for the British artillery to smash a way through for them. This the artillery did when word had been carried back telling of the plight of the infantry.

passages.context: The Twenty-fifth Brigade, to the south, had the good fortune to turn the flank of the Germans north of Neuve Chapelle. Then the entire Twenty-third Brigade forced its way to the orchard northeast of the village, where it met the Twenty-fourth Brigade, which included the First Worcesters, Second East Lancashires, First Sherwood Foresters, and the Second Northamptons. The Twenty-fourth Brigade had fought its way through from the Neuve Chapelle-Armentières road. As soon as this
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: There was also an additional delay in bringing up the reserves of the Fourth Corps. Thus it was not until 3.30 p. m. that three brigades of the Seventh Division, the Twentieth, Twenty-first, and Twenty-second Brigades were in their places on the left of the Twenty-fourth Brigade. Then the left moved southward toward Aubers. At the same time the Indian Corps, composed of the Garhwal Brigade and the Dehra Dun Brigade, forced its way through the Bois du Biez toward the ridge. St
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: By evening the British had gone forward as far as their artillery fire had been effective; and it was found necessary for them to stop to strengthen the new line which they had established. They had won Neuve Chapelle. They had advanced a mile. They had straightened their line, but they could go no farther.
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: On the following day, March 11, 1915, the British artillery was directed against the Bois de Biez and the trenches in the neighborhood of Pietre. The Germans, however, had recovered from the surprise of the great bombardment, and they made several counterattacks. Little progress was made on that day by either side. On that night, March 11, the Bavarian and Saxon reserves arrived from Tourcoing, and on the morning of March 12 the counterattack extended along the British front.
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: An attempt to use the British cavalry was unsuccessful on March 12. The Second Cavalry Division, in command of General Hubert Gough, with a brigade of the North Midland Division, was ordered to support the infantry offensive, it being believed that the cavalry might penetrate the German lines. When the Fifth Cavalry Brigade, under command of Sir Philip Chetwode, arrived in the Rue Bacquerot at 4 p. m., Sir Henry Rawlinson reported the German positions intact, and the cavalry
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: The attack of the Seventh Division against the Pietre Fort continued all the day of March 12, as did the attempt to take the Des Layes bridges from the Germans, who were valiantly defending their second line of trenches in the Bois du Biez. Probably the fiercest fighting of that day fell to the lot of the Twentieth Brigade, composed of the First Grenadiers, the Second Scots Guards, the Second Border Regiment, and the Second Gordons, with the Sixth Gordons, a Territorial batta
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: It was evident by the night of March 12 that the British could not gain command of the ridge and that the Germans could not retake Neuve Chapelle. Hence Sir John French ordered Sir Douglas Haig to hold and consolidate the ground which had been taken by the Fourth and Indian Corps, and suspend further offensive operations for the present. In his report General French set forth that the three days' fighting had cost the British 190 officers and 2,337 other ranks killed; 359 off

passages.context: The British soldiers who had been engaged in the fighting about Neuve Chapelle spent all of March 13, 1915, in digging trenches in the wet meadows that border the Des Layes. On the following day the two corps that had fought so valiantly were sent back to the reserve.
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: The German commanders, in the meantime, had been preparing for a vigorous counterattack. They planned to make their greatest effort fifteen miles north of Neuve Chapelle, at the village of St. Eloi, and trained a large section of their artillery against a part of the British front, which was held by the Twenty-seventh Division. The preparation of the Germans was well concealed on March 14 by the heavy mist that covered the low country. The bombardment started at 5 p. m., the
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: That night a counterattack was prepared. It was made at 2 a. m., on March 15, by the Eighty-second Brigade, which had the Eightieth Brigade as its support. The Eighty-second Brigade drove the Germans from the village and the trenches on the east. The Eightieth Brigade finished the task of regaining all of the ground that had been lost except the crater caused by the explosion of the mines. Among the regiments that made a most enviable record for themselves in this action were

passages.context: Before leaving the Neuve Chapelle engagement and what immediately followed it, it is well to give a brief survey of the actions along the line that supported it. To prevent the Germans from taking troops from various points and massing them against the main British attack, the British soldiers all along that part of the front found plenty of work to do in their immediate vicinity. Thus, on March 10, 1915, the First Corps attacked the Germans from Givenchy, but there had been
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: The attack on L'Epinette, a hamlet southeast of Armentières, was much more successful on the same day. The Seventeenth Brigade of the Fourth Division of the Third Corps advanced at noon, with the Eighteenth Brigade as its support. It advanced 300 yards on a front a half mile in length, carrying the village, which it retained in spite of all the counterattacks.
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: The work of the artillery was not confined to the main attack, for it was very effective in shelling the Quesnoy railway station east of Armentières, where German reenforcements were boarding a train for the front. The British artillery fire was effective as far as Aubers, where it demolished a tall church spire.
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: The work of the aviators, from March 10 to 12 inclusive, deserves special mention. Owing to the adverse weather conditions, it was necessary for them to fly as low as from 100 to 150 feet above the object of their attack in order to be sure of their aim. Nevertheless they destroyed one of the piers of the bridge over the Lys at Menin. This bridge carried the railroad over the river. They also wrecked the railway stations at Douai, Don, and Courtrai. The daring of the British
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: To summarize the fighting about Neuve Chapelle, it may be said that the British had advanced something more than a mile on a three-mile front, replacing the sag which had existed in their line by a sag in that of the Germans. The British had not won the ridges which were the key to Lille, but they had advanced their trenches close to those ridges. The entire moral effect was a gain for the British; but even that and the gain in advancing the front had been obtained at a too g

passages.context: The belief in the supposed superiority of the German artillery was so shaken in the minds of the General Staff as a result of the fighting on the Neuve Chapelle front that they shortly after issued an order to try a series of experiments on animals with asphyxiating gases.

passages.context: On the night of February 6, 1915, Germans exploded three mines at La Boisselle in front of the houses in the village which the French occupied, but the attempt of the Germans to advance was checked after a small amount of ground had been gained. The next day a counterattack carried out by a French company retook this ground, and inflicted a loss of 200 men. The French seized a wood north of Mesnil-les-Hurles on the night of February 7. Here the Germans had strongly establishe
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: During the first part of February, 1915, the Germans made a series of assaults on the Marie Therese works in the Argonne. Their force comprised about a brigade; but the French repulsed all attacks. Both sides suffered severe losses. On the night of February 9, there was an infantry engagement at La Fontenelle in the Ban de Sapt. Two battalions of Germans took part in the action and gained some ground which the French regained by counterattacks on the following day.
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: Actions in the Vosges continued in spite of heavy snow. The French carried Hill 937, eight hundred meters northwest of the farm of Sudelle, in the region north of Hartmannsweilerkopf.
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: About February 9, 1915, there was considerable activity on the part of the German artillery in Champagne, especially before Rheims. The city being again bombarded. There was also a lively cannonade in the region of Lens, around Albert, between the Avre and Oise, in the neighborhood of Soissons, and at Verneuil, northeast of Vailly. In Lorraine the Germans, after having pushed back the French main guard, succeeded in occupying the height of the Xon beacon and the hamlet of Nor
passages.title: The Story of the Great War, Volume V (of 12)

passages.context: Cover skin and avoid standing water when you can, so fewer mosquitoes bite. A plant on the skin does not replace that, and it does not treat diseases mosquitoes can carry.
passages.title: camp

passages.context: Camp site: pick flat ground out of a drainage, off the ridge, and clear of dead limbs. Face the opening away from the night wind. A spot near a stream is handy and also a flood risk, so step uphill a little. This is planning, not a permit to camp where rules forbid it.
passages.title: camp

passages.context: Sleep: insulation under you matters as much as the cover over you. Change out of wet clothes before you lie down, and keep a dry layer in the bag. Food and scented items stay outside the sleep spot. A closed shelter still needs air. This note does not treat cold injury.
passages.title: camp

passages.context: Kitchen: cook and store food downwind of where you sleep, and seal it so animals are not fed. Drown the fire or stove and feel for heat before you leave. Strain cloudy water, then boil it, before it goes in the pot. Known food only. This is not a foraging menu.
passages.title: camp

passages.context: Sanitation: carry waste out when the land requires it. Otherwise dig a small cathole well away from water, camp, and trails, then cover it. Soap stays out of the creek. Hands are cleaned away from the stream. This is a hygiene reminder, not a medical treatment.
passages.title: camp

passages.context: Leave the site: pack out what you carried in, put back natural cover you moved, and drown the fire until it is cold. The next person should not be able to tell you cooked there. A waypoint you saved stays on your device. Erasing the camp from the land is the point.
passages.title: camp

passages.context: The white-tailed deer is the common deer of the East, brown with a white belly and a tail it raises like a white flag when alarmed. Also called whitetail, white-tail deer, deer, buck, doe. Look for brown coat, white underside, tail raised like a white flag; bucks carry antlers from late summer to winter. Deer are the main big-game animal in New England; check your state's season and tag rules before hunting.
passages.title: White-tailed deer

passages.context: The moose is the largest deer, with a long face, a hanging dewlap, and broad flat antlers on bulls. Also called Alces, bull moose, cow moose. Look for huge with a long face, dewlap, and broad flat antlers on bulls; dark body on long pale legs. Watch from at least 50 yards (about 45 m). If one lays its ears back or raises its hackles, back away and put a tree between you.
passages.title: Moose

passages.context: The elk is a large deer with a pale rump, a dark neck, and branching antlers on bulls. Also called wapiti, Cervus canadensis, bull elk. Look for large with a pale rump and branching antlers; bugling calls in fall. Elk are rare in New England; a big brown deer there is more likely a moose or white-tailed deer.
passages.title: Elk

passages.context: The black bear is the only bear in the East, black or brown, with a straight face profile and no shoulder hump. Also called bear, American black bear, Ursus americanus. Look for black or brown with a straight muzzle and no shoulder hump; tall pointed ears. Make noise on the trail, store food and trash away from camp, and if you meet one, stand tall, talk firmly, and back away slowly.
passages.title: Black bear

passages.context: The eastern coyote is a slim, dog-like wild canine with a bushy tail carried low and pointed ears. Also called eastern coyote, coywolf, Canis latrans, brush wolf. Look for slim dog-like with a bushy low tail and pointed ears; yips and howls at night. If one comes close, make yourself big, shout, and throw something toward it.
passages.title: Coyote

passages.context: The red fox is a small wild canine with a red coat, black legs, and a white tail tip. Also called fox, Vulpes vulpes. Look for red coat, black legs, white tail tip; bushy tail longer than half its body. Watch from a distance; foxes are usually shy.
passages.title: Red fox

passages.context: The bobcat is a medium wild cat with a short bobbed tail, tufted ears, and a spotted coat. Also called wildcat, Lynx rufus, bay lynx. Look for short tail with a black tip, tufted ears, spotted coat; tail tip black on top, white below. Bobcats avoid people; enjoy the sighting from where you are.
passages.title: Bobcat

passages.context: The porcupine is a slow, round rodent covered in barbed quills. Also called porky, Erethizon dorsatum, quill pig. Look for round quill-covered body, slow waddle; chewed bark high on trees. Leave it alone and keep dogs away. A pet with quills needs a vet.
passages.title: Porcupine

passages.context: The raccoon is a gray, masked, ring-tailed animal that raids camps and trash at night. Also called coon, Procyon lotor, trash panda. Look for black mask and ringed tail; handprint-like tracks near water. Lock food away at night and keep a clean camp.
passages.title: Raccoon

passages.context: The striped skunk is a black animal with white stripes down its back that sprays a strong musk when threatened. Also called skunk, Mephitis. Look for black with white stripes down the back; stamps its feet and raises its tail before spraying. Back away slowly if it stamps or turns.
passages.title: Striped skunk
