passages.context: The beaver is a large water rodent with a flat paddle tail that builds dams and lodges. Also called American beaver, Castor canadensis. Look for flat paddle tail, dam and cut sapling stumps; tooth-chewed pointed stumps near water. Beaver ponds flood trails and make routes longer; plan around them.
passages.title: Beaver

passages.context: The snowshoe hare is a northern hare with huge furry hind feet whose coat turns white in winter. Also called varying hare, Lepus americanus, snowshoe rabbit. Look for large back feet, coat white in winter and brown in summer; brown in summer, white in winter. Hares are legal small game in many states; check your state's rules.
passages.title: Snowshoe hare

passages.context: The wild turkey is a large dark bird with a bare red-blue head and a fanned tail. Also called turkey, Meleagris gallopavo, gobbler, tom turkey. Look for large dark bird with a bare head and fanned tail; toms gobble in spring. Turkey season has its own rules; identify the bird and what is beyond it before every shot.
passages.title: Wild turkey

passages.context: The ruffed grouse is a brown or gray barred woodland bird with a fan tail and a dark neck ruff. Also called partridge, Bonasa umbellus, grouse, pa'tridge. Look for brown barred bird with a fan tail and dark neck ruff; drumming sound like a starting engine in spring. Grouse are upland game in New England; check season rules.
passages.title: Ruffed grouse

passages.context: The bald eagle is a large raptor whose adults have a white head and tail and a yellow bill. Also called eagle, Haliaeetus leucocephalus, American eagle. Look for large dark bird with a white head and tail on adults; young birds are mottled brown for four years. Watch and photograph from a distance, especially near nests.
passages.title: Bald eagle

passages.context: The great horned owl is a large owl with ear tufts, yellow eyes, and a deep hooting call. Also called hoot owl, Bubo virginianus, cat owl. Look for large owl with ear tufts and yellow eyes; white throat patch. Enjoy it from a distance, especially near nests in late winter.
passages.title: Great horned owl

passages.context: The Canada goose is a large goose with a black neck and head and a white chin strap. Also called honker, Branta canadensis, goose. Look for black neck and head with a white chin strap; V-shaped flocks with loud honking. Geese are migratory birds with federal and state season rules; check both.
passages.title: Canada goose

passages.context: The timber rattlesnake is a heavy-bodied venomous snake with a broad triangular head and a rattle on its tail. Also called timber rattlesnake, rattler, Crotalus horridus. Look for thick body, triangular head, a rattle on the tail; dark crossbands on a yellow or dark body. Rattlesnakes are rare and protected in much of New England. Back away slowly and walk around.
passages.title: Rattlesnake

passages.context: The copperhead is a venomous snake with a copper-colored head and tan hourglass bands. Also called Agkistrodon contortrix, highland moccasin. Look for copper head, tan body with hourglass bands; bands narrow on the back and wide on the sides. Copperheads live in southern New England's rocky woods. Back away slowly.
passages.title: Copperhead

passages.context: The cottonmouth is a heavy, dark venomous water snake that gapes to show a white mouth. Also called water moccasin, Agkistrodon piscivorus. Look for heavy dark water snake with a white mouth when it gapes; swims with its body high on the water. Cottonmouths do not live in New England; a dark snake in water there is almost always a northern water snake.
passages.title: Cottonmouth

passages.context: The eastern garter snake is a slim, harmless snake with three pale stripes along its body. Also called garter snake, garden snake, Thamnophis sirtalis. Look for slim, three pale stripes along the body; often basks on paths and rocks. It is harmless; let it go on its way.
passages.title: Garter snake

passages.context: The northern water snake is a common, non-venomous banded brown snake found in and near water. Also called water snake, Nerodia sipedon. Look for banded brown snake near water; round pupils. It is not venomous; give it room.
passages.title: Northern water snake

passages.context: The blacklegged tick, or deer tick, is a tiny dark tick that spreads Lyme disease, anaplasmosis, and babesiosis. Also called deer tick, Ixodes scapularis, Lyme tick. Look for tiny dark tick; adult females have an orange-red body and black plate. Check your whole body after time outside, and remove ticks with fine tweezers pulled straight out.
passages.title: Blacklegged (deer) tick

passages.context: The American dog tick is a larger brown tick with cream markings that can carry Rocky Mountain spotted fever. Also called dog tick, wood tick, Dermacentor variabilis. Look for larger brown tick with white-cream markings on the back; common in grassy fields and trail edges. Remove it with fine tweezers close to the skin and wash the bite.
passages.title: American dog tick

passages.context: The lone star tick is a reddish-brown tick whose females have one white dot on the back; its bites are linked to a red-meat allergy. Also called Amblyomma americanum, turkey tick. Look for reddish-brown tick with one white dot on the back of females; aggressive biter, spreading north. Remove it with fine tweezers close to the skin.
passages.title: Lone star tick

passages.context: The black widow is a shiny black spider with a red hourglass under its belly whose bite needs medical care. Also called widow spider, Latrodectus. Look for shiny black spider with a red hourglass underneath; messy webs under rocks, logs, and outhouse seats. Shake out gloves, boots, and firewood before use.
passages.title: Black widow

passages.context: The bald-faced hornet is a black-and-white wasp that builds a gray paper nest in trees and defends it fiercely. Also called white-faced hornet, Dolichovespula maculata. Look for black and white wasp with a grey paper nest the size of a football; nests hang from branches or eaves. Walk wide around nests.
passages.title: Bald-faced hornet

passages.context: The yellowjacket is a black-and-yellow wasp that nests in the ground and stings repeatedly. Also called yellow jacket, ground wasp, Vespula. Look for black and yellow wasp that nests underground; busy hole in the ground. Watch for ground nests when clearing a camp or trail.
passages.title: Yellowjacket

passages.context: The wild boar, or feral hog, is a dark bristly pig with a long snout that can be aggressive. Also called feral hog, feral pig, wild pig, Sus scrofa. Look for dark bristly pig with a long snout; rooted-up ground. Feral hogs are not established in New England; report one to your state wildlife agency.
passages.title: Wild boar (feral hog)

passages.context: A family emergency plan says how you will reach each other, where you will meet near home and out of the neighborhood, and who an out-of-area contact is. Also called family plan, where do we meet, meeting place, family emergency card. Look for a meeting spot near home and one farther away; an out-of-area contact everyone knows. Write the plan down, give every family member a card, and practice it twice a year.
passages.title: Family emergency plan and meeting points

passages.context: A child who is lost should stay in one place, hug a tree, make noise, and answer when called; searchers find children who stay put far faster. Also called kid lost in woods, hug a tree, child lost hiking, teach kids if lost. Look for a whistle on the child's jacket; bright clothing. Teach: stop, hug a tree, blow the whistle three times, stay put, and answer anyone calling your name. Practice it as a game.
passages.title: What to teach a child about being lost in the woods

passages.context: Children can call 911 from any phone, even a locked one, and should say what happened, where they are, and stay on the line. Also called teach kids to call 911, child emergency call, what to say to 911. Look for how to reach emergency call on your phone's lock screen; the child knows their address. Teach your address, how to place an emergency call on a locked phone, and to answer the dispatcher's questions and stay on the line.
passages.title: How a child calls 911

passages.context: Children lose heat faster than adults; an infant with hypothermia can have bright red, cold skin and very low energy. Also called baby hypothermia, infant cold, keeping kids warm, child too cold. Look for bright red, cold skin in a baby; a quiet, floppy, or very sleepy child. Dress children in one more layer than adults, cover the head, change wet clothes at once, and warm a cold child against your body in a dry blanket.
passages.title: Keeping children warm and spotting cold stress in infants

passages.context: Children dehydrate quickly with vomiting, diarrhea, heat, or fever; a dry mouth, few wet diapers, no tears, and unusual sleepiness are warning signs. Also called child dehydrated, kid fever, baby dehydration signs, when to take child to doctor. Look for fewer wet diapers or no urine for many hours; no tears when crying, a dry mouth, sunken eyes. Give small, frequent sips of fluid or oral rehydration solution, keep the child cool, and watch urine and alertness.
passages.title: Dehydration and fever in a child

passages.context: A few short rules prevent most outdoor harm to children: check for ticks, avoid leaves of three, stay within reach near water, and never touch a gun. Also called kids safety outdoors, children and guns, kids near water, kids ticks. Look for a tick check after every outing; a life jacket on near water. Teach: if you see a gun, don't touch, leave, tell an adult. Keep children within arm's reach near water and do a full tick check at night.
passages.title: Kids outdoors: ticks, poison ivy, water, and firearms

passages.context: When tap water is unsafe, infant formula should be ready-to-feed, or mixed with bottled water or water that was boiled and cooled. Also called baby formula water, boil water notice baby, formula during outage. Look for a boil-water notice; flooding near the well. Use ready-to-feed formula when you can; otherwise use bottled water or water brought to a rolling boil for one minute and cooled. Clean bottles in safe water.
passages.title: Infant formula when the water is unsafe

passages.context: A closed car heats up fast even on a mild day and can kill a child within minutes; in winter, a running car can fill with exhaust. Also called child left in car, kid in hot car, baby in car heat. Look for a child alone in a car; a sweaty, red, or unresponsive child. If you see a child alone in a hot car, call 911 at once and follow the dispatcher's directions. Make a habit of checking the back seat every time you leave the car.
passages.title: A child left in a vehicle is an emergency

passages.context: Pets need their own emergency kit and a plan for where they can stay, because many shelters only take service animals. Also called pet emergency kit, evacuate with pets, dog ate something toxic, pet poison. Look for food, water, medicines, leash, carrier, and records; a list of pet-friendly hotels or friends. Pack a pet kit, plan pet-friendly places to stay, and take pets with you if you evacuate.
passages.title: Pet kit, pet evacuation, and pet poisoning

passages.context: Children take their cue from adults; calm, simple, honest words and a job to do help them feel safer. Also called kids scared storm, calm a child, explain disaster to kids, child anxiety emergency. Look for a child clinging, crying, or very quiet; questions repeated many times. Get down to their level, say what is happening in a few words, tell them what you are doing to keep them safe, and give them a small task.
passages.title: Talking to children during an emergency

passages.context: After a disaster, families reunite fastest when everyone knows the meeting places and the out-of-area contact ahead of time. Also called find family after disaster, separated from family, reunification. Look for the planned meeting spot; an out-of-area contact who relays messages. Go to the planned meeting place, text the out-of-area contact, and register with official shelters or reunification services.
passages.title: Reuniting a family after a storm or evacuation

passages.context: A pickup plan names who can collect each child, how the school will reach you, and what happens if roads or phones are down. Also called school emergency pickup, who picks up the kids, school lockdown parent. Look for the school's emergency and release policy; backup adults on the authorized pickup list. Learn the school's plan, add backup adults to the pickup list, and tell children who may collect them.
passages.title: School or daycare pickup when phones or roads fail

passages.context: Hiking with a baby or toddler needs a carrier that fits both of you, extra warmth and sun protection for the child, and short, flexible plans. Also called hiking with a baby, child carrier backpack, toddler on trail. Look for the child's face, hands, and feet staying warm or shaded; the carrier's weight limit. Check the child often, dress them warmer than you since they are not moving, take breaks, and avoid steep or icy ground.
passages.title: Child carriers and trail safety with little ones

passages.context: In a group, life-saving medicines such as an epinephrine auto-injector or an inhaler must stay with the person who needs them, with a backup someone else knows about. Also called who carries epipen, family medicines trip, inhaler on hike. Look for an epinephrine auto-injector with the allergic person; a spare inhaler with another adult. Decide before leaving who carries what, show others where it is, and keep medicines protected from heat and freezing.
passages.title: Shared kit: who carries the meds and the inhaler

passages.context: Pets suffer in heat and cold like people do; during an outage they need shade or warmth, water, and their food and medicines. Also called dog in heat, pets cold weather, pets during outage. Look for heavy panting, drooling, or weakness in heat; shivering or lethargy in cold. Keep pets indoors with you, give plenty of water, never leave them in a parked car, and bring them when you go to a warming or cooling center that accepts pets.
passages.title: Pets in a power outage, heat, or cold

passages.context: After a close call, a death, or seeing an animal harvested, children need brief, age-appropriate words, honest answers, and permission to have feelings. Also called kid saw something scary, child grief, explaining death to child, child after hunting harvest. Look for questions, drawings, or play about the event; clinginess or nightmares. Answer simply and honestly, keep routines, and let them talk or not; tell them it is okay to feel sad or confused.
passages.title: Helping children after a hard event

passages.context: Many states have youth days or apprentice licenses with special rules on age, supervision, and hunter education; they change by year. Also called youth deer season, kids hunting license, apprentice license. Look for the state's minimum age and supervision distance; a hunter-education course requirement. Read your state agency's current youth-hunting page and follow its supervision rules.
passages.title: Youth seasons and mentored hunts

passages.context: A teenager in crisis needs an adult who listens calmly, takes their words seriously, and connects them with help. Also called teen depressed, teenager suicidal, help my teen. Look for withdrawal, giving things away, or talk of death; sudden changes in sleep, school, or friends. Listen without judging, ask directly about suicide if worried, lock up guns and medicines, and call or text 988 together.
passages.title: Supporting a teenager in crisis

passages.context: A small paper card with emergency contacts, allergies, medicines, and conditions helps responders when a phone is locked or dead. Also called medical info card, emergency contacts on paper, ICE contact. Look for names and numbers of two contacts; allergies, medicines, and conditions. Make a card for each family member, update it when medicines change, and add emergency contacts to your phone's lock-screen medical info.
passages.title: Emergency contact and medical card

passages.context: Older adults are at higher risk in heat, cold, and outages, especially if they live alone or rely on medical devices. Also called check on elderly parent, older neighbor heat, senior in power outage. Look for no answer by phone during an outage or heat wave; confusion, weakness, or a cold or hot home. Call or visit twice a day during extreme weather or outages, help them reach a cooling or warming center, and make sure they have water and medicines.
passages.title: Checking on older relatives and neighbors

passages.context: Drowning is quick and silent; children need a watcher whose eyes stay on them and a life jacket near open water. Also called kids drowning, child near pond, life jacket kids, swimming safety kids. Look for a designated adult watcher with no phone; a properly fitted life jacket. Name one adult watcher at a time, keep young children within arm's reach, and use life jackets on boats and near rivers and ponds.
passages.title: Children and water

passages.context: A safe fire site is on bare mineral soil, clear of overhanging branches, dry grass, and roots, and downwind from your shelter. Also called where to build a fire, fire ring, keep a fire from spreading, fire pit. Look for bare soil or sand, or an existing ring; a cleared circle about 10 feet (3 m) wide. Scrape away leaves and duff to bare soil, build a ring of rocks, keep water or a shovel at hand, and keep it small. Check local rules first.
passages.title: Choosing a fire site

passages.context: Tinder is fine dry material that catches a spark, kindling is pencil-sized sticks that carry the flame, and fuel is the larger wood that burns for hours. Also called what is tinder, what burns best, fire materials, birch bark, fatwood. Look for tinder: birch bark, fatwood shavings, dry grass, cattail fluff, cotton with petroleum jelly; kindling: dry twigs from pencil lead to thumb thick.
passages.title: Tinder, kindling, and fuel

passages.context: A teepee fire is a cone of kindling leaned over a nest of tinder, lit from the windward side so the flame climbs. Also called how to start a campfire, teepee fire lay, start a fire. Look for tinder bundle in the center; kindling leaning inward like a tent. Place the tinder bundle, lean kindling around it, leave a gap on the windward side, light the tinder, and add small fuel as it catches. Blow gently at the base and add bigger pieces slowly.
passages.title: Building and lighting a basic fire (teepee)

passages.context: In rain, use dry material from under cover: dead branches still on trees, inner bark, and shaved wood, and protect the flame under a tarp. Also called fire in the rain, wet wood fire, damp tinder, fire in snow. Look for dead lower branches that snap; split wet logs to reach dry centers.
passages.title: Starting a fire in rain or with wet wood

passages.context: A fire in snow needs a platform of green logs or stones so it does not sink and go out. Also called fire on snow, build a platform for a fire. Look for a platform of green logs, flat rocks, or a layer of sticks; a windbreak. Stamp down the snow, lay a log platform, and build the fire on top. Keep dry tinder against your body, and feed it slowly.
passages.title: Starting a fire in snow

passages.context: A fire is out only when the ashes are cold to the touch; drown it, stir it, and drown it again. Also called put out the campfire, drown the fire, cold fire, douse. Look for steam or hissing means it is still hot; no glowing embers. Let the fire burn down, pour water on the embers, stir the ashes and soil with a stick, and add more water until nothing hisses. Feel for heat with the back of your hand.
passages.title: Putting a fire out completely

passages.context: A camp stove is more controlled and leaves less trace than an open fire, but any stove, grill, or charcoal burner must never be used indoors, in a tent, or in a garage. Also called cook on a stove, charcoal grill indoors, camping stove safety. Look for stoves burn liquid or gas fuel; charcoal makes carbon monoxide. Cook outdoors on a stable, flat surface, away from tents and dry grass, and have water handy. Let it cool before refueling.
passages.title: Camp stove versus open fire

passages.context: Fire rules vary by state, town, and land, and bans are common in dry or windy weather, so check the official source before you light one. Also called can I build a fire, burn ban, campfire permit. Look for a burn ban or a red flag warning; state, town, or land-manager rules. Check with the local fire department, the state forest service, or the land manager, and follow any ban. If fires are banned, use a stove only if rules allow.
passages.title: Is a fire legal here? Fire bans and permits

passages.context: Never burn poison ivy, treated lumber, painted wood, plastic, or trash; the smoke is toxic. Also called toxic smoke, burn poison ivy, treated lumber, trash fire. Look for poison ivy smoke carries irritating oil; treated lumber has chemicals. Burn only clean, dry, untreated wood. Pack out trash.
passages.title: What not to burn

passages.context: Smoke drifts downwind, so sit upwind or to the side, and dry wood burns cleaner. Also called smoke in my face, sit upwind of a fire, smoky fire. Look for smoke blowing toward your seat; a smoky fire from wet wood. Move your seat upwind, burn dry wood, and keep the fire small. If it keeps smoking, stir and add dry fuel.
passages.title: Smoke, wind, and where to sit

passages.context: A signal fire is a fire built to be seen from a distance, with green boughs for white smoke by day and bright fuel at night. Also called fire to be found, smoke signal, three fires. Look for three fires in a triangle is a distress signal; green leaves make dense smoke. Build it on an open spot, keep tinder dry and ready, and light it when an aircraft or searchers are close. Add green boughs for smoke by day.
passages.title: Signal fire

passages.context: A ferrocerium rod throws hot sparks when scraped, and it works wet; matches and lighters are easier but fail when wet or empty. Also called how to use a ferro rod, fire steel, waterproof matches, bic lighter. Look for scrape the rod down with a sharp spine, keeping it close to the tinder; carry two ways to light. Hold the rod near the tinder and pull the striker backward fast. Carry a lighter, matches in a waterproof case, and a ferro rod as a backup.
passages.title: Ferro rod, matches, and lighters

passages.context: A viable ember is glowing red and spreads when you blow on it; a dead ember is black and cool. Also called viable ember, char cloth, keep a fire overnight. Look for a bright orange glow when blown on; char cloth or punky wood catches a spark. Place the ember in a nest of fine tinder, fold the tinder around it, and blow gently until it flames. Bank a fire at night with large logs and ash.
passages.title: Keeping and moving an ember

passages.context: If you are hungry in the woods, eat the food you carried and focus first on water, shelter, warmth, and being found, because a person can go weeks without food but only days without water. Also called I am hungry, no food in the woods, need to eat, starving lost. Look for a hunger that feels urgent but is not an emergency; packed food, even small amounts.
passages.title: Hungry in the woods

passages.context: The danger zone is 40 to 140 F (4 to 60 C), where bacteria multiply fast, so perishable food should not stay out more than two hours, or one hour above 90 F. Also called how long can food sit out, bacteria grow in food, two hour rule, food temperature danger zone. Look for perishable food left out on a counter or picnic table; food not kept cold in a cooler.
passages.title: Danger zone: 40 to 140 F

passages.context: Use a food thermometer: 165 F (74 C) for poultry and leftovers, 160 F (71 C) for ground meats and egg dishes, and 145 F (63 C) for whole cuts of meat and fish with a three-minute rest. Also called what temperature to cook chicken, how done should venison be, meat thermometer, ground meat temperature. Look for poultry and reheated food: 165 F; ground beef, pork, and ground game: 160 F.
passages.title: Safe minimum cooking temperatures

passages.context: Leftovers are safe for three to four days in the fridge and picnic or cooler food is safe only if it stayed at 40 F or below; when in doubt, throw it out. Also called is this food still good, leftovers how long, cooler food melted ice, can I eat this. Look for how long it sat in the danger zone; a cooler with ice still present and food cold.
passages.title: Are leftovers, picnic food, or cooler food still safe?

passages.context: Wash hands and tools, keep raw meat separate from ready-to-eat food, and cook to a safe temperature. Also called wash hands before eating, keep raw meat separate, clean cutting board outdoors. Look for hands washed with soap or sanitizer; separate cutting boards and knives. Wash hands with soap and treated water before touching food, bag raw meat separately, wash utensils, and keep the cooler in shade.
passages.title: Food hygiene in the field

passages.context: A closed refrigerator keeps food safe about 4 hours without power; a full freezer holds for about 48 hours (24 if half full) if the door stays shut. Also called power outage food, how long does a fridge stay cold, freezer without power, throw out food. Look for a thermometer in the fridge at 40 F or below; ice crystals still in the freezer food.
passages.title: Food in the fridge and freezer during an outage

passages.context: Safe jerky starts with heating the meat to a safe internal temperature before or during drying, and the drying alone does not kill bacteria. Also called dry meat, venison jerky, dehydrating meat. Look for lean meat sliced thin; heat to 160 F (71 C), poultry to 165 F, then dry at 130 to 140 F (54 to 60 C). Follow USDA guidance: marinate in the fridge, steam or oven-heat to the right internal temperature, then dry. Store in a cool dry place.
passages.title: Making jerky safely

passages.context: Low-acid foods such as meat and vegetables must be canned in a pressure canner following the USDA guide, because boiling-water canning cannot make them safe from botulism. Also called canning venison, botulism, low-acid canning, pressure canner. Look for a pressure canner with a tested gauge; a bulging lid, spurting liquid, or a bad smell. Follow the USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning for your food, jar size, and altitude. Check each jar seal before storage.
passages.title: Home canning: pressure canner for meat and vegetables

passages.context: Food allergies can cause hives, swelling, or trouble breathing within minutes; carry any prescribed epinephrine and tell your group. Also called food allergy outdoors, allergic reaction to nuts, epinephrine on a trip. Look for hives, swelling of the lips or tongue, wheezing; vomiting or dizziness after eating. Know your allergens, tell your group, carry medicine, and avoid new wild foods. Use epinephrine as prescribed and call 911.
passages.title: Allergies to wild or familiar foods

passages.context: Gut and chill fish quickly; cook it to 145 F; spoiled fish smells sour, feels slimy, and has cloudy eyes. Also called how to clean a fish, is the fish bad, fish smell. Look for fresh: clear eyes, firm flesh, mild smell; spoiled: sour smell, slime, sunken or cloudy eyes. Gut the fish soon after catching, keep it on ice, wash your hands, and cook it to 145 F. Check the state health department's fish advisories for mercury and other contaminants.
passages.title: Cleaning fish and spoilage signs

passages.context: Shellfish can carry toxins from algal blooms, and cooking does not remove them, so follow the official closure notices. Also called clams closed, paralytic shellfish poisoning, red tide, mussels safe. Look for a posted closure or red tide notice; numbness around the mouth after eating shellfish. Check the state shellfish closure page before you harvest; if you cannot confirm that the area is open, do not eat shellfish from it.
passages.title: Shellfish closures and red tide

passages.context: The day-hike essentials are the few items that let you get through an unplanned night: navigation, light, sun protection, first aid, a knife, fire, shelter, extra food, extra water, and extra clothes. Also called ten essentials, what to bring hiking, hiking checklist, day pack list. Look for map and compass as well as a phone; headlamp with spare batteries. Pack the same essentials for every hike, even a short one, and leave a trip plan with someone at home.
passages.title: Day-hike essentials checklist

passages.context: A deer-hunt day kit covers the hunt itself, getting an animal out, and getting yourself home: license and tags, orange, a sharp knife, gloves, a drag rope, light, water, and first aid. Also called what to bring deer hunting, hunting pack list, deer hunting gear checklist. Look for license, tags, and a pen or zip ties for tagging; hunter orange hat and vest.
passages.title: Deer-hunt day kit

passages.context: A 72-hour kit holds what each person needs for three days without help: water, food, light, radio, first aid, medicines, warmth, copies of documents, and cash. Also called go bag, bug out bag, 72 hour kit, emergency kit, car emergency kit. Look for a gallon of water per person per day; a week of prescription medicines where possible.
passages.title: 72-hour bag, car kit, and home outage kit

passages.context: When a key item is left behind, safer substitutes and a changed plan beat improvising something risky: a phone light in short bursts, a multi-tool or sharp-edged stone, and turning back before dark. Also called forgot my knife, no flashlight, forgot lighter, no fire starter, improvise gear. Look for phone battery level; how much daylight is left. Shorten the trip, start back early, save phone battery for calls and short light, and borrow from a partner.
passages.title: Forgot your knife, light, or fire starter

passages.context: Layers let you adjust warmth: a base layer that moves sweat, an insulating layer, and a wind and rain shell; wool and synthetics stay warm when damp, while wet cotton pulls heat away fast. Also called layering, cotton kills, what to wear hiking, wool vs cotton, base layer. Look for cotton jeans or a cotton hoodie on a cold, wet day; shivering when you stop.
passages.title: Clothing layers: wool and synthetics versus cotton

passages.context: A headlamp keeps your hands free; spare batteries or a charged backup, and a dim red mode that protects night vision, make it last the night. Also called headlamp, red light mode, spare batteries, flashlight for camping. Look for batteries tested before the trip; a red or dim setting. Carry a headlamp and spares on every outing, keep batteries warm in cold weather, and use red mode around camp and when reading a map.
passages.title: Headlamp, spare batteries, and red mode

passages.context: Safe knife use means cutting away from your body and others, keeping a blood circle clear around you, and keeping the blade sharp so it does not slip. Also called knife safety, sharpen a knife, cut away from yourself, dull knife. Look for a clear arm's length around you; a firm grip and a stable work surface. Cut away from your body, close or sheath the knife when not using it, and sharpen at a steady, shallow angle on a stone or rod.
passages.title: Knife safety and a basic edge

passages.context: Hollow-fiber water filters must be kept from freezing once wet, because ice can crack the fibers without any visible sign and let germs through. Also called hollow fiber filter frozen, sawyer filter care, backflush filter, water filter cold. Look for a filter used on a cold trip; slower flow over time. In freezing weather keep a used filter in an inside pocket and in your sleeping bag at night, and backflush it as the maker directs.
passages.title: Water filter care

passages.context: A useful first-aid kit matches your trip and training: bandages and gauze, tape, gloves, blister care, pain relievers, personal medicines, and for bleeding, pressure dressings and a commercial tourniquet if you have trained with it. Also called first aid kit list, what to put in a first aid kit, trauma kit, IFAK. Look for personal medicines and an epinephrine auto-injector if prescribed; gloves and a pressure dressing.
passages.title: First-aid kit contents

passages.context: Camp stoves and fuel are safe used outdoors in open air, set on a stable surface away from tents and brush, with fuel stored cool and closed. Also called camp stove safety, propane safety, white gas stove, cooking in a tent. Look for a stable, flat base; no tent fabric, overhanging branches, or dry grass nearby. Cook outside, light the stove before leaning over it, let it cool before refueling, and pack fuel apart from food.
passages.title: Stove and fuel safety

passages.context: Blisters come from friction, heat, and moisture; boots that fit, dry socks, and treating hot spots early prevent most of them. Also called blisters hiking, hiking boot fit, hot spot on foot, prevent blisters. Look for a warm, rubbing hot spot; heel lifting in the boot. Break boots in before a trip, wear wool or synthetic socks, stop at the first hot spot, and cover it with tape or moleskin.
passages.title: Boot fit and blister prevention

passages.context: A sleeping bag's temperature rating is a lab estimate; most people need a bag rated colder than the night, plus an insulated pad under them. Also called sleeping bag rating, how warm a sleeping bag, sleeping pad R value, cold at night camping. Look for the comfort versus limit rating; a pad's insulation (R-value) for cold ground. Choose a bag rated below the expected low, add a warm pad, wear a dry hat and base layer, and eat before bed.
passages.title: Sleeping bag temperature ratings

passages.context: A pack fits when the hip belt carries most of the weight on the hip bones and the shoulder straps hug without carrying the load. Also called backpack fit, hip belt, pack hurts shoulders, adjust a pack. Look for hip belt centered on the hip bones; load lifters snug at an angle. Loosen everything, buckle the hip belt first, then snug the shoulder straps, load lifters, and sternum strap. Pack heavy items close to your spine.
passages.title: Fitting a backpack

passages.context: A small repair kit of tape, cord, a needle and strong thread, safety pins, and a few zip ties fixes most broken straps, torn shells, and gear failures. Also called repair kit, fix a torn jacket, broken strap, duct tape repair. Look for duct or repair tape wrapped on a bottle or pole; spare cord and a buckle. Patch holes with tape on both sides, sew or pin torn straps, lash broken parts with cord, and keep a wet sleeping bag in a dry bag.
passages.title: Field repair: tape, cord, and needle

passages.context: A length of strong cord lets you hang a tarp, rig a clothesline, lash a splint, or hang food; knowing a few knots makes it useful. Also called paracord, what rope to carry, cordage, rope for camping. Look for about 50 feet of thin, strong cord; rope rated for the job if it holds people. Carry cord for camp jobs and learn a bowline, a taut-line hitch, and two half hitches.
passages.title: Rope and cordage basics

passages.context: Binoculars help you identify animals and people before acting; a rangefinder measures distance to keep shots within your practiced range. Also called binoculars, rangefinder, glassing, how far is that deer. Look for a steady rest when glassing; identifying the whole animal. Glass from a rest, range a few landmarks around your stand, and use binoculars, not a rifle scope, to look at things you are not sure of.
passages.title: Binoculars and rangefinders in practice

passages.context: Trekking poles take strain off knees on descents, add balance on stream crossings and ice, and can hold up a tarp. Also called hiking poles, walking sticks, trekking pole height. Look for elbow at about a right angle on flat ground; longer for downhill, shorter for uphill. Adjust the length to the slope, use the straps correctly, and plant poles ahead on crossings.
passages.title: Trekking poles

passages.context: A folding saw is safer and more efficient than a hatchet for most camp wood; both need a clear swing zone and a stable work position. Also called hatchet safety, folding saw, chopping wood safely, axe safety. Look for a clear arc with no people or branches; wood on a stable base, not held by your foot. Saw dead, down wood, kneel or stand so a missed swing goes into the ground, and sheath tools when done.
passages.title: Saw and hatchet safety

passages.context: Winter trails need traction such as microspikes or snowshoes, insulated boots, extra layers, and more daylight planning. Also called snowshoes, microspikes, ice cleats, winter hiking gear. Look for ice under snow on trails; deep snow that makes you posthole. Carry traction, a warm spare layer, an insulated bottle, and a headlamp, and turn back early.
passages.title: Winter travel gear

passages.context: A phone drains fast in cold and when searching for signal; a charged power bank and battery-saving settings keep it working for calls and maps. Also called phone battery dying, power bank, save phone battery, charge phone outdoors. Look for battery level and temperature; airplane mode when you don't need signal. Keep the phone warm in an inside pocket, turn on low-power or airplane mode, dim the screen, and carry a charged power bank.
passages.title: Phone battery and backup power

passages.context: Satellite SOS devices and some phones can send an emergency message from places with no cell signal; a personal locator beacon alerts search and rescue directly. Also called satellite SOS, personal locator beacon, PLB, inReach, emergency beacon. Look for a clear view of the sky; the device registered and tested before the trip. Learn how to send an SOS before you need it, keep it on your body, and use it only for real emergencies.
passages.title: Satellite SOS and messengers

passages.context: A whistle carries farther than your voice and takes little energy; a signal mirror flashes sunlight to aircraft or searchers miles away. Also called emergency whistle, signal mirror, three whistle blasts. Look for three blasts or three flashes as a distress signal; a whistle on the pack strap or jacket. Blow three blasts and repeat; aim the mirror flash at aircraft or distant searchers using your fingers as a sight.
passages.title: Whistle and signal mirror

passages.context: EPA-registered repellents such as DEET, picaridin, or oil of lemon eucalyptus on skin, and permethrin on clothing, reduce tick and mosquito bites. Also called bug spray, DEET, permethrin, picaridin, mosquito repellent. Look for the EPA registration on the label; permethrin for clothes and gear, never skin. Use repellent on exposed skin as the label directs, treat boots and pants with permethrin, and do a tick check after.
passages.title: Insect repellent and tick-treated clothing

passages.context: How much water you need depends on heat, effort, and distance; a rough start is about a half liter per hour of moderate hiking, more in heat. Also called how much water hiking, water bottles, hydration bladder. Look for dark urine or thirst; hot, dry, or high-altitude conditions. Carry enough to reach the next sure source plus extra, and a filter or tablets to treat more.
passages.title: How much water to carry

passages.context: Before a hunt you need a valid license and any tags for the animal, the hunter orange your state requires, and this season's official rules, which change every year. Also called hunting license, deer tag, what do I need to hunt, hunter orange, blaze orange. Look for license and tags on you, not at home; orange hat and vest where the state requires it.
passages.title: Before you hunt: license, tags, orange, and this year's rules

passages.context: Legal shooting light is the window each day when hunting is allowed; many states use about 30 minutes before sunrise to 30 minutes after sunset, but the exact rule is set by each state and sometimes by species. Also called shooting hours, legal shooting time, half hour before sunrise, when can I shoot. Look for sunrise and sunset for your exact spot; the state's own rule for the species.
passages.title: Legal shooting light

passages.context: Field firearm safety comes down to four habits: treat every gun as loaded, keep the muzzle pointed in a safe direction, keep your finger off the trigger until you are ready to shoot, and be sure of your target and what is beyond it. Also called gun safety, hunting gun safety, muzzle control, treat every gun as loaded, firearm rules. Look for muzzle never sweeps a person, including yourself; finger rests along the frame, outside the trigger guard.
passages.title: Firearm safety in the field

passages.context: Before any shot you must be certain of the species, sex if it matters for your tag, and that a safe backstop such as rising ground stops the bullet; anything uncertain means no shot. Also called identify before you shoot, not sure what it is, is it a deer, backstop, what is behind the target. Look for whole animal seen, not just a patch of brown or a sound; no house, road, trail, or person in the line of fire.
passages.title: Know your target and what is beyond it

passages.context: An ethical shot aims at the heart and lungs from a broadside or slightly quartering-away angle within the range you have practiced, so the animal goes down quickly. Also called where to shoot a deer, ethical shot, vital zone, heart lung shot, after the shot. Look for the animal standing still and broadside; a clear lane with no branches in the path.
passages.title: Shot placement and what to do after the shot

passages.context: Following a hit deer means starting at the spot it stood, finding hair and blood, and moving slowly from sign to sign while marking each spot. Also called blood trail, tracking a wounded deer, following blood, lost blood trail, how long to wait before tracking. Look for bright red, frothy blood often means a lung hit; dark blood or green matter can mean a gut hit and a longer wait.
passages.title: Tracking a hit deer and reading a blood trail

passages.context: When a hit animal cannot be found, the ethical next steps are a careful grid search, a second person's eyes, and, where the state allows it, a leashed tracking dog. Also called can't find my deer, lost the blood trail, wounded deer lost, deer ran off. Look for the last marked sign; water, thick cover, and downhill paths nearby.
passages.title: When you cannot find the animal

passages.context: Field dressing removes the internal organs soon after the kill so the body heat can escape and the meat cools quickly. Also called gutting a deer, field dress, clean a deer, how to gut a deer. Look for gloves on, sharp knife, clean water or wipes; belly opened shallow so the gut is not cut. Tag the animal first if your state requires it, open the body from the pelvis toward the ribs with the blade edge up, remove the organs, then prop the cavity open in shade.
passages.title: Field dressing a deer

passages.context: Game meat stays safe when it is cooled below 40 °F (4 °C) quickly; in warm weather that means skinning, quartering, and icing within hours. Also called meat care warm weather, is my deer meat spoiled, hanging a deer, cooling venison, game meat spoiled. Look for air temperature above 40 °F means the clock is running; a sour or rotten smell, slime, or green color means spoiled.
passages.title: Keeping game meat cool and spotting spoiled meat

passages.context: Chronic wasting disease is a fatal prion disease of deer, elk, and moose; no human case has been confirmed, but health agencies advise people not to eat meat from an infected animal. Also called CWD, chronic wasting disease, zombie deer, sick looking deer, deer disease. Look for a thin, drooling, stumbling, or unafraid deer; animals found dead.
passages.title: Chronic wasting disease (CWD) and deer

passages.context: Game meat is safest cooked to a measured temperature: whole cuts of venison to at least 145 °F (63 °C) with a 3-minute rest, ground venison to 160 °F (71 °C), and wild birds to 165 °F (74 °C). Also called venison temperature, cook deer meat, ground venison temperature, wild game cooking. Look for a food thermometer in the thickest part; ground meat cooked through. Use a thermometer, keep raw game apart from cooked food, and wash hands and boards after handling raw meat.
passages.title: Cooking venison and wild game safely

passages.context: Tree-stand safety means staying attached to the tree from the moment you leave the ground until you are back on it, with a full-body harness and a lifeline or tether. Also called tree stand, deer stand fall, safety harness, full body harness, climbing a stand. Look for full-body harness worn and connected; stand straps and chains checked before each season.
passages.title: Tree-stand safety

passages.context: Crossing a fence, ditch, log, or stream with a firearm is safe only with the action open and the gun unloaded, set down on the far side with the muzzle pointed away. Also called crossing a fence with a gun, climbing over a log with a gun, crossing a stream with a rifle. Look for action open and chamber empty; muzzle pointed away from you and others.
passages.title: Crossing fences and obstacles with a firearm

passages.context: Tularemia is a bacterial disease people can catch from handling or eating rabbits, hares, and rodents; gloves and thorough cooking prevent most cases. Also called rabbit fever, tularemia, cleaning rabbits, squirrel hunting safety. Look for a rabbit or squirrel that is slow, sick, or found dead; white spots on the liver. Wear gloves when skinning and cleaning, cook the meat thoroughly, and wash hands and tools afterward.
passages.title: Small game: rabbits, squirrels, and tularemia

passages.context: Ducks, geese, and other migratory birds are hunted under federal rules plus state rules, which differ from deer rules, including shot type and a federal duck stamp for many hunters. Also called duck hunting rules, goose hunting, migratory bird hunting, duck stamp, waterfowl regulations. Look for a federal duck stamp and state permits where required; non-toxic shot required for waterfowl.
passages.title: Waterfowl and migratory birds have their own rules

passages.context: Turkey hunting has its own risks because hunters wear camouflage and use calls, so another hunter can mistake a person for a bird. Also called turkey hunting, spring turkey safety, gobbler hunting, turkey call safety. Look for no red, white, or blue clothing, which can look like a gobbler's head; a tree trunk wider than your shoulders at your back.
passages.title: Turkey hunting safety

passages.context: Quartering means cutting a large animal into its four legs plus the backstraps, neck, and other meat so it can be carried out in loads and cooled faster. Also called quarter a deer, pack out meat, gutless method, boning out a deer. Look for clean game bags for each quarter; a sharp knife and a spare blade. Skin one side at a time, take the front and hind quarters, backstraps, and tenderloins, bag each piece, and hang or lay the bags in shade to cool before carrying.
passages.title: Quartering and packing out game

passages.context: Skinning removes the hide so meat can cool and stay clean; hanging lets the carcass cool and drain in cold, shaded, animal-proof conditions. Also called skin a deer, hang a deer, how long to hang venison, deer gambrel. Look for a stable gambrel or rope and a strong limb or beam; air at or below 40 °F (4 °C) for hanging. Hang by the hind legs or the head, skin from the top down with the blade edge out, and keep the carcass cold and covered from flies and animals.
passages.title: Skinning and hanging a deer

passages.context: Home butchering divides a deer into a few simple groups: backstraps and tenderloins for steaks, hind-quarter roasts, shoulder and neck for stew, and trim for grinding. Also called butcher a deer, venison cuts, backstrap, tenderloin, deer processing at home. Look for silver skin and fat trimmed off; a clean, cold work surface. Work cold and clean, trim fat, silver skin, and bloodshot meat, wrap tightly, label, and freeze.
passages.title: Basic venison butchering cuts

passages.context: Most states require you to tag an animal right away, keep the tag with it during transport, and report or check in the harvest within a set time. Also called tag a deer, check in deer, register harvest, transport deer legally. Look for the tag filled out and attached as your state requires; the state's online, phone, or station check-in. Read your state agency's current tagging and check-in page before the season and follow it exactly.
passages.title: Tagging, transport, and checking in game

passages.context: If you hunt where chronic wasting disease is found, ask a processor to process your animal by itself so its meat is not mixed with others. Also called deer processor CWD, individual processing, commercial processing venison. Look for the processor's policy on batch versus individual processing; test results before you eat the meat. Ask for individual processing, get the animal tested, and keep the meat frozen and unused until the result comes back.
passages.title: Using a processor when CWD is a concern

passages.context: Getting an animal out of water, swamp, or thick cover comes after your own safety: cold water and deep mud can kill. Also called deer in the water, deer in a swamp, retrieve deer thick brush. Look for water depth, current, and temperature; ice that may not hold. Bring a partner and a rope, wait for light if needed, and reach the animal from shore or shallow water where you can.
passages.title: Recovering game in water or thick cover

passages.context: A ground blind hides you at ground level, but it also hides you from other hunters, so safe setup matters. Also called ground blind, pop-up blind, hunting blind safety. Look for orange on the outside of the blind where required; a clear, safe shooting lane. Put orange on and around the blind as your state requires, know your shooting lanes and backstops, and keep the gun pointed out the window only when ready.
passages.title: Ground blind safety

passages.context: Mentoring a new or young hunter means close supervision, short trips, and teaching safety before success. Also called take a kid hunting, mentor hunt, youth hunter, new hunter safety. Look for the new hunter within arm's reach when handling a gun; a completed hunter-education course where required. Keep sessions short and comfortable, review the firearm rules often, and check your state's youth and apprentice rules.
passages.title: Hunting with a young or new hunter

passages.context: Black bears are drawn to carcasses, gut piles, and camp food, and a moose can charge if crowded, especially a cow with a calf or a bull in the rut. Also called bear at my deer, bear near camp, moose charge, bear safety hunting. Look for fresh bear sign near a gut pile or meat pole; a moose with ears back and hackles raised. Hang meat away from sleeping areas, store food sealed, approach a kill carefully and make noise, and give moose plenty of room.
passages.title: Black bear and moose around camps and carcasses

passages.context: Birds keep best when the crop and entrails are removed soon after the kill and the body is cooled. Also called clean a turkey, gut a pheasant, field dress grouse, dress a duck. Look for gloves on; crop and intestines removed. Remove the entrails and crop, wipe the cavity, and cool the bird quickly; pluck or skin at home.
passages.title: Field dressing birds

passages.context: Lead bullets can break into small fragments in meat, and scavengers such as eagles can be poisoned by lead in gut piles; non-lead options exist. Also called lead bullet fragments, copper bullets, non-toxic shot, lead in venison. Look for fragments spread several inches from the wound channel; federal non-toxic shot rules for waterfowl. Trim generously around the wound channel, consider copper or other non-lead ammunition, and follow any rules where you hunt.
passages.title: Lead versus non-lead ammunition

passages.context: Ethical hunting means taking only shots you can make cleanly, using the animal well, and respecting landowners, other hunters, and the law. Also called hunting ethics, fair chase, wanton waste, respect landowners. Look for permission in hand on private land; a plan to recover and use the meat. Practice before the season, pass on doubtful shots, recover and use what you take, and leave gates and land as you found them.
passages.title: Hunting ethics: no waste, respect for land and people

passages.context: Hunting on private land needs the owner's permission, and posting and trespass rules differ from state to state; Yehsa has no property-owner map. Also called hunting private land, landowner permission, posted land, trespass hunting. Look for posted signs or paint marks on trees; a written or verbal permission you can show. Ask permission early, carry the owner's contact, learn your state's posting rules, and check official public-land maps.
passages.title: Land access, permission, and trespass

passages.context: Trapping usually needs its own license or education course and has strict rules on trap types, placement, checking times, and seasons. Also called trapping license, how to trap, trap rules, snare rules. Look for the state's trapper-education requirement; trap check intervals. Take your state's trapper-education course and follow its current rules.
passages.title: Trapping is tightly regulated

passages.context: Trail cameras record whatever passes, including people, so place them where you have permission and think about privacy. Also called trail camera, game camera privacy, cellular trail cam. Look for the landowner's permission; trails used by hikers or neighbors. Get permission, aim cameras at game trails rather than paths people use, and check whether your state limits cellular cameras.
passages.title: Game cameras: etiquette and privacy

passages.context: Deer rely on smell, and your scent drifts downwind in a widening cone, so hunters set up with the wind blowing from the deer toward them. Also called wind direction hunting, scent cone, deer smell me, play the wind. Look for wind direction from a light feather, milkweed fluff, or powder; thermals rising in the morning warmth and sinking in the evening.
passages.title: Wind direction and your scent

passages.context: Dragging a deer is hard work that strains the back and heart, especially in cold weather and for people who do not exercise. Also called drag a deer, heart attack dragging deer, deer sled, moving a deer out. Look for chest pain, shortness of breath, or dizziness; a long or uphill drag. Use a sled or cart, get help, take frequent breaks, and quarter a large animal rather than drag it far.
passages.title: Dragging a deer without hurting yourself

passages.context: A solo hunter should leave a plan with someone: where you will park and sit, when you will be back, and when they should call for help. Also called solo hunting, hunting alone safety, tell someone where I hunt. Look for a marked map or pin of your stand; a check-in time. Leave the plan, carry a whistle, light, and first aid, and stick to your return time or update it.
passages.title: Hunting alone: leave a plan

passages.context: Deer scat is a pile of small, dark, oval or acorn-shaped pellets, often 20 to 50 together, that shows where deer have fed or bedded. Also called deer droppings, deer poop, deer pellets, deer poo, deer dung. Look for pellets about 1/2 to 3/4 inch (1.5 to 2 cm) long, often with a small point or dimple at one end; dark and shiny when fresh, dull and dry or crumbly when old.
passages.title: Deer scat

passages.context: A deer track is a split, heart-shaped hoof print made by two pointed toes, about 2 to 3 1/2 inches (5 to 9 cm) long. Also called deer track, deer prints, deer hoof print, whitetail track, deer sign. Look for two teardrop toes forming a heart with the point toward travel; two dewclaw dots behind the print in mud, snow, or when running.
passages.title: Deer tracks

passages.context: A rub is a sapling or small tree where a buck has scraped off bark with his antlers, mostly in fall before and during the rut. Also called buck rub, antler rub, rubs on trees, scraped bark, deer sign. Look for bark stripped from one side of a small tree, often 1 to 4 inches (2.5 to 10 cm) thick, from knee to waist height; pale fresh wood, shredded bark curls on the ground, and broken twigs.
passages.title: Deer rubs

passages.context: A scrape is a patch of bare earth that a buck paws clear under an overhanging branch and marks with scent, mostly in the weeks before the rut. Also called buck scrape, deer scrape, scrape under a branch, licking branch, deer sign. Look for a pawed oval of bare dirt, often 1 to 3 feet (30 to 90 cm) across; a chewed or broken licking branch about head height above it.
passages.title: Deer scrapes

passages.context: Deer sign is the tracks, scat, rubs, scrapes, beds, and browsed plants that deer leave, and reading it shows where they travel, feed, and rest. Also called deer sign, signs of deer, how to scout for deer, deer scouting, where are the deer. Look for trails and tracks between thick cover and food; scat piles, oval beds pressed in leaves or snow.
passages.title: Reading deer sign

passages.context: Orienting a map means turning it so north on the map points to north on the ground, after allowing for declination, so the map matches what you see. Also called set the map, orient the map, line up map and compass, turn the map to north, map and compass basics. Look for the map's north arrow or meridian lines; the compass needle settled and away from metal.
passages.title: Orienting a map with a compass

passages.context: Declination is the angle between where a compass needle points (magnetic north) and true north on the map; it differs by place and slowly changes over the years. Also called compass doesn't match the map, compass and map disagree, magnetic variation, declination angle, adjust for declination. Look for the declination diagram and year printed on the map; a compass with an adjustable declination setting.
passages.title: Declination: magnetic versus true north

passages.context: True north points to the North Pole, magnetic north is where a compass needle points, and grid north follows the vertical grid lines printed on a map; the small angles between them matter over distance. Also called grid north, true north vs magnetic north, three norths, which north. Look for the three-arrow diagram in a topographic map's margin; grid lines (UTM) on the map.
passages.title: True north, magnetic north, and grid north

passages.context: A bearing is the direction to a target measured in degrees clockwise from north; you take it from the map or a landmark, then walk it by sighting from object to object. Also called follow a bearing, take a bearing, walk a compass heading, shoot a bearing, azimuth. Look for the direction-of-travel arrow on the compass; the needle boxed in the orienting arrow.
passages.title: Taking and following a compass bearing

passages.context: Contour lines join points of equal elevation, so their shape and spacing show the land: close lines are steep, wide lines are gentle, and Vs pointing uphill mark streams and draws. Also called contour lines, topo map lines, reading a topographic map, saddle ridge valley, squiggly lines on a map. Look for contour interval printed in the margin; closed rings for hilltops, with tick marks for depressions.
passages.title: Contour lines and terrain features

passages.context: Distance on a map is measured against its scale bar, and on the ground you track it with a pace count: the number of your double steps in 100 meters on your normal stride. Also called pace count, how far have I walked, measure distance on a map, pacing. Look for the scale bar in the map margin; your own tested pace count. Measure your pace count on a known 100 m course, count every second step while walking, and tie a knot or move a bead at each 100 m.
passages.title: Measuring distance and keeping a pace count

passages.context: A GPS or phone gives a fast position but needs battery and sky view; a paper map and baseplate compass keep working when the screen dies or the signal drops. Also called GPS not working, phone died navigation, do I need a compass if I have a phone, GPS in canyon. Look for battery below half on a long day; deep canyons, heavy cover, or cliffs blocking the fix.
passages.title: GPS and phone versus map and compass

passages.context: When you realize you are lost, the first job is to stop moving, calm down, and work from your last known point; staying put is usually safest if you cannot work it out. Also called I'm lost, what to do if lost, turned around in the woods, don't know where I am, STOP lost. Look for the last place you were sure of; streams, ridges, or roads you crossed.
passages.title: Lost? Stop, think, observe, plan

passages.context: Terrain association uses long features to guide you: a handrail is something you walk alongside, a catching feature stops you if you overshoot, and aiming off means deliberately aiming to one side of a target on a line feature. Also called handrail navigation, catching feature, aiming off, terrain association, follow a ridgeline. Look for a stream, ridge, trail, or field edge running your way; a road, river, or lake beyond your target.
passages.title: Handrails, catching features, and aiming off

passages.context: A phone's compass is a magnetic sensor that metal, magnets in cases, vehicles, and a skipped calibration can throw off by many degrees. Also called phone compass wrong, calibrate phone compass, compass app not accurate. Look for a magnetic phone case or mount; readings that swing when you move near a truck or rifle. Calibrate by moving the phone in a figure-eight away from metal, remove magnetic cases, and cross-check against a baseplate compass or the sun.
passages.title: When a phone compass is unreliable

passages.context: A stream is safe to cross only when it is shallow, slow, and has a clear landing; knee-deep fast water can knock an adult down. Also called crossing a river, ford a stream, safe to cross a creek, fast water crossing. Look for water above the knee or moving faster than a walk; muddy, rising water after rain. Scout for a wide, shallow, braided spot, unbuckle the pack's hip belt, face upstream with a stick or partner, and shuffle your feet.
passages.title: Stream crossings: when to go around

passages.context: A baseplate compass has a clear base with a direction-of-travel arrow, a rotating housing marked in degrees with an orienting arrow and lines, and a magnetic needle whose red end points to magnetic north. Also called baseplate compass, orienting arrow, compass housing, direction of travel arrow. Look for the red end of the needle; the degree ring on the housing.
passages.title: Parts of a baseplate compass

passages.context: Moving at night is slower and riskier; it works only on a known trail or a sure handrail with a good light and a careful bearing. Also called walking in the dark, night hike navigation, lost at night. Look for a bright headlamp and spare batteries; a trail, road, or stream edge to follow. Shorten legs between landmarks, count paces, check the compass often, and stop and camp if the ground gets rough.
passages.title: Navigating at night

passages.context: The sun gives only a rough direction: it rises in the east, sets in the west, and in the northern hemisphere is generally to the south at midday, with big seasonal shifts. Also called sun direction, find north without compass, shadow stick, which way is east. Look for a stick's shadow tip moving from west to east over 15-20 minutes; time of day and season.
passages.title: Rough direction from the sun

passages.context: In the northern hemisphere the North Star, Polaris, sits almost due north; the two outer stars of the Big Dipper's cup point to it. Also called north star, Polaris, big dipper north, find north at night. Look for the Big Dipper's pointer stars; a moderately bright star alone in its area. Follow the pointer stars about five times their gap to Polaris, then pick a ground landmark below it to hold your direction.
passages.title: Stars as a rough north reference

passages.context: Marking your own route with removable flagging or noted landmarks makes the return trip easier, especially in thick woods or snow. Also called mark my trail, flagging tape, find my way back, blaze a trail. Look for bright, removable flagging tape; waypoints saved only if you chose to. Tie flagging at eye level where you can see the next one, look back often so you know the return view, and remove the flagging on your way out.
passages.title: Marking a route for yourself

passages.context: In fog or a whiteout you lose landmarks and depth; most often the safest choice is to stop, shelter, and wait unless a sure handrail leads you out. Also called lost in fog, whiteout, can't see in snowstorm, fog navigation. Look for no visible landmarks beyond a few yards; snow or fog hiding drop-offs. Stop, get warm and sheltered, and wait it out, or follow a known handrail with compass and pace count, staying together.
passages.title: Whiteout or fog: stay put or follow a sure handrail

passages.context: An altimeter estimates your height from air pressure, and matching that height to a contour on the map helps narrow down where you are along a trail or slope. Also called altimeter navigation, barometer altitude, elevation to find location. Look for a known elevation to calibrate at the trailhead; weather changes shifting the reading. Calibrate at a known height, recheck at known points, and combine the reading with the trail, stream, or ridge you are on.
passages.title: Altimeter or barometer as a rough navigation aid

passages.context: A map's scale sets how much detail it can show; a 1:24,000 topographic map shows small streams and contours, while a small-scale map leaves out trails, cliffs, and new roads. Also called map scale, 1:24000, zoom limits, what a map pack shows. Look for the scale and date in the margin; missing new trails, logging roads, or beaver flooding. Use the largest-scale map you can get for foot travel and expect changes on the ground since the map's date.
passages.title: Map scale and what a map does not show

passages.context: On unmapped back roads the vehicle is shelter, a big visible target, and a supply cache, so staying with it is often safer than walking out. Also called car stuck on back road, leave the car or walk, unmarked forest road. Look for fuel, weather, and daylight left; distance to the last known road or house. Stay with the vehicle when stuck unless help is close and the way is sure; walking out is safer by daylight on a known road.
passages.title: Driving versus walking when the road is not on the map

passages.context: Resection finds your own position by taking bearings to two or three landmarks you can identify on the map and drawing back-bearings; intersection finds a distant point from two known spots. Also called triangulation, resection, find my position with compass, intersection navigation. Look for two or three distinct, mapped landmarks far apart in direction; back-bearings: add or subtract 180°.
passages.title: Resection and intersection

passages.context: Grid coordinates locate a point using the map's grid lines: read the easting (left to right) first, then the northing (bottom to top). Also called UTM coordinates, grid reference, read right then up, give my location coordinates. Look for the grid line labels along the map edges; a coordinate scale or ruler. Read right, then up; give the coordinates and the datum to rescuers if asked, or read latitude and longitude from your phone.
passages.title: Reading grid coordinates on a map

passages.context: A turnaround time is the hour you turn back no matter where you are, set so you are out before dark or bad weather; a trip plan tells someone your route and return. Also called turnaround time, trip plan, leave a plan, how late to hike. Look for sunset time and forecast; your pace on the way in. Set the turnaround time before you start, keep it, and leave your route and return time with someone who will call for help.
passages.title: Turnaround time and trip plans

passages.context: Choose a shelter site away from hazards overhead and underfoot: dead branches, rockfall, flood channels, game trails, and low cold pockets. Also called widowmaker, dead tree over camp, flood channel, rockfall, bad campsite. Look for dead limbs or leaning trees overhead (widowmakers); dry washes, gullies, and stream banks that can flood.
passages.title: Where not to camp or build a shelter

passages.context: A debris hut is a small, wedge-shaped shelter of a ridgepole, ribs, and a thick layer of dry leaves or other debris, built to trap body heat. Also called leaf hut, insulated stick hut, hut made of leaves and sticks, debris shelter. Look for a long ridgepole on a stump, rock, or tripod; ribs steep enough to shed water.
passages.title: Debris hut (how to build)

passages.context: A lean-to is a sloped roof with an open side, built against a crossbar between two trees or posts, often with a fire reflector wall opposite it. Also called lean to shelter, three-sided shelter, lean-to fire reflector, a-frame lean-to. Look for a crossbar between two supports at about chest height; a roof sloping toward the wind with the open side away from it.
passages.title: Lean-to with a fire reflector

passages.context: A tarp shelter is a sheet of waterproof fabric pitched over a ridgeline and staked down; it is the fastest shelter to set up. Also called tarp A-frame, poncho tent, how to set up a tarp, tarp lean-to. Look for a taut ridgeline between two trees at waist height; tarp draped over it with edges staked low.
passages.title: Rigging a tarp or poncho shelter

passages.context: The ground pulls heat out of you faster than the air does, so insulation under you matters before the roof. Also called bed of boughs, sleeping pad, insulate from the ground, warm bed. Look for a 6 to 8 inch (15 to 20 cm) pressed layer of dry boughs, leaves, or grass; a pad or pack under your torso and hips. Build the bed first, then the shelter. Pile dry leaves, pine boughs (cut ends down), or grass, add a pad or pack, and refresh each night.
passages.title: Ground insulation: why the ground comes first

passages.context: A shelter door is anything that closes the entrance against wind and cold, such as a pack, a debris pile, or a tarp. Also called close the entrance, block the opening, door for a debris hut. Look for a gap just big enough to crawl in; a door that can be closed from the inside. Use your pack, a bundle of branches stuffed with leaves, a spare tarp, or a slab of snow. Close it from the inside after you crawl in, and leave a small gap for air.
passages.title: What I can use for a shelter door

passages.context: A windbreak stops moving air from stealing heat, while insulation traps still air around you; a good shelter does both. Also called windbreak, what keeps me warm, wind vs cold shelter. Look for windbreak: a wall, tarp, or log between you and the wind; insulation: dry layers, boughs, and a bed. Block the wind first, then add insulation under and around you. Keep it dry and make the space small to hold heat.
passages.title: Stopping wind versus staying insulated

passages.context: Layering uses a wicking base, a warm insulating middle, and a windproof, waterproof outer layer that you adjust to stay dry and warm. Also called what to wear, dress in layers, wool or cotton, wet clothes, how to layer. Look for wool or synthetic base layers, not cotton; an insulating mid-layer like fleece or down. Vent before you sweat, add layers when you stop, and swap wet layers for dry ones as soon as you can. Keep a spare dry layer in a waterproof bag.
passages.title: Clothing as shelter: layering

passages.context: Burning charcoal, a stove, a lantern, or even a candle in a closed shelter can fill it with carbon monoxide, which has no smell and can kill in your sleep. Also called stove in a tent, charcoal in a shelter, candle in a snow cave, carbon monoxide in a shelter. Look for a closed tent, snow cave, car, or hut; headache and drowsiness.
passages.title: No fuel burning in a closed shelter

passages.context: If stranded in a car in a snowstorm, staying with the vehicle is usually safest; keep the tailpipe clear and run the engine only a little. Also called stranded in snow, stay with the car, car in a snowbank, exhaust pipe blocked. Look for blowing or falling snow with low visibility; the exhaust pipe at risk of blocking.
passages.title: Stuck in a car in a snowstorm

passages.context: A snow shelter uses snow's insulating quality, and it needs a vent hole and a roof about a foot thick to be safe. Also called tree well shelter, snow trench, snow cave vent, packed snow hut. Look for a tree well with low branches overhead; a trench or cave with a roof at least 12 inches (30 cm) thick. Dig a pit under an evergreen, roof it with branches and snow, line the floor with boughs, and cut a vent. Keep a tool inside and keep the entrance lower than the sleeping area.
passages.title: Snow shelters: tree-pit and ventilation

passages.context: A space blanket is a thin reflective sheet that holds in some body heat; a bivy is a waterproof shell for a sleeping bag. Also called emergency blanket, mylar blanket, bivy sack, survival blanket. Look for a very light sheet that reflects heat back; a bivy keeps wind and rain off a bag. Wrap a space blanket around you under clothes or in a shelter, with a pad or dry layers under you. Use it as a roof or wind block too. Add insulation; it does not warm by itself.
passages.title: Space blanket and bivy: what they will and won't do

passages.context: For a storm pitch, set the tent low and tight with the narrow end into the wind, and guy out every line. Also called set up a tent in the wind, tent in a storm, stake out a tent. Look for a flat, drained site away from dead trees; the door facing away from the wind. Choose a protected spot, stake every corner and guy line, and stow the pack inside. Put rocks or logs on the stakes in soft ground. Avoid ridges and open meadows.
passages.title: Tent site and storm pitching

passages.context: Place a fire off the opening of a shelter and far enough that sparks cannot reach the roof or bedding. Also called how close should a fire be, fire next to tent, sparks on a tent. Look for a fire 6 to 10 feet (2 to 3 m) from a tarp or tent; a reflector wall behind the fire. Keep the fire small and downwind of the shelter, away from the door and dry fabric. Use a ring of rocks or a pit. Put it out before you sleep.
passages.title: Fire placement near a shelter

passages.context: Different weather needs a different shelter: a steep tarp for rain, a low wedge for wind, a snow shelter for deep snow, and netting for insects. Also called bug shelter, rain shelter, mosquito shelter. Look for rain: steep pitch and a drip line; wind: low and streamlined, back to the wind. Pick the shelter that fits what the weather is doing, and use netting or a head net when insects are bad.
passages.title: Shelter for rain, wind, snow, and bugs

passages.context: A group shelter shares body heat and takes less material per person; a solo shelter must be smaller and better insulated. Also called share body heat, sleeping together, shelter for two. Look for two people sharing a bag or insulation hold heat better; a smaller space is warmer. Share a larger shelter where possible, huddle with insulation under all, and take turns keeping the vent and fire.
passages.title: Group versus solo shelter

passages.context: In plain terms, thicker is warmer: about 3 feet of dry debris on a hut and 6 to 8 inches under you, with a small vent. Also called thickness of debris, how thick should the leaves be. Look for 3 feet (1 m) of debris on a hut; 6 to 8 inches (15 to 20 cm) under you. Add more until you can no longer feel the cold coming through, and keep it dry. Leave a vent.
passages.title: How much insulation is enough?

passages.context: Black bear scat is a large tubular or piled dropping, often full of berries, seeds, nut shells, grass, or hair, that means a bear has been in the area. Also called bear droppings, bear poop, bear dung, black bear scat, bear sign. Look for thick tubes about 1.5 to 2 inches (4 to 5 cm) wide, or loose piles; packed with berries, seeds, or grass in summer and fall.
passages.title: Bear scat

passages.context: Coyote and fox scat is a twisted, rope-like dropping full of hair and small bones, with a tapered end, often left in the middle of a trail. Also called coyote droppings, fox scat, fox poop, coyote poop, canine scat. Look for coyote scat about 3/4 to 1 inch (2 to 2.5 cm) wide; fox scat thinner; packed with fur, bone, berries, or seeds. Scat on a trail or at a junction is a territory marker. It tells you which predators use the area.
passages.title: Coyote or fox scat

passages.context: Moose scat is a pile of large oval pellets of compressed wood fiber in winter, or soft clumps like a cow pie in summer. Also called moose droppings, moose poop, moose nuggets, moose pellets. Look for pellets about 1 to 1 1/2 inches (2.5 to 4 cm) long, much bigger than deer; sawdust-like texture when broken. Fresh piles mean moose are using the area; give any moose plenty of room.
passages.title: Moose scat

passages.context: Raccoon scat is a blunt-ended, tubular dropping often full of seeds and shell bits, left in piles called latrines on logs, rocks, roofs, or at tree bases. Also called raccoon droppings, raccoon poop, raccoon latrine, coon scat. Look for dark tubes about 3/4 inch (2 cm) wide with blunt ends; many droppings of different ages in one spot. A latrine means raccoons use the site regularly. Keep food and trash locked away.
passages.title: Raccoon scat

passages.context: Rabbit and hare scat is a scatter of round, slightly flattened, pea-sized pellets of chewed plant fiber. Also called rabbit droppings, rabbit poop, rabbit pellets, hare droppings, bunny poop. Look for round, about 1/4 to 1/2 inch (0.6 to 1.3 cm) across, flattened like a thick coin; light brown and fibrous inside. Lots of pellets near brush and browsed twigs mean rabbits or hares feed and hide there.
passages.title: Rabbit or hare scat

passages.context: A black bear track is a wide print with five toes in an arc and a broad pad, the hind print looking like a flat-footed human foot. Also called bear track, bear prints, bear paw print, black bear track, bear sign. Look for front print about 4 to 6 inches (10 to 15 cm) wide with claw dots; hind print longer, up to about 7 inches (18 cm), with a heel. Fresh tracks mean a bear is close. Make noise, keep food sealed, and keep dogs leashed.
passages.title: Bear tracks

passages.context: A canine track has four toes with claw marks around a triangular pad, and an X shape can be drawn through the space between toes and pad. Also called coyote track, fox track, dog track, canine prints, wolf track.
