Look for oval print; coyote about 2 1/2 inches (6 cm) long, fox smaller; wild canines walk in a straight, direct line; dogs wander. A straight, purposeful line of oval prints is usually a coyote or fox; a zigzagging line beside a person's tracks is usually a dog.
passages.title: Coyote, fox, or dog tracks

passages.context: A raccoon track has five long, finger-like toes, like a small human handprint, usually in mud near water. Also called raccoon track, raccoon prints, coon track. Look for front print about 2 to 3 inches (5 to 8 cm) with separated fingers; hind print longer, like a small foot. Raccoon tracks near camp mean you should lock up food at night.
passages.title: Raccoon tracks

passages.context: A moose track is a large split-hoof print over 4 inches (10 cm) long, shaped like a deer track but much bigger. Also called moose track, moose prints, moose hoof print. Look for blunt or pointed heart shape, about 4 to 6 inches (10 to 15 cm) long; deep in mud or snow, with dewclaws often showing. Fresh tracks mean moose are near; give them room, especially in fall and in calving season.
passages.title: Moose tracks

passages.context: A wild turkey track is a large bird print with three long forward toes and a short back toe, about 4 to 5 inches (10 to 13 cm) long. Also called turkey track, turkey prints, bird tracks. Look for middle toe longest and straight ahead; long stride of many prints in a line. Fresh tracks near fields, roosts, or dusting spots mean turkeys use the area.
passages.title: Turkey tracks

passages.context: A bobcat track is a round print about 2 inches (5 cm) across with four toes, no claw marks, and a three-lobed pad. Also called bobcat track, cat track, lynx track, bobcat prints. Look for round, not oval like a canine; leading edge of the pad has two notches making three lobes. A round print with no claws is a cat; bobcats often walk with hind feet placed in the front prints.
passages.title: Bobcat tracks

passages.context: Rabbit and hare tracks come in groups of four: two long hind feet side by side in front of two small front feet, one behind the other. Also called rabbit track, hare track, bunny prints, snowshoe hare track. Look for Y-shaped or triangle-shaped track group; snowshoe hare hind prints very large and splayed in snow. The big hind prints land ahead of the front prints, so the wide end of the group points the way the animal went.
passages.title: Rabbit or hare tracks

passages.context: Plan on at least one gallon (about 4 liters) of drinking water per person per day for emergencies, and more in heat, with illness, or for children and nursing mothers. Also called how much water do I need, gallon per day, dehydration signs, water per person. Look for pale yellow urine means you are drinking enough; dark urine, dry mouth, headache, and dizziness mean you need more.
passages.title: How much drinking water to plan for

passages.context: Clear water from a stream, lake, or spring can still carry germs, so treat it unless you know it is safe; clear does not mean clean. Also called can I drink from the stream, is creek water safe, clear water safe, wild water. Look for clear but untreated water can hold Giardia, Cryptosporidium, bacteria, and viruses; fuel, chemical, or flood water is not made safe by boiling.
passages.title: Is this water safe to drink?

passages.context: Boiling is the most reliable way to kill germs: bring water to a rolling boil for one minute, or three minutes above 6,500 feet (2,000 m). Also called boil water to make it safe, rolling boil, how long to boil, boil at altitude. Look for large bubbles breaking the surface; settle or strain cloudy water first.
passages.title: How to boil water

passages.context: Plain unscented household bleach can disinfect clear water, but it works less well than boiling against Giardia and Cryptosporidium. Also called bleach to purify water, drops of bleach per gallon, chlorine bleach water. Look for 8 drops of 6% bleach per gallon (6 drops of 8.25%), double for cloudy water; wait 30 minutes.
passages.title: Disinfecting water with household bleach

passages.context: A portable filter strains out parasites and bacteria; most do not remove viruses or chemicals. Also called water filter, straw filter, pump filter, how fine a filter, backpacking filter. Look for pore size about 1 micron or less stops Giardia and Cryptosporidium; 0.3 micron or less also stops most bacteria.
passages.title: Portable water filters: what they remove

passages.context: Filtering removes parasites and bacteria and clears the water, and a disinfectant afterward handles viruses that pass through. Also called filter and treat, layer treatment, virus protection water. Look for filter or settle first; then boil, or add bleach or a chlorine dioxide tablet. When you are in doubt or in a place with viruses of concern, filter first and then disinfect the filtered water. This also saves disinfectant and gives it more reliable contact.
passages.title: Filter first, then disinfect

passages.context: Cloudy water hides germs from disinfectant and clogs filters, so let it settle and strain it first. Also called muddy water, silty water, turbid water, clear up cloudy water. Look for silt or particles in the water; a clean cloth or coffee filter. Let the water sit until the silt sinks, pour the clear top through a clean cloth or coffee filter, then boil, filter, or disinfect.
passages.title: Cloudy water: settle or pre-filter

passages.context: Water contaminated with fuel, chemicals, sewage, or flood debris cannot be made safe by boiling or bleach, so do not use it to drink. Also called fuel in the water, flood water, chemical spill water, dead animal in stream. Look for an oily sheen or fuel smell; flood water with sewage or farm runoff.
passages.title: Water that cannot be made safe in the field

passages.context: Store treated water in clean, food-grade containers with tight lids, away from sun and heat. Also called what to use for a water bottle, store clean water, water jug, hydration bladder. Look for food-grade plastic or stainless steel; a lid that seals. Wash containers with soap and rinse, fill with treated water, label them with the date, and replace commercial water as the package says. In the field, use a pot, a bottle, or a clean bag.
passages.title: Containers and storing treated water

passages.context: In New England, water is usually near: look for streams in valley bottoms, springs, ponds, and melted snow; moving water is better than still. Also called where to find water in the woods, stream or spring, snow for water, water in Maine. Look for valley bottoms and seeps where several slopes meet; springs and clear running streams.
passages.title: Finding water in New England woods

passages.context: Melt snow or ice in a pot and treat the water; eating snow lowers body temperature and uses energy. Also called melt snow, eat snow, drink from snow. Look for a pot with a little water in it to start; clean white snow, not yellow or near a road. Start with a little water in the pot so it doesn't scorch, add snow gradually, and boil it. Melt it with a stove or fire, or in a bag against the body only if needed.
passages.title: Melting snow and ice for water

passages.context: Rain is a good source if you collect it in clean containers, and you should treat it if it passed over roofs or leaves. Also called catch rain water, tarp water catchment, rain barrel. Look for a tarp funneling water into a clean pot; rain caught directly is cleaner. Set clean containers out, rig a tarp to funnel rain into them, and let the first few minutes of rain wash dust off. Treat the water if it is for drinking.
passages.title: Collecting rain

passages.context: Giardia and Cryptosporidium are tiny parasites in surface water that cause days of diarrhea, cramps, and nausea; boiling or the right filter stops them. Also called beaver fever, parasite in water, cryptosporidium, giardia. Look for watery diarrhea, gas, cramps, and nausea one to two weeks after drinking; found in streams, lakes, and ponds, even clear ones. Boil water or use a filter rated for 1 micron or smaller. Wash your hands with soap and clean water before eating.
passages.title: Giardia and Cryptosporidium

passages.context: Tablets disinfect water when boiling is not possible; follow the label for dose and wait time. Also called water purification tablets, iodine tablets, micropur, aquamira drops. Look for chlorine dioxide tablets kill most germs including Cryptosporidium after the label wait time; iodine tablets are less reliable against Cryptosporidium. Read the label, pre-filter cloudy water, add the tablet, and wait the full time (often 30 minutes to 4 hours for Cryptosporidium).
passages.title: Iodine and chlorine dioxide tablets

passages.context: UV treatment works only on clear water in a working unit, and solar disinfection needs clear plastic bottles in strong sun for many hours. Also called steripen, UV light water, sodis, solar water disinfection. Look for clear, not cloudy, water; a charged, working UV unit. Pre-filter, treat with the UV unit as directed, and carry a backup like tablets or a pot. Use solar disinfection only as a last resort.
passages.title: UV purifiers and solar disinfection

passages.context: When water is short, use the cleanest water for drinking and wound care, and a little soap and treated water for hands. Also called wash hands without water, hand sanitizer, dishes in the field, hygiene when water is short. Look for a small amount of soap and water for hands; alcohol-based sanitizer when hands are not greasy.
passages.title: Washing hands, dishes, and wounds when water is scarce

passages.context: Dig a latrine or cathole at least 200 feet (60 m) from water, trails, and camp to keep your drinking water clean. Also called where to go to the bathroom outdoors, cathole, toilet in the woods, poop in the woods. Look for a hole 6 to 8 inches (15 to 20 cm) deep; 200 feet from any stream, pond, or spring. Dig a small hole, use it, cover it with soil, and wash your hands. Pack out toilet paper if the rules require it.
passages.title: Latrine placement away from water

passages.context: Mix infant formula with bottled, boiled-and-cooled, or properly treated water when the tap is unsafe. Also called infant formula and boil water, safe water for baby, mix formula. Look for a boil-water notice or a flood; bottled water for babies. Use bottled or boiled water (cooled to room temperature before mixing, per the label), wash bottles with safe water, and use ready-to-feed formula if you can.
passages.title: Baby formula when tap water is unsafe

passages.context: Never drink radiator or boiler water, seawater, urine, or water that has fuel or chemicals in it. Also called radiator water, urine, seawater, toilet tank. Look for antifreeze in radiators; salt in seawater and urine. Use another source; if you must use pool water, treat and filter it, and use a toilet tank only if it is clean, not a bowl.
passages.title: Water sources never to drink

passages.context: A flooded well must be tested and disinfected following health-department or EPA directions; do not invent a mix. Also called flooded well, shock chlorinate a well, well water after flood. Look for flood water over the wellhead; cloudy or odd-tasting water. Use bottled or boiled water until the well is tested and cleared. Contact your health department or a certified lab, and follow their disinfection steps.
passages.title: Well disinfection after a flood

passages.context: Food: eat known cultivated food or packaged rations before foraging. Do not taste unknown plants, mushrooms, or unfamiliar meat. Herbology notes in this repo are cautions, not a menu. Hunger is not a reason to experiment.
passages.title: food

passages.context: Pack food you already eat, with the first night's portion on top of the bag. Eat small amounts through the day. A pot and a spoon you have used at home beat a new wild food. This sets no calorie target and no meal plan for a clinic.
passages.title: food

passages.context: Cook known food until it is hot through, and keep raw scraps away from the cooked pot. Seal or hang leftovers so animals are not invited to where you sleep. A bulging can or a sour smell means you discard it. Do not taste food to decide if it has turned.
passages.title: food

passages.context: Berries, fish, and greens are a local-rules question, and only for kinds you already know from a source outside this note. If you are not sure, it does not go in your mouth. Mushrooms are not a trial. Cultivated food is the plan. Wild food is not a backup menu and not a dose guide.
passages.title: food

passages.context: Navigation: the sun rises generally east and sets generally west. A map and compass beat guesswork. If you are lost, staying put and making yourself visible is often safer than wandering. This is not a complete orienteering manual.
passages.title: navigation

passages.context: Walk to a landmark you can name, a boulder, a saddle, or a distinct tree, then pick the next. Count paces on a stretch you already measured so distance is a number. Stop while the last sure point is still clear. Turning around is a plan, not a failure.
passages.title: navigation

passages.context: A shoreline, a ridge, or a stream can be a handrail you keep beside you. Know which side you are on, and which bend means you have gone too far. A handrail is a landscape line. It is not a street. If it splits and you cannot say which branch, you stop.
passages.title: navigation

passages.context: If you are unsure, sit and sketch a circle of possible places instead of a hopeful dot. Signal from an open spot. Move only toward a feature you can name, in daylight, and camp if dusk is close. These notes do not replace a map you can read, and they do not invent a trail.
passages.title: navigation

passages.context: Shelter and fire: get out of wind and wet ground first. A small contained fire needs clear fuel, a safe distance from brush, and a way to put it out. Do not light a fire where local rules forbid it. This is a planning note, not a wilderness course.
passages.title: shelter_fire

passages.context: Pick the site before the flame. Choose ground that sheds rain, above a flood line, and clear of dead trees that can drop limbs. Face the opening away from the wind. A finger-width of dry insulation under you holds more heat than a tall roof. This is planning, not a building code.
passages.title: shelter_fire

passages.context: Build a fire only where rules allow it, on scraped mineral soil, with fuel upwind and a way to drown it. Start with tinder and pencil twigs, and add thicker wood after the flame is honest. Feel the ashes cold before you leave. A banned day or a hard wind means no flame.
passages.title: shelter_fire

passages.context: Without a fire, stay dry, covered, and off the ground, and keep the wind off your back. Any flame inside a closed shelter can foul the air, so leave a vent and do not sleep against a heater. Wet clothes next to the skin steal heat even in mild air. This does not treat a cold injury.
passages.title: shelter_fire

passages.context: Signaling: three of anything (whistle blasts, bright flashes, fires) is a common distress pattern. A mirror or light aimed at rescuers is a signal, not a weapon. Tell another person where you are going before you travel.
passages.title: signaling

passages.context: A whistle carries farther than a shout and spends less breath. Three short blasts, a pause, then three again is the pattern to repeat. If you hear a reply, answer the same way and stay where you can be seen. Yelling until you are hoarse does not mark your location.
passages.title: signaling

passages.context: Put bright gear in an open sight line, in a straight line or a large X. Flash a mirror toward a ridge or an aircraft in short groups of three, then stop so you do not dazzle someone close. Day smoke and a night flame are signals only where fire is legal and contained.
passages.title: signaling

passages.context: An arrow of stones or packs can show the way you left, if you must leave, and only where the sky can see it. Tell a person your route, your return time, and the color of your pack before you go. If you are unsure, signal and stay visible. This is how to be found, not a radio trick.
passages.title: signaling

passages.context: Tools and cordage: a knife, cord, and container solve more camp problems than improvising from scratch. Keep edges covered. Natural cord from bark or roots only comes from plants you are allowed to cut and can identify. This is not a weapons guide.
passages.title: tools_cordage

passages.context: Use the knife away from your body, on a firm surface, and sheath it when you move. A dull edge slips, so a small stone belongs with the blade. Do not throw it, and do not pry with the only knife you have. A covered edge does not cut the bottle in the pack. This is handling, not a fight.
passages.title: tools_cordage

passages.context: Carry cord you already trust before you strip a living plant. A few meters can hang a pot clear of flame, tie a shelter ridge, or repair a strap. Learn two knots you can also undo. Wet natural fiber swells and can jam a knot you tied while it was dry.
passages.title: tools_cordage

passages.context: A needle, a little tape, and cord stop a small tear from becoming a lost strap or a split handle. Brighten a tool handle so it shows against leaves. A lighter in a dry bag is the simple spark; practice it at home. This note does not teach you to burn the country.
passages.title: tools_cordage

passages.context: Water: carry known-safe water when you can. If you must treat water in the field, boiling is the straightforward heat method. Cloudy water should be settled or strained before boiling. This is an offline reminder, not a guarantee the water is safe, and not a substitute for emergency services.
passages.title: water

passages.context: Containers matter. A closed bottle or a pot you can heat beats a leaky bag. Keep the drinking bottle capped and off the ground, and refill it when you pass a source you mean to treat. A spare empty container is how you carry water away from the source.
passages.title: water

passages.context: Where to look: green growth on a dry slope, a dark seep, or a stream in the lowest line of a valley are clues. Flowing water is a better clue than a still pool. Clues are not proof. Settle the grit, then boil, and still treat the result as uncertain.
passages.title: water

passages.context: Snow and ice need melting before you drink them, and melting spends fuel you may need for warmth. Eating snow when you are already cold cools you further. Salt water and urine are not drinking water. This reminder sets no liter quota and no chemical dose.
passages.title: water

passages.context: Carry more than the first hour seems to need, then drink small amounts through the day instead of emptying the bottle at once. In heat, rest in shade before you feel dizzy. If someone stops sweating or grows confused, stop travel and get human help. This is not a medical threshold.
passages.title: water

passages.context: Weather: dark building clouds, sudden wind, and thunder mean you should leave high ground and open water. Cold plus wet clothing steals heat. This note does not forecast a local storm.
passages.title: weather

passages.context: Read the sky you have. A hard wind shift, a fast drop in temperature, and a dark towering cloud are reasons to leave ridges and lone tall trees. A shorter gap between flash and thunder only means the cell is closer. Do not wait for a forecast you cannot make. Get lower.
passages.title: weather

passages.context: Wind that rises and holds one direction often comes before rain. Face the shelter away from it, and weight anything that can blow away. Blowing dust is a reason to seek a low sturdy spot, not a hilltop. This note is not a warning siren and not a local forecast.
passages.title: weather

passages.context: A clear night is often colder than a cloudy one. Put the rain layer on before you are soaked, and keep a hat where you can reach it. Stop early enough to camp in daylight. The plan is to be dry before the wind arrives, not after.
passages.title: weather

passages.context: Heat is a travel cost: still air, a high sun, and no shade. Move earlier and later, rest at midday, and cover your head. Pushing on through dizziness is a reason to stop and get help, not a goal. This note does not set a temperature rule.
passages.title: weather

passages.context: We take great pleasure in presenting to the attention of students and investigators of the Secret Doctrines this little work based upon the world-old Hermetic Teachings. There has been so little written upon this subject, not withstanding the countless references to the Teachings in the many works upon occultism, that the many earnest searchers after the Arcane Truths will doubtless welcome the appearance of this present volume.
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: The purpose of this work is not the enunciation of any special philosophy or doctrine, but rather is to give to the students a statement of the Truth that will serve to reconcile the many bits of occult knowledge that they may have acquired, but which are apparently opposed to each other and which often serve to discourage and disgust the beginner in the study. Our intent is not to erect a new Temple of Knowledge, but rather to place in the hands of the student a Master-Key w
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: There is no portion of the occult teachings possessed by the world which have been so closely guarded as the fragments of the Hermetic Teachings which have come down to us over the tens of centuries which have elapsed since the lifetime of its great founder, Hermes Trismegistus, the "scribe of the gods," who dwelt in old Egypt in the days when the present race of men was in its infancy. Contemporary with Abraham, and, if the legends be true, an instructor of that venerable sa
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: From the land of the Ganges many advanced occultists wandered to the land of Egypt, and sat at the feet of the Master. From him they obtained the Master-Key which explained and reconciled their divergent views, and thus the Secret Doctrine was firmly established. From other lands also came the learned ones, all of whom regarded Hermes as the Master of Masters, and his influence was so great that in spite of the many wanderings from the path on the part of the centuries of tea

passages.context: The lifework of Hermes seems to have been in the direction of planting the great Seed-Truth which has grown and blossomed in so many strange forms, rather than to establish a school of philosophy which would dominate, the world's thought. But, nevertheless, the original truths taught by him have been kept intact in their original purity by a few men each age, who, refusing great numbers of half-developed students and followers, followed the Hermetic custom and reserved their
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: "O, let not the flame die out! Cherished age after age in its dark cavern--in its holy temples cherished. Fed by pure ministers of love--let not the flame die out!"
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: These men have never sought popular approval, nor numbers of followers. They are indifferent to these things, for they know how few there are in each generation who are ready for the truth, or who would recognize it if it were presented to them. They reserve the "strong meat for men," while others furnish the "milk for babes." They reserve their pearls of wisdom for the few elect, who recognize their value and who wear them in their crowns, instead of casting them before the
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: There are those who have criticized this attitude of the Hermetists, and who have claimed that they did not manifest the proper spirit in their policy of seclusion and reticence. But a moment's glance back over the pages of history will show the wisdom of the Masters, who knew the folly of attempting to teach to the world that which it was neither ready or willing to receive. The Hermetists have never sought to be martyrs, and have, instead, sat silently aside with a pitying
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: And the spirit of persecution has not as yet died out in the land. There are certain Hermetic Teachings, which, if publicly promulgated, would bring down upon the teachers a great cry of scorn and revilement from the multitude, who would again raise the cry of "Crucify! Crucify."
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: In this little work we have endeavored to give you an idea of the fundamental teachings of The Kybalion, striving to give you the working Principles, leaving you to apply therm yourselves, rather than attempting to work out the teaching in detail. If you are a true student, you will be able to work out and apply these Principles--if not, then you must develop yourself into one, for otherwise the Hermetic Teachings will be as "words, words, words" to you.
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: "The lips of wisdom are closed, except to the ears of Understanding"--The Kybalion.
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: From old Egypt have come the fundamental esoteric and occult teachings which have so strongly influenced the philosophies of all races, nations and peoples, for several thousand years. Egypt, the home of the Pyramids and the Sphinx, was the birthplace of the Hidden Wisdom and Mystic Teachings. From her Secret Doctrine all nations have borrowed. India, Persia, Chaldea, Medea, China, Japan, Assyria, ancient Greece and Rome, and other ancient countries partook liberally at the f
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: In ancient Egypt dwelt the great Adepts and Masters who have never been surpassed, and who seldom have been equaled, during the centuries that have taken their processional flight since the days of the Great Hermes. In Egypt was located the Great Lodge of Lodges of the Mystics. At the doors of her Temples entered the Neophytes who afterward, as Hierophants, Adepts, and Masters, traveled to the four corners of the earth, carrying with them the precious knowledge which they wer
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: But among these great Masters of Ancient Egypt there once dwelt one of whom Masters hailed as "The Master of Masters." This man, if "man" indeed he was, dwelt in Egypt in the earliest days. He was known as Hermes Trismegistus. He was the father of the Occult Wisdom; the founder of Astrology; the discoverer of Alchemy. The details of his life story are lost to history, owing to the lapse of the years, though several of the ancient countries disputed with each other in their cl
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: As the years rolled by after his passing from this plane of life (tradition recording that he lived three hundred years in the flesh), the Egyptians deified Hermes, and made him one of their gods, under the name of Thoth. Years after, the people of Ancient Greece also made him one of their many gods--calling him "Hermes, the god of Wisdom." The Egyptians revered his memory for many centuries-yes, tens of centuries-- calling him "the Scribe of the Gods," and bestowing upon him
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: Even to this day, we use the term "hermetic" in the sense of "secret"; "sealed so that nothing can escape"; etc., and this by reason of the fact that the followers of Hermes always observed the principle of secrecy in their teachings. They did not believe in "casting pearls before swine," but rather held to the teaching "milk for babes"; "meat for strong men," both of which maxims are familiar to readers of the Christian scriptures, but both of which had been used by the Egyp
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: And this policy of careful dissemination of the truth has always characterized the Hermetics, even unto the present day. The Hermetic Teachings are to be found in all lands, among all religions, but never identified with any particular country, nor with any particular religious sect. This because of the warning of the ancient teachers against allowing the Secret Doctrine to become crystallized into a creed. The wisdom of this caution is apparent to all students of history. Th
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: But there were always a few faithful souls who kept alive the Flame, tending it carefully, and not allowing its light to become extinguished. And thanks to these staunch hearts, and fearless minds, we have the truth still with us. But it is not found in books, to any great extent. It has been passed along from Master to Student; from Initiate to Hierophant; from lip to ear. When it was written down at all, its meaning was veiled in terms of alchemy and astrology so that only
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: In the early days, there was a compilation of certain Basic Hermetic Doctrines, passed on from teacher to student, which was known as "THE KYBALION," the exact significance and meaning of the term having been lost for several centuries. This teaching, however, is known to many to whom it has descended, from mouth to ear, on and on throughout the centuries. Its precepts have never been written down, or printed, so far as we know. It was merely a collection of maxims, axioms, a

passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: So that according to the Teachings, the passage of this book to those ready for the instruction will attract the attention of such as are prepared to receive the Teaching. And, likewise, when the pupil is ready to receive the truth, then will this little book come to him, or her. Such is The Law. The Hermetic Principle of Cause and Effect, in its aspect of The Law of Attraction, will bring lips and ear together--pupil and book in company. So mote it be!

passages.context: "The Principles of Truth are Seven; he who knows these, understandingly, possesses the Magic Key before whose touch all the Doors of the Temple fly open."--The Kybalion.

passages.context: The Seven Hermetic Principles, upon which the entire Hermetic Philosophy is based, are as follows:
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: These Seven Principles will be discussed and explained as we proceed with these lessons. A short explanation of each, however, may as well be given at this point.
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: This Principle embodies the truth that "All is Mind." It explains that THE ALL (which is the Substantial Reality underlying all the outward manifestations and appearances which we know under the terms of "The Material Universe"; the "Phenomena of Life"; "Matter"; "Energy"; and, in short, all that is apparent to our material senses) is SPIRIT which in itself is UNKNOWABLE and UNDEFINABLE, but which may be considered and thought of as AN UNIVERSAL, INFINITE, LIVING MIND. It als
passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: This Principle embodies the truth that there is always a Correspondence between the laws and phenomena of the various planes of Being and Life. The old Hermetic axiom ran in these words: "As above, so below; as below, so above." And the grasping of this Principle gives one the means of solving many a dark paradox, and hidden secret of Nature. passages.title: The Kybalion

And yet this Hermetic Principle was enunciated thousands of years ago, by the Masters of Ancient Egypt. This Principle explains that the differences between different manifestations of Matter, Energy, Mind, and even Spirit, result largely from varying rates of Vibration. Fro

passages.title: The Kybalion

passages.context: This Principle embodies the truth that "everything is dual"; "everything has two poles"; "everything has its pair of opposites," all of which were old Hermetic axioms. And more than this, as many students and practitioners of modern mental science know, every material condition dep
